teile.einleitung: Puberty is the time when a child becomes an adult. Hormones cause a growth spurt and the development of the sexual characteristics. Feelings, thoughts and the brain also change during this exciting time.
wichtigste: Typical of puberty are a growth spurt and the development of the sexual characteristics.
In girls it usually starts between 8 and 13 years, in boys a little later.
In boys the hormone testosterone is especially important.
In girls the ovaries produce mainly oestrogens.
The very first period is called menarche.
Boys’ voices break because the larynx and vocal cords grow.
Spots appear because the sebaceous glands produce more sebum.
Mood swings are normal in puberty.

abschnitte.text: **Puberty** usually starts in girls between 8 and 13 years and in boys between about 9 and 14 years. It lasts several years. Everyone has their own pace, and earlier or later are both normal. The word comes from the Latin pubertas, which means sexual maturity.

The brain gives the starting signal by stimulating the pituitary gland. This makes the sex glands produce more hormones. In boys the testicles produce mainly **testosterone**. In girls the ovaries produce mainly **oestrogens**.

There is a **growth spurt**, in which you can grow several centimetres a year. Hair grows under the arms and in the private area, and you sweat more. The sebaceous glands produce more sebum, so many teenagers get spots. Washing regularly helps, but spots often cannot be prevented completely.

In girls the breasts grow and the hips become wider. At some point the first period begins, the **menarche**. In boys the penis and testicles grow, the shoulders become broader and a beard begins to sprout. Because the larynx and vocal cords grow, boys’ voices **break** and become deeper.

The brain also changes a great deal in puberty. Feelings can become more intense, and moods sometimes swing quickly. Many teenagers want to become more independent and argue more often with their parents. This is a normal part of growing up, and it helps to talk about it with people you trust.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance that triggers changes in the body.
The very first period of a girl.
The time when boys’ voices become deeper.
A gland in the skin that produces an oily substance.
Physical features that distinguish women and men.

gewusst: Girls also get a slightly deeper voice in puberty, but you hardly hear it.
Teenagers often become tired later in the evening because their body clock shifts in puberty.
The part of the brain responsible for planning and reasoning is only finished at about 20 to 25 years.

teile.einleitung: Nodes of Ranvier are small gaps in the nerve fibres. They make sure that nerve signals are passed on especially fast. They are named after a French doctor.
wichtigste: A node of Ranvier is a gap between two sections of myelin.
It is only about 1 micrometre wide.
At the nodes there are especially many voltage-gated sodium channels.
The section between two nodes is called an internode.
In the peripheral nervous system, a node lies between two Schwann cells.
Nodes of Ranvier typically occur in vertebrates.

abschnitte.text: Nerve cells have long extensions, the **axons**. Many axons are surrounded by a fatty sheath, the **myelin**. It works rather like the insulation of a cable. But the sheath is not continuous: at regular intervals there are small **gaps**. These gaps are called **nodes of Ranvier**. They are only about **1 micrometre** wide, that is, one thousandth of a millimetre.

abschnitte.titel: The man who gave it its name
abschnitte.text: The nodes are named after the **French doctor** and researcher **Louis-Antoine Ranvier**. He described them in the 19th century when he examined nerve tissue under the microscope. Ranvier was very interested in the fine structure of tissues. His discovery later helped us to understand why some nerves are so fast.

The myelinated section between two nodes is called the **internode**. It is much longer than the node itself. In the **peripheral nervous system**, that is, in the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, one **Schwann cell** in each case forms the myelin of an internode. A node therefore lies between two Schwann cells. Right next to the node lies the **paranode**. There the loops of myelin are anchored to the axon.

At the nodes there are especially many **voltage-gated sodium channels**. Through them, sodium ions flow into the axon when a nerve signal passes. Under the myelin this hardly happens. That is why the signal jumps from node to node. This is called **saltatory conduction**, from the Latin word for jumping. In this way signals are passed on much faster and more economically than in nerve fibres without myelin.

Nodes of Ranvier typically occur in **vertebrates**, that is, in fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Many invertebrates have no such myelin sheath. Some of them, such as squid, achieve fast signals instead with especially thick nerve fibres. If the myelin in a human is damaged by a disease, for example in multiple sclerosis, the signals become slower.

gewusst: In the fastest nerve fibres of a human, signals travel more than a hundred metres per second.
Without myelin and nodes, our nerves would have to be much thicker to conduct equally fast.

teile.einleitung: Psychosomatics deals with the interaction of mind and body. Worries and stress can cause physical complaints, and physical illnesses can affect mood. The word is made up of the Greek words for soul and body.
wichtigste: Psychosomatics studies how mind and body influence each other.
The biopsychosocial model explains illness as an interplay of biological, psychological and social factors.
With lasting stress, the adrenal cortex releases more cortisol.
Tension headache is often partly caused by stress.
Positive expectations can have an effect: this is the placebo effect.
Negative expectations can strengthen complaints: this is the nocebo effect.

abschnitte.text: If you are excited, you may get a tummy ache. If you have had worries for a long time, you sleep badly or have a headache. **Psychosomatics** studies such connections. The word comes from the Greek “psyche” for soul and “soma” for body. Today illness is often explained with the **biopsychosocial model**: biological, psychological and social factors work together.

The researcher **Hans Selye** shaped the modern understanding of stress. He described the **“general adaptation syndrome”**: the body reacts to strain with alarm, adaptation and, if it lasts too long, exhaustion. With lasting stress, the **adrenal cortex** releases more of the hormone **cortisol**. In the short term it helps to provide energy. But if the stress lasts long, it can harm the body.

Some complaints are especially often partly caused by stress and tension. One example is **tension headache**, which feels like pressure around the head. The stomach and gut also often react sensitively. In a **somatoform disorder**, a person has physical complaints without doctors finding a sufficient physical cause. The complaints are real all the same and deserve good treatment.

It is astonishing how strongly expectations work. If someone firmly believes in a treatment, they may feel better even if the tablet contains no active ingredient. This is called the **placebo effect**. The other way round, negative expectations can cause or strengthen complaints. This is the **nocebo effect**. If you read a lot about side effects, for example, you sometimes notice them more.

In psychosomatics, body and mind are treated together. Besides medical treatment, talking, relaxation exercises and exercise often help. Enough sleep, breaks and time with friends protect against constant stress. In Switzerland, many hospitals have their own departments for psychosomatics.

gewusst: The word placebo is Latin and means “I shall please”.
Laughing and exercise can also help to break down stress hormones in the body again.

teile.einleitung: The pupil is the black hole in the middle of your eye. Light falls into the eye through it so that you can see. It can get bigger and smaller, depending on how bright it is.
wichtigste: The pupil lets light into the eye.
In bright light it gets smaller.
In the dark it gets bigger.
In humans the pupil is round.
It looks black because hardly any light comes back out of it.
Goats have horizontal pupils, cats in the daytime narrow slits.

abschnitte.text: Around the pupil lies the coloured **iris**. It is blue, green or brown, for example. The pupil itself is a hole in the iris. **Light** gets into the inside of the eye through this hole. At the back of the eye, the light hits the retina, which passes the images on to the brain.

The iris contains small muscles. They change the size of the pupil all by themselves. In **bright light** the pupil becomes **smaller**, so that not too much light falls into the eye. In the **dark** it becomes **bigger**, so that as much light as possible gets in. You can try this out: look into one eye in the mirror, close it briefly and open it again. The pupil first becomes large and then quickly smaller.

The pupil is not a black spot but an opening. It looks **black** because **hardly any light comes back out of it**. The light is almost completely swallowed up inside the eye. With photos taken with a **flash**, it is different: the bright flash hits the well-supplied layers of blood vessels at the back of the eye. Some of the red light comes back, and so **red eyes** appear in the photo.

In humans the pupil is **round**. In animals there are quite different shapes. **Goats** and sheep have **horizontal, elongated** pupils. This lets them survey their surroundings well and spot enemies early. The **domestic cat** often has a **narrow, slit-shaped** pupil in the daytime. In the dark it becomes almost circular and large.

gewusst: Eye doctors shine a small lamp into the eye to check whether the pupil narrows properly.
Cats’ eyes glow in the dark because behind their retina there is a layer that reflects light back.

teile.einleitung: Periodisation is a term from training theory. The training is divided into sections with different aims, so that athletes are in top form at the right time.
wichtigste: Periodisation divides the training year into sections with aims.
The smallest section is the microcycle, usually about a week.
A mesocycle lasts about 3 to 6 weeks.
Lev Matveyev distinguished preparation, competition and transition periods.
In tapering the amount of training is reduced before a competition.
Double periodisation has two peaks in the year.

abschnitte.text: Nobody can be in top form the whole year. That is why trainers plan the year in **sections**. Each section has its own **focus**, for example stamina, strength or technique. This approach is called **periodisation**. The aim is to reach **peak form** at the most important competitions.

The smallest planning section is the **microcycle**. It usually lasts a few days to a week. Several microcycles form a **mesocycle** of about **3 to 6 weeks**. Often it ends with an easier week for recovery. Several mesocycles make up the **macrocycle**, for example a whole season.

The Soviet training scientist **Lev Matveyev** divided the training year into three periods. In the **preparation period** the foundations are built. In the **competition period** the competitions are the focus. After that follows the **transition period**. It serves for physical and mental recovery, but you stay active with light exercise.

In **double periodisation** there are two preparation and competition periods per year. This suits, for example, athletes with an indoor and an outdoor season. In **block periodisation**, described among others by **Vladimir Issurin**, each block concentrates on a few abilities. The blocks follow in a planned order.

Shortly before an important competition people often train less. This approach is called **tapering**. The **volume** of training falls, but the **intensity** is partly kept. In this way the body recovers from the hard work and is fresh on the day of the competition. In school sport and in clubs, too, a good plan helps to avoid overloading.

gewusst: Matveyev’s model shaped training theory for many decades.
Recovery is a fixed part of training, because in the rest after the load the body becomes stronger.

teile.einleitung: Many medicines cannot simply be bought at the chemist’s. For them you need a doctor’s **prescription**. On it the doctor writes down which medicine you should take and how.
wichtigste: You need a prescription to receive prescription-only medicines.
A prescription states, among other things, the name of the medicine and the dose.
The old abbreviation “Rp.” stands for the Latin “recipe”, meaning take!
In Switzerland, **Swissmedic** decides whether a medicine needs a prescription.
In Switzerland antibiotics are only available on a doctor’s prescription.
You normally have a prescription filled at the chemist’s.

abschnitte.text: Some medicines can do harm if used wrongly. That is why you may only get them with a **doctor’s prescription**. They are called **prescription-only**. The doctor first checks whether the medicine is suitable and what amount is right. One example is **antibiotics**, which work against bacteria and in Switzerland are only available on prescription.

A prescription states, among other things, the **name of the medicine** and the **dose**, that is, how much to take and when. It also has the name of the patient, the date and the doctor’s signature. In the past, every prescription began with the abbreviation **“Rp.”**. It stands for the Latin **“recipe”**, which means take! Today prescriptions are often issued electronically too.

In Switzerland, **Swissmedic**, the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products, checks all medicines. Swissmedic also decides whether a medicine **needs a prescription** or may be sold freely. The authority has its seat in Bern. Some medicines are available without a prescription after advice at the chemist’s. Others, such as mild painkillers, can be bought freely in small packs.

Normally you have a prescription filled at the **chemist’s**. A special feature of many doctors’ practices in **German-speaking Switzerland**, however, is **self-dispensing**: doctors there may hand out medicines directly in the practice. Whether this is allowed is decided by each canton itself. If you need a medicine for a long time, you often get a **repeat prescription**. It is valid for several collections so that you do not have to go back to the doctor every time.

gewusst: The word “Rezept” comes from the same Latin word as the abbreviation “Rp.”.
Cooking recipes are also called Rezept in German because, like a medical prescription, they write down what you should take.

teile.einleitung: Nursing professionals (in German Pflegefachpersonen) look after sick, injured and old people. They work in hospital, in the old people’s home or with people at home, and that round the clock.
wichtigste: Nursing professionals measure values, give medicines and help with personal care.
In hospital they work day and night.
They do shift work in the morning, in the evening and at night.
In the past people often said nurse.
FaGe stands for Fachfrau or Fachmann Gesundheit (healthcare assistant), a three-year apprenticeship.
The sick get medicines according to the doctor’s plan.

abschnitte.text: In hospital **nursing professionals** look after the sick all day. They measure **temperature**, pulse and blood pressure. They help with **washing** and dressing when someone cannot do it alone. They observe how the sick are doing and report changes to the doctor. Often they are also there to listen and to comfort.

The doctor decides which **medicine** someone needs. The nursing professional brings it to the bed at **fixed times**. She takes great care that every person gets the right medicine in the right amount. Everything is carefully recorded in a **plan**. In this way fewer mistakes happen.

Sick people need help in the night too. That is why in hospital there are nursing staff **day and night**. The work is divided into **shifts**: early shift, late shift and night shift. Several groups take turns. This is called **shift work**. People also work at weekends and on public holidays.

After school in Switzerland you can do the apprenticeship as a **Fachfrau or Fachmann Gesundheit** (healthcare assistant), **FaGe** for short. It lasts **three years**. You work, for example, in hospital, in the old people’s home or with the **Spitex**, the nursing care at home. Whoever wants to become a qualified nursing professional afterwards attends a **college of higher education** or a **university of applied sciences**.

In the past people often said **nurse** (in German Krankenschwester, literally “sick sister”). Today the job is called **Pflegefachfrau** or **Pflegefachmann**, because many men also work in nursing. The job is demanding and important. In Switzerland many new nursing professionals are being sought, because more and more older people need care.

gewusst: The Briton Florence Nightingale is regarded as the founder of modern nursing.
On 12 May, the birthday of Florence Nightingale, International Nurses Day is celebrated.

teile.einleitung: Right at the top of the nose lies a small piece of mucous membrane with which we smell. This is the **olfactory mucous membrane**. It is only a few square centimetres in size but can tell thousands of scents apart.
wichtigste: The olfactory mucous membrane is only a few square centimetres in size on each side of the nose.
It lies in the area of the upper nasal conchae.
Bowman’s glands make the mucus that covers the smell cells.
Scent substances must first dissolve in the mucus.
The nerve fibres pass through the ethmoid bone to the brain.
“Olfactory” means: relating to the sense of smell.

abschnitte.titel: Right at the top of the nose
abschnitte.text: The **olfactory mucous membrane** lies in the uppermost part of the nasal cavity, in the area of the **upper nasal conchae**. Nasal conchae are curved ridges on the side wall of the nose. The olfactory mucous membrane is only **a few square centimetres on each side of the nose**, about as big as a postage stamp. In it sit millions of smell cells. The technical word for everything that concerns the sense of smell is **olfactory**.

The smell cells are covered by a thin layer of mucus. This mucus is made by **Bowman’s glands**. Scent substances from the air must first **dissolve in the mucus** before the smell cells can recognise them. The mucus is constantly renewed and washes old scent substances away. In this way the nose is soon ready again for new smells.

In normal breathing, only little air flows all the way up to the olfactory mucous membrane. When we want to smell something carefully, we **sniff**. We draw in the air briefly and strongly. This brings **more scent substances up** to the olfactory mucous membrane. In this way we also smell faint scents better.

We also smell a lot when we eat. While chewing, the aromas rise **from behind through the throat** into the nose. Much of what we call taste is really smell. That is why food often tastes bland when you have a cold. If the nose is blocked, the aromas no longer reach the olfactory mucous membrane.

The nerve fibres of the smell cells have to reach the brain. To do so they pass through a skull bone, the **ethmoid bone**. It has many small holes, like a sieve, hence the name. Above it lies the **olfactory bulb**, a part of the brain. There the signals are collected and passed on.

gewusst: Dogs have a much larger olfactory mucous membrane than humans and so a far better sense of smell.
With colds, the sense of smell can fail almost completely for some time.

teile.einleitung: Wheelchair basketball is basketball played in a wheelchair. As in normal basketball, you throw a ball into a basket. The sport is fast, exciting and is part of the Paralympic Games.
wichtigste: In **wheelchair basketball** you throw a ball into a basket from a wheelchair.
The basket hangs at the same height as in normal basketball.
There are **5 players** per team on the court.
It is played in especially nimble **sports wheelchairs**.
Wheelchair basketball is a **Paralympic sport**.

abschnitte.text: Two teams of **5 players** each face each other. The aim is to throw the ball into the opponents’ basket. The basket hangs at the same height as in basketball on foot, at about 3 metres. Whoever has the ball may push only twice and must then dribble, pass or shoot it. This replaces the travelling rule of normal basketball.

The game is not played in an everyday wheelchair but in a light **sports wheelchair**. Its wheels are set at an angle. This makes it very nimble and it does not tip over so easily. At the front a bar protects the feet in collisions. The players have to drive, handle the ball and watch the game all at the same time.

Not all players have the same physical abilities. That is why each person is given a **points value** according to their mobility. The points of all the players on the court together must not exceed a certain limit. This keeps the game fair. In many leagues, people without a disability may also play.

Wheelchair basketball arose after the Second World War in the USA, when injured soldiers wanted to do sport again. Soon the game spread to many countries. It has been part of the programme since the first Paralympic Games in 1960 in Rome. In Switzerland too there are clubs and a championship.

gewusst: Good players can turn the wheelchair so fast that they outplay their opponents as in dribbling.
If you tip over in the wheelchair, you can often get up again yourself and carry on playing.

teile.einleitung: Some people feel sick in a car, on a ship or on a plane. This is **travel sickness**. It is unpleasant but usually harmless and stops as soon as the journey is over.
wichtigste: The technical term for travel sickness is **kinetosis**.
Typical signs are nausea, paleness, sweating and dizziness.
It arises when the eyes and the sense of balance send conflicting messages to the brain.
In a car it helps to look out of the window into the distance.
On a ship it is best to sit in the middle.
Children of school age are especially often affected.
Ginger is often used as a natural remedy.

abschnitte.text: In technical language, travel sickness is called **kinetosis**, after the Greek word for movement. Depending on the means of transport, people also speak of seasickness or car sickness. Typical signs are **nausea**, yawning, cold sweat, a pale face and sometimes vomiting. The complaints often begin slowly and get stronger with time. After the journey they usually pass quickly.

In the inner ear sits the **balance organ**. It senses when the body moves or sways. But if you read a book in the car, your eyes report that you are standing still. The brain thus receives conflicting messages and reacts to them with nausea. That is why many people feel ill when reading or playing on their phone during a journey.

In a car it helps to look **out of the window into the distance**, because then the images from the eyes match the movement you feel. A seat at the front, fresh air and a light meal before the journey are also good. On a ship it is best to sit **in the middle**, because that is where it sways least. **Ginger** is often used as a natural remedy. For severe complaints there are also medicines from the chemist’s.

**Children of school age** suffer especially often from travel sickness. Small children under two, on the other hand, are rarely affected. In many people the tendency becomes weaker in adulthood. If you are exposed to a movement for longer, for example several days on a ship, you often get used to it.

Even in space there is a form of travel sickness. It is called **space sickness**. In weightlessness the balance organ lacks its familiar sense of up and down. Many astronauts therefore feel unwell in the first days. After that the body usually gets used to the new situation.

gewusst: The word “nausea” for sickness comes from the Greek word for ship.
In simulators and in games with VR goggles you can also get similar complaints.

teile.einleitung: A percentile helps to compare a value with many others. At the paediatrician’s, percentile curves show, for example, how tall a child is compared with children of the same age.
wichtigste: Percentiles divide ordered data into a hundred equal parts.
The 50th percentile is the median, that is, the middle.
At the 75th percentile, 75 out of 100 children of the same age are equally tall or shorter.
Between the 3rd and the 97th percentile lie 94 per cent of children.
What matters is that a child roughly follows its own curve.
There are separate curves for girls and boys.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from **“per centum”**, that is, “by the hundred”. You arrange many values by size and divide the row into **100 equal parts**. A **percentile** says what per cent of the values are equal or smaller. The **50th percentile** is the **median**: one half lies below, the other above.

At the paediatrician’s, height and weight are entered in a **percentile curve**. If a child is at the **75th percentile** for height, about three quarters of children of the same age are equally tall or shorter. At the **97th percentile**, 97 out of 100 are equally tall or shorter. Only about **3** out of 100 are taller. This is not a school report, only a comparison.

Much more important than the exact number is the **course**. A healthy child usually follows roughly **its own curve**. If it moves clearly up or down away from it, the doctor looks more closely. Girls and boys grow on average at different speeds and reach different heights. That is why there are **separate curves** for them.

Below the **3rd percentile** lie 3 per cent of children, above the **97th percentile** likewise 3 per cent. In between remain 100 minus 3 minus 3, that is, **94 per cent**. Another example: in a group of 20 children distributed like the population, 25 per cent lie below the **25th percentile**. That is 20 times 0.25, that is, **5 children**.

Percentiles are also used in **statistics**, in school and in business. In tests you can use them to show how a result compares with many others. Special names go to the **quartiles**: the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles divide the data into four quarters. In this way large amounts of data can be described simply.

gewusst: A child at the 50th percentile is exactly average in height, and a child at the 10th percentile can still be completely healthy.
At the check-ups at the paediatrician’s the growth curve is often continued over many years.

teile.einleitung: Sleep is not the same all night. It consists of different stages that repeat in cycles. Specialists distinguish REM sleep and non-REM sleep.
wichtigste: A distinction is made between REM sleep and non-REM sleep.
A sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes in adults.
In a night you go through about 4 to 6 cycles.
The most time is spent in light sleep N2.
In the falling-asleep stage N1 you are easiest to wake.
A hypnogram shows the sleep stages over the course of the night.

abschnitte.text: Sleep divides into **non-REM sleep** and **REM sleep**. In REM sleep the eyes move quickly, and you often dream vividly. A complete **sleep cycle** lasts about **90 minutes** in adults. In a normal night you go through about **4 to 6** such cycles.

The time from turning off the light to falling asleep is called **sleep latency**. Then follows the **falling-asleep stage N1**. In it you are easiest to wake. Sometimes the body suddenly twitches, which is a harmless **hypnic jerk**.

Adults spend the largest part of the night in **light sleep N2**. In the EEG, short patterns appear, the **sleep spindles**. In **deep sleep N3** the brain is slow and the body recovers especially well. If you are woken from deep sleep, you are often groggy.

Specialists show the course of a night in a **hypnogram**. It looks like a staircase that goes up and down several times. On it you can see: at the start of the night there is more deep sleep, towards morning longer REM phases.

gewusst: In REM sleep most muscles are almost paralysed, so you do not act out your dreams.
Short moments awake in the night are normal, and you usually forget them by morning.

teile.einleitung: Sleep is a natural state of rest into which humans and many animals fall every day. We spend about a third of our life asleep. Yet while we rest, our body is anything but idle.
wichtigste: In sleep the body recovers, and the brain processes what has been learned.
Children of school age need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night.
Children grow mainly in sleep, because a lot of growth hormone is released then.
Sleep runs in cycles of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep.
In REM sleep we dream especially vividly.
A dark, quiet room helps with falling asleep.
Anyone who sleeps too little is often tired, irritable and finds it hard to concentrate.

abschnitte.text: Sleep is a state in which we hardly notice our surroundings and move little. Unlike in a faint, though, you can be woken at any time. Sleep is controlled by the **inner clock** in the brain. It makes sure that we become tired in the evening and awake in the morning. The hormone **melatonin**, which is made in the dark, helps with this.

A night consists of several **sleep cycles**, each lasting about 90 minutes. After falling asleep, first comes light sleep and then **deep sleep**, in which it is hard to wake up. After that comes **REM sleep**, named after the rapid eye movements under the closed lids. In a night you go through four to six such cycles. Towards morning, REM sleep becomes longer and deep sleep shorter.

Almost all people dream every night, even if they do not remember it in the morning. We have especially colourful and strange **dreams** in REM sleep. So that we do not act out the dreams with our body, the muscles are almost paralysed in this phase. Researchers suspect that dreams help to process experiences and feelings. Bad dreams are called **nightmares**.

In sleep the brain sorts the experiences of the day and stores what has been learned in the **memory**. Anyone who sleeps well after studying remembers vocabulary better. In deep sleep the body releases a lot of **growth hormone**, which is why children grow mainly at night. In addition, muscles recover and the **immune system** is strengthened. Without sleep a person cannot stay healthy in the long run.

Babies sleep 14 to 17 hours a day, spread over many short naps. School children need about 9 to 12 hours, teenagers about 8 to 10 hours. Adults usually manage with 7 to 9 hours. In puberty the inner clock shifts, which is why teenagers are awake late in the evening and tired in the morning. Too little sleep makes you **irritable**, unable to concentrate and more prone to illness.

A dark, quiet and rather cool room helps with falling asleep. The blue light of **screens** slows the making of melatonin, so you should put away your phone and tablet before sleeping. Fixed times for going to bed and getting up help the inner clock. Exercise during the day makes you pleasantly tired in the evening. A heavy meal or drinks with caffeine shortly before sleeping, by contrast, disturb a good night’s rest.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sleep phase with rapid eye movements in which we dream especially vividly.
A very restful sleep phase in which it is hard to wake up.
A hormone that is made in the dark and makes us tired.
A pacemaker in the brain that controls the day-night rhythm.

gewusst: Dolphins always sleep with only one half of the brain, so that they can surface to breathe.
In the wild, giraffes often manage with less than five hours of sleep a day.
During sleep you turn over many times each night without noticing.

teile.einleitung: The Red Cross is a worldwide relief movement. It helps people in need, for example in wars, disasters and natural catastrophes. It was founded by Henri Dunant of Geneva, which is why it has an especially close link with Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Swiss **Henri Dunant** from **Geneva** founded the Red Cross movement.
At the beginning the Red Cross looked after mainly **wounded soldiers**.
Henri Dunant received the first **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1901.
Many countries use the **Red Crescent** instead of the Red Cross.
The Red Cross organisation of Switzerland is called the **SRK**.
**World Red Cross Day** is on **8 May**.

abschnitte.text: **Henri Dunant** was born in 1828 in **Geneva**. In 1859 on a journey he came to Solferino in Italy, where a great battle had taken place shortly before. Thousands of wounded soldiers lay there without help. Together with people from the area, Dunant organised help for all the wounded, no matter which side they were on. Later he wrote about it in the book “A Memory of Solferino”.

Dunant’s book moved many people. In 1863 he founded a committee in Geneva with other citizens, which became the **International Committee of the Red Cross** (ICRC). A year later several states signed the first **Geneva Convention**. It protects **wounded soldiers** and all who help them. The ICRC still has its seat in Geneva today.

The emblem is a red cross on a white background. It is the Swiss flag with its colours reversed, as an honour to Switzerland. In many countries the **Red Crescent** is used instead. Later the **Red Crystal** was added as another protective emblem. All the emblems mean the same: help is given here neutrally, and these people must not be attacked.

In **1901** the **Nobel Peace Prize** was awarded for the first time. Henri Dunant was one of the first two winners. He received it for founding the Red Cross. His birthday, **8 May**, is now **World Red Cross Day**. On this day, people all over the world remember the work of the movement.

In Switzerland there is the **Swiss Red Cross**, **SRK** for short. It offers, for example, first aid courses, looks after blood donations, supports older people and helps families in need. Many people take part as volunteers. Organisations such as the Samaritans also belong to the Red Cross family of Switzerland.

gewusst: The Red Cross and the Red Crescent are present in almost all countries of the world.
The ICRC has itself received the Nobel Peace Prize several times for its work.

teile.einleitung: Psychotherapy is the treatment of mental problems and illnesses using scientifically recognised methods, above all through conversation. There are different schools that differ in their ideas. What they all have in common is that a good relationship between therapist and patient is very important.
wichtigste: Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis.
The Swiss psychiatrist Carl Gustav Jung founded analytical psychology.
Carl Rogers developed client-centred talk therapy.
In systemic therapy, relationships in the social environment are at the centre.
The therapeutic relationship is seen as one of the most important factors that make therapy work.
Since 2022, basic insurance pays for psychological psychotherapy when a doctor refers the patient.

abschnitte.text: The Viennese doctor **Sigmund Freud** founded **psychoanalysis** around 1900. He assumed that unconscious wishes and conflicts influence our behaviour. In therapy they are meant to become conscious through conversation. An important term is **transference**: feelings from earlier relationships are directed at the therapist. These feelings can then be understood together.

The Swiss psychiatrist **Carl Gustav Jung** first worked together with Freud but then went his own way. He founded **analytical psychology**. Jung was especially interested in dreams, symbols and myths. Terms such as “introverted” and “extraverted” go back to him. He lived and worked for a long time in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich.

The American **Carl Rogers** developed **client-centred talk therapy**. He considered three basic attitudes to be central: **empathy**, that is, understanding with feeling, appreciation and genuineness. Another major school is **behavioural therapy**. It helps to change distressing thoughts and habits step by step. Today it is one of the best-studied methods.

**Systemic therapy** does not look only at a single person. At the centre are the **relationships in the social environment**, for example in the family, at school or at work. Problems are understood as part of a system. That is why several family members often take part in the sessions.

Research shows that one of the most important factors in every psychotherapy is the **therapeutic relationship**. You have to feel understood and safe. In Switzerland, the **referral model** has applied since July 2022. Since then, psychological psychotherapy has been paid for by **basic insurance** on **a doctor’s referral**. Before that, psychologists mostly had to work under medical supervision so that the health insurer would pay.

gewusst: Freud often had his patients lie on a couch so that they could relax and talk freely.
Today there are many different psychotherapy methods, which are studied scientifically.

teile.einleitung: The plague is a serious infectious disease that is caused by a bacterium. In the 14th century, as the “Black Death”, it killed a large part of the people in Europe.
wichtigste: The plague is caused by a bacterium.
The great wave of plague in the 14th century is called the Black Death.
In 1347 merchant ships brought the plague to Europe.
About a third of the population of Europe died then.
Alexandre Yersin, born in the canton of Vaud, discovered the germ in 1894.
The word quarantine comes from the Italian word for forty.
Today the plague can be treated with antibiotics.

abschnitte.text: The plague is caused by a rod-shaped **bacterium**. It is called **Yersinia pestis**. Often it is passed on by **fleas** that have lived beforehand on infected rats or other rodents. In **bubonic plague** the lymph nodes, for example in the armpit or on the neck, swell into painful lumps. If the germ attacks the lung, this is called **pneumonic plague**. It is passed directly from person to person by coughing.

In the autumn of **1347** merchant ships from the area of the Black Sea brought the plague to **Messina** in Sicily. From there it spread over the whole of Europe. The area of present-day Switzerland was also hit. Estimates speak of about **25 million deaths**, roughly **a third** of the population of Europe at that time. This pandemic is called the **Black Death**.

At that time nobody knew how the disease arises. Many believed it came from **bad air**. In Venice ships from plague areas had to wait **40 days** before anyone was allowed ashore. In Italian forty is **“quaranta”**. From this arose the word **quarantine**. In the 17th century some plague doctors wore a mask with a long **beak** in which fragrant herbs were placed.

The researcher **Alexandre Yersin** was born in 1863 in **Aubonne** in the canton of Vaud. In **1894** he investigated a plague epidemic in **Hong Kong**. In doing so he found the germ. Later the bacterium was named after him. Yersin spent a large part of his life in Vietnam.

Because the plague is caused by a bacterium, today it can be treated with **antibiotics**. Early treatment is important. In some parts of the world the germ still occurs in wild rodents. That is why there are isolated cases today too. In Europe, however, the plague has long since disappeared.

gewusst: After the Black Death the plague kept returning in waves in Europe for centuries.
The bacterium Yersinia pestis bears the name of the researcher Alexandre Yersin, born in Vaud.

teile.einleitung: Besides the blood groups A, B, AB and O there is another important feature of the blood: the **rhesus factor**. It helps to decide which blood a person may receive in a blood transfusion.
wichtigste: The rhesus factor is named after the rhesus monkey.
Rhesus positive means: the red blood cells carry the feature D.
In Europe about 85 per cent of people are rhesus positive.
Rhesus negative people make antibodies only after contact with rhesus positive blood.
Blood group A with a positive rhesus factor is written A+ for short.
The rhesus factor is inherited from the parents.

abschnitte.titel: A monkey gave it its name
abschnitte.text: The rhesus factor is named after the **rhesus monkey**. Researchers carried out experiments with the blood of these monkeys around 1940. **Karl Landsteiner**, who had already discovered the blood groups A, B and O, was involved. They came across a new feature of the red blood cells. It was given the name of the monkey.

The most important rhesus feature is called **D**. If the red blood cells carry this feature, a person is **rhesus positive**. If it is missing, they are **rhesus negative**. In Europe about **85 per cent** of people are rhesus positive. Together with the blood group, this is written briefly, for example **A+** or O-.

With blood groups A and B you have antibodies against foreign blood groups from early childhood. With the rhesus factor it is different. A rhesus negative person has **no antibodies against the feature D from birth**. They only make them once they have had **contact with rhesus positive blood**. **Antibodies** are defence substances of the immune system.

That is why a rhesus negative person should **not receive rhesus positive blood**. Their body could make antibodies that destroy foreign blood cells. In a further transfusion that would be dangerous. Before every blood transfusion it is therefore checked carefully whether the blood matches. In Switzerland, Blutspende SRK (the Red Cross blood donation service) collects the donated blood.

Like the blood group, the rhesus factor is **inherited from the parents**. Every person receives one gene for it from each parent. Rhesus positive is the stronger gene. That is why two rhesus positive parents can still have a rhesus negative child. The rhesus factor does not change throughout life.

gewusst: Besides the feature D, the rhesus system has many other but less important features.
How common rhesus negative is varies greatly from one part of the world to another, and in East Asia it is rare.

teile.einleitung: The collecting duct is the last section in the fine system of tubes in the kidney. Here it is decided how much water and salt the body keeps and how concentrated the urine becomes. This is controlled mainly by hormones.
wichtigste: The collecting duct joins the **distal tubule** through a **connecting tubule**.
Under the influence of a hormone, water channels made of **aquaporin-2** are built into the cell membrane.
If the body has to save water, the urine is **concentrated** in the collecting duct.
**Principal cells** take up sodium and give off potassium.
**Intercalated cells** give off protons or bicarbonate.
The medicine **amiloride** blocks the sodium channels (ENaC).

abschnitte.text: The kidney filters the blood in many tiny units, the **nephrons**. The filtered primary urine flows through various small tubes, the **tubules**. After the **distal tubule** it reaches the **collecting duct** through a short **connecting tubule**. Several nephrons open into one shared collecting duct. The collecting ducts run through the renal medulla and release the finished urine at the renal papilla into the renal pelvis.

If the body has too little water, the pituitary gland releases the hormone **ADH**, also called **antidiuretic hormone** or vasopressin. It causes water channels made of **aquaporin-2** to be built into the membrane of the collecting duct cells. Through these channels water flows from the urine back into the tissue. The urine is **concentrated** as a result and the amount becomes smaller. Without ADH the channels are missing, and a large amount of dilute urine is produced.

For water to leave the collecting duct, the surrounding tissue has to be very rich in salt and other substances. In the **inner medulla**, **urea** also leaves the collecting duct. There it raises the **osmolarity**, that is, the amount of dissolved particles. As a result, additional water is drawn out of the collecting duct. In this way the kidney can produce urine that is much more concentrated than the blood.

In the wall of the collecting duct there are two important types of cell. The **principal cells** take up sodium through sodium channels, the **ENaC**, and give off **potassium**. The hormone **aldosterone** strengthens this work. The **intercalated cells** regulate the acid-base balance. Depending on the type, they give off **protons** or **bicarbonate**.

Some medicines act specifically on the collecting duct. **Amiloride** blocks the sodium channels **ENaC** in the principal cells. Then less sodium, and with it less water, is taken back, and the amount of urine rises. Because less potassium is given off as well, amiloride is counted among the **potassium-sparing diuretics**. Diuretics are medicines that promote the excretion of water.

gewusst: Each day the kidney filters far more fluid than is finally excreted as urine, because almost all of it is taken back.
If the effect of ADH is missing, those affected can produce very large amounts of dilute urine.

teile.einleitung: In every cell there are tiny protein factories, the **ribosomes**. They read off a set of building instructions and use it to build proteins. Without ribosomes no cell could live.
wichtigste: Ribosomes consist of rRNA and proteins.
They carry out **translation**, a step of protein synthesis.
The tRNA brings the amino acids to the ribosome.
Eukaryotic ribosomes in the cytoplasm have the value 80S.
Several ribosomes on the same mRNA form a polysome.
Ribosomes have no membrane envelope.

abschnitte.text: **Ribosomes** are tiny particles that occur in all cells. They consist of **ribosomal RNA**, rRNA for short, and **proteins**. Each ribosome has two parts, a large and a small subunit. Unlike organelles such as lysosomes or mitochondria, ribosomes have **no membrane envelope**. They lie freely in the cell plasma or sit on the endoplasmic reticulum.

The building instructions for a protein come as **mRNA** from the cell nucleus. The ribosome reads them off and builds up the protein building block by building block. This process is called **translation**. The building blocks are **amino acids**. The **tRNA** brings them to the ribosome, and each tRNA carries a particular amino acid.

Often several ribosomes read the same mRNA at the same time, one behind the other. Such a group is called a **polysome**. In this way the cell can quickly make many copies of the same protein from one set of instructions. The size of ribosomes is given by the **sedimentation coefficient**, measured in **S** for Svedberg. It shows how fast particles sink in a centrifuge.

The ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells, including those of humans, have the value **80S**. Bacteria have smaller ribosomes with the value 70S. Because **bacterial ribosomes are built differently**, some antibiotics can block them specifically. One example is **tetracycline**. The bacteria can then no longer make proteins, while human cells are hardly disturbed.

gewusst: A single cell can contain millions of ribosomes.
For working out the structure of ribosomes, three researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009, among them Ada Yonath.

teile.einleitung: Pro Juventute is a Swiss foundation that works for children and young people. Best known is its helpline 147. There, young people can always find someone who will listen.
wichtigste: Pro Juventute is a Swiss foundation for children and young people.
You can turn to the 147 helpline with any worries and questions.
The 147 helpline can be reached around the clock.
A call is free of charge, and the conversations are confidential.
You can also reach 147 by text message, chat and email.
Adults can find help from Dargebotene Hand (the Helping Hand) on the number 143.
In an acute emergency threatening life, you dial 144 for the ambulance service.

abschnitte.text: The name **Pro Juventute** comes from Latin and means “for the youth”. The organisation was founded in 1912 and is a **foundation**. It supports children, young people and their families all over Switzerland. This includes counselling, courses for parents and projects on subjects such as media, money or free time. Many people also know the **Pro Juventute stamps**, which the foundation sells to raise money.

The **147 helpline** is there for children and young people. You can get in touch with **any worries and questions**: arguments with friends, trouble at home, stress at school, heartache or simply a bad feeling. The helpline can be reached **around the clock**, also at night and at weekends. A call is **free of charge**. As well as by telephone, you can also get in touch by **text message, chat and email**.

The conversations with the 147 helpline are **confidential**. This means that what you tell them stays between those involved. You do not have to give your name. The specialists listen, take your worries seriously and look for solutions together with you. Sometimes it helps just to talk to someone about it. Nobody has to be left alone with their problems.

Besides 147, there are other numbers that you should know. **Dargebotene Hand** is there on **143** for adults who need someone to talk to. In an acute emergency threatening life, you dial **144** for the ambulance service. You reach the police on 117 and the fire brigade on 118. It is worth knowing these numbers by heart.

The history of Pro Juventute also includes a sad chapter. From 1926 to 1973 the charity project **“Kinder der Landstrasse”** (“Children of the Road”) took Yenish children away from their families. The Yenish are a minority in Switzerland who used to travel around a lot. Today this practice is seen as a serious injustice. The foundation has apologised for it.

gewusst: Every year the 147 helpline receives a very large number of enquiries from children and young people from all over Switzerland.
Pro Juventute has been issuing stamps for over a hundred years.

teile.einleitung: Prokaryotes are living things made of a single, very simply built cell. They have no cell nucleus. They include the bacteria and the archaea, the oldest forms of life on Earth.
wichtigste: Prokaryotes have no cell nucleus with a nuclear envelope.
They include the two domains of bacteria and archaea.
Their ring-shaped chromosome lies in the nucleoid.
They have smaller 70S ribosomes.
The cell wall of most bacteria consists mainly of murein.
Many move along using rotating flagella.

abschnitte.text: The word **prokaryote** comes from Greek and means roughly “before the nucleus”. In plants, animals, fungi and humans, the **eukaryotes**, the genetic material lies in a cell nucleus with a **nuclear envelope**. Prokaryotes have no such nucleus. Their cells are usually only a few thousandths of a millimetre across and so much smaller than most eukaryote cells. You can only see them under the microscope.

The prokaryotes make up two of the three great **domains** of life: the **bacteria** and the **archaea**. Bacteria live almost everywhere, in the soil, in water and in our gut. Many are useful, some make us ill. Archaea look similar to bacteria but differ in their metabolism and structure. Some live in extreme places, such as hot springs or very salty water.

The genetic material of a bacterium is usually a single **ring-shaped chromosome**. It lies freely in the cell plasma in an area called the **nucleoid**. In addition there are often small rings of DNA, the **plasmids**. They can carry features such as resistance to antibiotics. To make proteins, prokaryotes have **70S ribosomes**, which are smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes.

Most bacteria have a firm **cell wall** made of **murein**. It gives the cell its shape and protection. Many bacteria move along using **flagella**. These are long threads that turn like a propeller. Bacteria usually multiply by simple cell division: one cell becomes two. Under good conditions this happens very quickly in some species.

The Danish doctor **Hans Christian Gram** developed a staining method in 1884 that is still important today. With the **Gram stain**, bacteria are divided into two groups according to the structure of their cell wall: Gram-positive and Gram-negative. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick layer of murein and stain dark violet. This helps doctors to choose the right antibiotic.

gewusst: On and in the human body there live roughly as many bacterial cells as there are body cells.
Prokaryotes existed on Earth for billions of years before there were plants and animals.

teile.einleitung: Oxygen is a gas that we breathe in with every breath. Almost all living things need it to get energy from food. It is made mainly by green plants and algae.
wichtigste: Oxygen is a colourless gas with no smell.
About one fifth of the air is oxygen.
In chemistry, oxygen has the symbol O.
Plants and algae make oxygen using sunlight.
The blood carries oxygen from the lungs to all cells.
Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water.
Plant roots need air in the soil too.

abschnitte.text: Green plants and algae take in carbon dioxide and water. With the energy of sunlight they build sugar from them and give off **oxygen** in the process. This process is called **photosynthesis**. A large part of the oxygen comes from tiny algae in the sea. Without plants there would hardly be any oxygen in the air.

When you breathe in, oxygen reaches the **lungs**. There it passes into the blood and is carried to all cells by the red blood cells. The cells need it to get energy from food. In hospital, a small device is sometimes clipped onto the finger, a **pulse oximeter**. It shines light through the finger and measures how much oxygen the blood is carrying.

Fish use their **gills** to breathe the oxygen that is dissolved in the water. Warm water can take up less oxygen than cold water. In a warm pond, fish therefore sometimes gasp for air at the surface. In an aquarium, an **air pump** blows small bubbles into the water so that enough oxygen gets in.

Roots need oxygen as well. They get it from small air holes between the crumbs of soil. If you water a potted plant far too much, these holes fill with water. Then the roots lack air, they can rot and the plant dies. That is why many flowerpots have a hole at the bottom, so that surplus water can drain away.

Oxygen combines easily with other substances. This is called **oxidation**. A cut apple turns brown in the air because substances in the apple react with oxygen. Iron also rusts with oxygen and water. A fire burns only if there is enough oxygen.

gewusst: The symbol O comes from the Latin name “Oxygenium”.
Very cold, liquid oxygen is light blue.
A few drops of lemon juice stop an apple from turning brown quickly.

teile.einleitung: The peripheral nervous system includes all the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. It joins the central nervous system to muscles, skin and organs in the whole body.
wichtigste: Brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system, all the other nerves the peripheral one.
A nerve cell is called a neuron in technical language.
The axon passes signals on to other cells.
Myelin sheaths around the nerve fibres make the conduction faster.
The sciatic nerve is the longest and thickest nerve.
The somatic nervous system controls conscious movements.

abschnitte.text: The nervous system has two large parts. **Brain** and **spinal cord** form the **central nervous system**. All the other nerves belong to the **peripheral nervous system**. “Peripheral” means “at the edge”. These nerves run like cables into every corner of the body. They report what we feel and carry commands to the muscles.

A nerve cell is called a **neuron**. The short, branched **dendrites** take in signals. The long **axon** carries signals away from the cell body to other cells. Many axons are wrapped in **myelin sheaths** made of myelin. They insulate the fibre like the sheath of a cable. The signal then jumps from gap to gap and is much faster, in thick fibres up to about **120 metres per second**.

The **sciatic nerve** is the longest and thickest nerve of the body. It runs from the lower back through the buttock into the leg and is about as thick as a finger at its thickest point. The **ulnar nerve** lies directly under the skin at the elbow. If you knock the “funny bone”, it tingles right into the little finger. The **auditory and balance nerve** carries signals from the inner ear to the brain.

The **somatic nervous system** controls the skeletal muscles that we move consciously. It also carries conscious perceptions such as touch or pain. The **autonomic nervous system** works without our will. It regulates, for example, heartbeat, breathing and digestion. It includes the **sympathetic nervous system**, which activates the body, and the **parasympathetic nervous system**, which provides rest and recovery.

From the brain emerge **twelve pairs of cranial nerves**. They supply mainly the head and neck, for example eyes, ears and face. From the spinal cord the **spinal nerves** emerge on both sides. They branch into the trunk, arms and legs. If a nerve is injured, the place can go numb or a muscle can become weak.

gewusst: The fastest nerve fibres carry signals at over 400 kilometres per hour.
The “funny bone” is not a bone at all, but the ulnar nerve, which is hardly protected there.

teile.einleitung: Primary urine is the first fluid that is filtered out of the blood in the kidneys. It is not yet urine: the body takes back almost all of it. Only a small remainder becomes the urine that we pass.
wichtigste: Primary urine is formed in the renal corpuscles when blood is filtered.
It resembles blood plasma, but without the large proteins.
About 99 per cent of the primary urine returns to the blood.
This process is called reabsorption.
Most of it is taken back in the proximal tubule.
In a healthy person, glucose is almost completely recovered.

abschnitte.text: Each kidney is made up of about a million tiny units, the **nephrons**. At the start of each nephron lies a tangle of fine blood vessels, the **glomerulus**. There, water with small dissolved substances is pressed out of the blood. Blood cells and large **proteins** stay in the blood because they are too big for the filter. The filtered fluid is the primary urine. In an adult about 180 litres of it are formed per day.

In its composition, primary urine is very similar to **blood plasma**, except that the large proteins are missing. It contains water, salts, glucose, amino acids and waste products such as urea. Because the dissolved particles are about as concentrated as in the blood, it is **isotonic** with blood plasma. If all of the primary urine were passed out, the body would very quickly lose far too much water and valuable substances.

That is why the body takes back about **99 per cent** of the primary urine. This process is called **reabsorption**. Most of it happens in the first section of the kidney tubules, the **proximal tubule**. Glucose is taken up there by **cotransport with sodium**: a transport protein carries sodium and glucose along together. Only about 1.5 litres of final urine are left each day, that is, the urine we pass.

In a healthy person, practically no glucose is found in the urine. But the transporters can only take up a certain amount. If the blood sugar rises above about **160 to 180 mg/dl**, they are overloaded and glucose appears in the urine. This limit is called the **renal threshold**. Sugar in the urine can be a sign of diabetes, which is why it is often tested for at medical check-ups.

gewusst: The kidneys filter a person’s entire blood supply many times a day.
From about 180 litres of primary urine, only around 1.5 litres of urine are produced each day.

teile.einleitung: The shoulder connects the arm to the trunk. It lies between the neck and the arm. Thanks to it you can move the arm in almost any direction.
wichtigste: The shoulder lies between the neck and the arm.
At the back of the shoulder lies the flat shoulder blade.
Directly under the shoulder the upper arm begins.
Of all joints, the shoulder joint can be moved furthest in a circle.
Shrugging your shoulders often means: I don’t know.
In ice hockey, players wear large shoulder pads.

abschnitte.text: Several bones belong to the shoulder. At the front lies the **collarbone**, which you can feel easily under the skin. At the back lies the flat, triangular **shoulder blade**. Together they form the **shoulder girdle**. The **upper arm bone** attaches to the shoulder blade and begins directly under the shoulder.

The **shoulder joint** is a **ball-and-socket joint**: the round head of the upper arm bone lies in a shallow socket. That is why you can move the arm forwards, back, sideways and **in a circle**. No other joint in the body is so mobile. Many **muscles** and tendons hold the joint together and move the arm. You use the shoulder when throwing, swimming, climbing and reaching up.

With our shoulders we often show how we feel. Someone who **shrugs their shoulders** usually shows that they do not know something or that they do not care. Drooping shoulders can point to tiredness or sadness. Someone who is proud, on the other hand, often holds their shoulders straight. Such signs are called **body language**.

The shoulder appears in many sayings. Someone who **“gives someone the cold shoulder”** deliberately ignores them. Someone who **“takes something lightly”** (German: “auf die leichte Schulter nehmen”) does not take it seriously. **“Shoulder to shoulder”** means that people stick closely together. And someone who carries a lot of responsibility has “a lot on their shoulders”.

In sports with many collisions, the shoulder needs protection. In **ice hockey**, players wear large **shoulder pads** under the jersey. In American football too, they are part of the equipment. To keep the shoulder healthy, you warm it up before sport, for example with arm circles.

gewusst: The collarbone is one of the bones that break most often, often in falls onto the outstretched arm.
The German word “schultern” means to put something on your shoulder, but also to take on a task.

teile.einleitung: Psychiatry is the field of medicine that deals with mental illnesses. These include, for example, depression, anxiety disorders or psychoses. Psychiatrists are doctors who recognise and treat such illnesses.
wichtigste: A psychiatrist is a doctor and may prescribe medicines, a psychologist may not.
The Burghölzli is the long-established university psychiatric clinic in Zurich.
The psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler coined the term “schizophrenia”.
Antipsychotics are mainly used against psychoses.
Lithium has long been used as a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder.
A hallucination is a perception without an outside stimulus.

abschnitte.text: The two words sound similar but describe different professions. A **psychiatrist** has studied medicine and is a **doctor**. So she may **prescribe medicines**. A psychologist has studied psychology and treats mainly through conversation, if she has further training in psychotherapy. The two professions often work closely together.

In Zurich stands one of the best-known clinics in the world: the **Burghölzli**, today the University Psychiatric Clinic Zurich. It opened in 1870. The Swiss psychiatrist **Eugen Bleuler** worked there. At the beginning of the 20th century he coined the term **“schizophrenia”**. The young Carl Gustav Jung also worked at the Burghölzli.

In some mental illnesses, perception changes. A **hallucination** is a perception **without an outside stimulus**: someone hears voices, for example, although nobody is speaking. In a **psychosis**, a person temporarily loses touch with reality. In a **bipolar disorder**, phases of very low mood and very high mood alternate.

Mental illnesses are often treated with a combination of talking and medicines. Against psychoses, **antipsychotics** mainly help. In bipolar disorder, **lithium** has long been used as a mood stabiliser. Many people are treated as outpatients. A **day clinic** offers treatment during the day, and the patients spend the night at home.

Sometimes a person is in danger because of a serious illness but cannot see this for themselves. For such cases, Swiss law provides for **compulsory placement for care**. Here a person is taken to an institution for their own protection, even against their will. Strict rules apply for this, and the person concerned can have the decision reviewed by a court.

gewusst: Mental illnesses are common: many people are affected by them at some time in their lives.
The name Burghölzli goes back to a wooded hill in Zurich on which the clinic was built.

teile.einleitung: Pepsin is an enzyme in the stomach that breaks down proteins from food. It works in a strongly acid environment and was one of the first enzymes that researchers described.
wichtigste: Pepsin splits proteins into shorter pieces, called polypeptides.
It is made as an inactive precursor, pepsinogen.
The chief cells of the stomach lining make pepsinogen.
Hydrochloric acid and already active pepsin activate the pepsinogen.
Pepsin works best at a pH of about 1.5 to 2.
A tough layer of mucus protects the stomach wall.
Theodor Schwann was the first to describe pepsin, in 1836.

abschnitte.text: **Enzymes** are protein substances that speed up chemical reactions. Pepsin is such an enzyme in the **gastric juice**. It splits the long chains of the **proteins** from food into shorter pieces, the **polypeptides**. The further breaking down is taken over later by enzymes in the **small intestine**. Experts count pepsin among the **aspartic proteases**, because two aspartate residues act in its active site.

If the body made active pepsin at once, it could attack its own cells. That is why the **chief cells** of the stomach glands first release a harmless precursor: **pepsinogen**. The **parietal cells** make hydrochloric acid, the **mucous neck cells** make mucus. In the acid gastric juice a piece splits off from the pepsinogen, and active pepsin arises. Pepsin that has already formed speeds up this process further.

The gastric juice is strongly **acid**. Pepsin is adapted exactly to this environment. It works best at a **pH of about 1.5 to 2**. In the small intestine the environment is less acid, and there pepsin stops working. The stomach acid also helps to kill germs in food.

Why does the stomach not digest itself? The stomach wall is covered with a thick, tough **layer of mucus**. It keeps acid and pepsin away from the cells. This layer is constantly renewed. If the protection is disturbed, an inflammation or an ulcer can arise.

The German physiologist **Theodor Schwann** discovered pepsin in **1836** in gastric juice. It was one of the first animal enzymes to be described. The name comes from the Greek word for **digestion**. Schwann is also known for his work on cells.

gewusst: Pepsin is also used technically, for example in research, to break down proteins in a targeted way.
The layer of mucus in the stomach is formed anew all the time, so that the protection never tears.

teile.einleitung: Almost everyone knows hiccups: suddenly there is a “hic”, again and again. Behind it is a twitch of the diaphragm. Mostly hiccups are harmless and over after a few minutes.
wichtigste: In hiccups, the diaphragm twitches.
The “hic” arises because the glottis suddenly closes.
Eating too hastily can trigger hiccups.
Hiccups are mostly harmless and last a few minutes.
In Zurich German they are called “Hitzgi”.

abschnitte.text: The **diaphragm** is a large, flat muscle under the lungs. It helps with breathing in. In hiccups it suddenly and involuntarily contracts. As a result, air rushes quickly into the lungs.

Shortly after the twitch, the **glottis** in the larynx suddenly closes. The incoming air hits against it. This produces the typical sound “hic”. In **Zurich German**, hiccups are called “**Hitzgi**”.
Hiccups can arise from **eating too hastily**, from fizzy drinks or from very hot or cold food. Excitement or laughing can also trigger them. Often you do not know the reason at all.

Ordinary hiccups usually last **a few minutes** and are **harmless**. Many people **hold their breath briefly**, drink a glass of water in small sips or let someone give them a fright. Whether these home remedies really help is not firmly proven. If hiccups last a very long time, you should seek medical advice.

gewusst: Even small babies often have hiccups.
The technical term for hiccups is “singultus”.

teile.einleitung: The forward roll is one of the first gymnastics exercises that children learn. You roll forwards over your rounded back. In PE lessons it is called a forward roll. In German it is also playfully called a Purzelbaum, a “tumbling tree”.
wichtigste: In PE the somersault-style roll forwards is called a forward roll (Rolle vorwärts).
Before rolling, you tuck your chin to your chest.
The back is round like a ball.
You place your hands shoulder-width apart in front of your feet.
You practise on a soft mat, and a sloping mat helps beginners.
If you roll backwards, the exercise is called a backward roll.

abschnitte.text: For a good forward roll, you crouch down. You place your **hands** on the floor **shoulder-width apart in front of your feet**. Then you tuck your **chin to your chest**, as if you wanted to look at your tummy. That way it is not your head but your neck that touches the mat first. Your **back** becomes **round like a ball** so that you can roll off gently.

In PE lessons the Purzelbaum is called a **Rolle vorwärts**, a forward roll. You push off gently with your legs and roll forwards over your rounded back. The knees stay close to the body. At the end you come down on your feet and stand up, if possible without using your hands. In the **backward roll**, you roll the other way, backwards over your back.

Forward rolls are practised on a **soft mat**, never on a hard floor. For **beginners** a **sloping mat** is especially helpful: because it goes slightly downhill, you almost roll by yourself. At the beginning the teacher can help by supporting your back and neck. It is important never to put your whole weight on your head.

abschnitte.titel: From the roll to the somersault
abschnitte.text: The forward roll is a basis for many other exercises in floor gymnastics. Anyone who can do the roll safely later learns rolls with a run-up or a roll over an obstacle. A **somersault** is a flip **in the air** in which the hands do not touch the floor. That is much harder and needs a lot of practice and help from experts.

gewusst: The word Purzelbaum has been known for several centuries.
The forward roll trains balance and body awareness, which also helps in many other sports.

teile.einleitung: A traumatic brain injury is an injury to the head in which the brain is also affected. It can be mild, like a concussion, or life-threatening. Doctors assess the severity among other things with the Glasgow Coma Scale.
wichtigste: The mildest form is concussion.
The Glasgow Coma Scale rates eye opening and the verbal and motor response.
The lowest possible score is 3.
With 8 points or fewer, a traumatic brain injury counts as severe.
An epidural haematoma often shows a “lucid interval”.
A subdural haematoma typically arises from a tear of the bridging veins.
Sharply rising pressure in the head can lead to herniation of the brainstem.

abschnitte.titel: What a traumatic brain injury is
abschnitte.text: The word **trauma** means injury in medicine. In a **traumatic brain injury**, not only the head but also the **brain** is injured. Common causes are falls, traffic accidents and sports accidents. The mildest form is **concussion**. Typical are headache, nausea, dizziness and sometimes a brief loss of consciousness. Severe forms are life-threatening.

To assess the condition quickly, specialists use the **Glasgow Coma Scale**. It rates three areas: **eye opening**, the **verbal response** and the **motor response**, that is, the movements. For each area there are points. The highest score is 15, the **lowest possible score is 3**. With **8 points or fewer**, a traumatic brain injury counts as **severe**.

With a head injury there can be bleeding inside the skull. An **epidural haematoma** typically arises when the **middle meningeal artery** is injured, an artery on the dura mater. Often the person seems awake again at first, before their condition gets worse. This time is called the **lucid interval**. A **subdural haematoma** usually arises from the tearing of **bridging veins**, which run between the brain and the dura mater.

The skull is a firm capsule. According to the **Monro-Kellie doctrine**, the total volume of brain tissue, blood and **cerebrospinal fluid** has to stay the same. If bleeding or swelling is added, the **intracranial pressure** therefore rises. If it rises sharply, the **brainstem** can be squeezed, which controls vital tasks such as breathing. That is why a severe traumatic brain injury needs treatment in hospital immediately.

A **helmet** when cycling, skiing or inline skating clearly lowers the risk of severe head injuries. In athletes with many blows to the head, such as **boxers**, a progressive brain disease is sometimes seen. It is called **chronic traumatic encephalopathy**. After a concussion you should therefore recover enough before you do sport again.

gewusst: The Glasgow Coma Scale was developed in the 1970s in Glasgow in Scotland.
Even a mild concussion needs rest so that the brain can recover.

teile.einleitung: Every nerve cell has a small electrical voltage between inside and outside, even when it is not passing on a signal. This voltage is called the resting membrane potential. It is the basis for nerves being able to send signals at all.
wichtigste: The resting membrane potential of a nerve cell is about **minus 70 millivolts** (mV).
It is determined mainly by **potassium**.
Potassium is more concentrated **inside the cell**, sodium **outside the cell**.
Potassium ions constantly flow out of the cell through **potassium leak channels**.
The **Nernst equation** calculates the equilibrium potential of one kind of ion.
The **Goldman equation** takes several kinds of ion and their permeabilities into account.

abschnitte.text: The cell is surrounded by a thin **cell membrane**. Inside and outside there are dissolved, electrically charged particles, the **ions**. Because they are unevenly distributed, a voltage arises. In a resting nerve cell the inside is negatively charged, at about **minus 70 millivolts**. This voltage is measured with very fine electrodes.

Inside the cell there is a lot of **potassium**, while outside the cell there is a lot of **sodium**. The **sodium-potassium pump** makes sure, using energy, that these differences are kept up. It carries sodium out and potassium in. Without this pump the concentrations would even out over time.

In the membrane there are **potassium leak channels**, which are open even at rest. Through them potassium ions constantly flow out of the cell, because there is more of them inside. In doing so they take positive charge with them to the outside, and the inside becomes negative. But this charge pulls the potassium ions back again. A balance is reached. For sodium, the membrane is hardly permeable at rest, so it is mainly **potassium** that determines the resting membrane potential.

With the **Nernst equation** you calculate the **equilibrium potential** of a single kind of ion. For potassium in a neuron it is about **minus 90 mV**, for sodium about **plus 60 mV**. The real resting membrane potential, at about minus 70 mV, is close to the potassium value. The exact value is given by the **Goldman equation**, which takes several kinds of ion and their permeabilities into account.

The resting membrane potential is like a tensioned spring. When the nerve cell is stimulated, sodium channels open, and the inside becomes positive for a short time. This short signal is called an **action potential**. After that the cell restores the resting state. In this way nerves can pass on new signals very quickly, again and again.

gewusst: A large part of the energy that the brain uses goes to the sodium-potassium pumps.
Muscle cells and many other cells also have a resting membrane potential.

teile.einleitung: Before a cell divides, it has to double all of its genetic material. This process is called **replication**. Many enzymes work together in it, like in a small factory.
wichtigste: In replication, the DNA of a cell is doubled.
Replication is **semi-conservative**: each new double helix keeps one old strand.
Meselson and Stahl proved this in 1958 using heavy nitrogen.
Helicase unwinds the DNA at the replication fork.
DNA polymerase always extends a strand from 5' to 3'.
DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments together.

abschnitte.text: DNA is a **double helix** of two strands that looks like a twisted ladder. In replication the two strands separate, and a matching new strand is built for each. Each new double helix therefore consists of one old and one new strand. This kind is called **semi-conservative**, that is, half preserving. The researchers **Matthew Meselson** and **Franklin Stahl** proved this in 1958 with bacteria and heavy nitrogen.

The place where the DNA opens is called the **replication fork**. There the enzyme **helicase** unwinds the double helix and separates the two strands. In front of the fork, the DNA would become more and more twisted as a result, like a twisted telephone cable. **Topoisomerase** prevents this by releasing the tension. Other proteins hold the separated strands apart.

The new strand is built by **DNA polymerase**. But it cannot simply start from nothing. First the **primase** makes a short RNA starting piece, the primer. The polymerase then attaches building block after building block, always in the direction **from 5' to 3'**. These numbers name the two ends of a DNA strand.

Because the polymerase works in only one direction, it can build one of the two strands in one go. The other it builds in short pieces called **Okazaki fragments**. They are named after the Japanese researchers, the Okazakis. **DNA ligase** then joins these pieces into a continuous strand. In the end, two complete DNA molecules have been formed.

Many DNA polymerases have a **proofreading function**. They check every new building block and remove wrongly built-in ones again at once. As a result the error rate in replication is very low. If a mistake still remains, it is called a **mutation**. Other repair systems of the cell later correct many such mistakes.

gewusst: With every division, a human cell has to copy about three billion base pairs.
So that this goes fast enough, replication begins at many places on the DNA at the same time.

teile.einleitung: In an accident or emergency, every minute counts. The **chain of rescue** describes what has to happen one after another so that a person gets the best help. Every link is important, and the first links are in the hands of all of us.
wichtigste: The classic chain of rescue begins with immediate life-saving measures.
After the emergency call comes first aid.
For helpers, their own safety has top priority.
With the Rautek grip you pull an unconscious person out of danger.
The chain of survival of the European Resuscitation Council has 4 links.
In many cantons, first responders are alerted by smartphone app.
