abschnitte.text: The classic chain of rescue begins with the **immediate life-saving measures**, such as securing the scene of the accident. Then comes the **emergency call**, in Switzerland the number **144** for the ambulance service. After that comes **first aid** until experts arrive. The **rescue service** follows, and finally treatment in **hospital**. If one link fails, the whole chain is weakened.

For all helpers, their **own safety** has top priority. If you are injured yourself, you can no longer help anyone. On Swiss motorways, you put up the **warning triangle** at least **100 metres** behind the scene of the accident. A high-visibility vest makes helpers easier to see. Only when the place is secured do you look after the injured.

Sometimes an unconscious person has to be quickly taken out of a danger zone, for example out of a car. For this there is the **Rautek grip**. You reach through from behind under the armpits and take hold of one forearm of the person. In this way you can support them with your own body and pull them away. With an unconscious motorcyclist wearing a **full-face helmet**, you carefully take off the helmet so that they can breathe freely.

For cardiac arrest there is a chain of its own, the **chain of survival**. At the European Resuscitation Council it consists of **4 links**: recognition and emergency call, early chest compressions, early defibrillation and treatment afterwards. In **telephone resuscitation**, the emergency call centre guides laypeople over the telephone through the chest compressions. So nobody has to decide alone what to do.

In many cantons there are **first responders**. These are trained volunteers who are alerted by **smartphone app** when someone nearby has a cardiac arrest. They begin resuscitation **before the rescue service arrives**. Often they are on the scene faster than the ambulance. In this way the person affected gains valuable minutes.

gewusst: In cardiac arrest, the chance of survival falls markedly with every minute without help.
The Rautek grip is named after the Austrian jiu-jitsu teacher Franz Rautek.

teile.einleitung: A right-handed person is someone who prefers to do most things with the right hand. This applies to the great majority of people. That is why many objects and habits in everyday life are designed for right-handers.
wichtigste: Most people are right-handed.
A right-hander writes with the right hand.
The right hand is controlled mainly by the left half of the brain.
In right-handers the right hand is usually a little stronger.
Even small children often prefer to grasp and draw with one hand.
In Switzerland you usually shake hands with the right hand as a greeting.

abschnitte.text: Our brain has two halves. Interestingly, the **left half of the brain** mainly controls the **right** side of the body, and the right half the left. In right-handers the left half is especially well practised for fine hand movements. That is why writing, drawing or throwing with the right hand works better for them. This hand is usually also a little **stronger**.

Whether a child will be right-handed can often be seen early on. The child mostly **grasps and draws with the right hand**. But the preferred hand is often only quite certain at nursery or school age. A right-hander **writes with the right hand** and also uses it for most other activities. The great majority of people are right-handed, and only about one in ten is left-handed.

Many things in everyday life are designed for right-handers. When you lay the table, the **knife is on the right** of the plate and the fork on the left. The **computer mouse** is usually **to the right** of the keyboard. Scissors, tin openers and fountain pens are also often built for the right hand. In Switzerland you usually shake **hands** with the **right hand** as a greeting.

abschnitte.titel: Right and left are equally good
abschnitte.text: In the past, left-handed children were often forced to write with the right hand. Today we know that this **retraining** can do harm. That is why children are allowed to write with the hand that comes naturally to them. For left-handers there are special scissors and writing tools. A few people can use both hands almost equally well.

gewusst: In many animals too there are preferences for one side, for example in the paws of cats or dogs.
Experts call the preferred hand handedness.

teile.einleitung: In robot-assisted surgery, a robot helps doctors to operate. But the robot does not work alone: a human controls every movement. The technique is used today in many hospitals around the world, including in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The best-known surgical system is the **da Vinci system**, named after Leonardo da Vinci.
The surgeon sits at a **control console** and steers the robot arms with hand controls and pedals.
Most operations are **minimally invasive**: you operate through a few small cuts.
The camera and instruments get into the body through hollow sleeves, the **trocars**.
**Tremor filtering** evens out fine shaking of the hands.
Disadvantages are the high costs and the limited sense of touch.

abschnitte.text: A surgical robot has several **robot arms** to which fine instruments and a camera are attached. The surgeon does not sit directly at the operating table but at a **control console** in the same room. There he looks at an enlarged, three-dimensional image from inside the body. With hand controls and foot pedals he gives the movements. The robot transfers these movements exactly but decides nothing itself.

Most robot-assisted operations are **minimally invasive**. That means: instead of one large cut there are only a few small access points. Through these openings, hollow guide sleeves are inserted, the **trocars**. Through them the camera and instruments are pushed into the abdomen or chest. Small cuts can reduce pain, blood loss and recovery time.

Everyone’s hands tremble a little, even if you hardly notice it. **Tremor filtering** recognises this fine shaking and does not pass it on to the instruments. In addition there is **motion scaling**: large hand movements are reduced. At a ratio of 3 to 1, the instrument tip moves only 1.5 cm when the hand travels 4.5 cm. The small instruments can also be angled in many directions.

In 2001 the famous **“Operation Lindbergh”** took place. The surgeon Jacques Marescaux sat in New York and removed a patient’s gallbladder in Strasbourg. The commands went over a data line across the Atlantic. Such operations are called **telesurgery**. The name recalls the aviator Charles Lindbergh, who was the first to fly alone across the Atlantic.

Surgical robots make very precise work possible in places that are hard to reach. But they are very **expensive** to buy and maintain. There is also often no **haptic feedback**: the surgeon hardly feels how firm or soft the tissue is. So he has to rely heavily on the image. Experts are still studying in which operations the robot really brings advantages.

gewusst: In “Operation Lindbergh”, several thousand kilometres lay between the surgeon and the patient.
A surgical robot can reduce movements so much that very fine stitches become possible.

teile.einleitung: A hinge joint works like the hinge of a door: it can only move open and shut. In the body there are several such joints, for example in the fingers and at the elbow.
wichtigste: A hinge joint moves around only one axis.
It allows bending and straightening.
The middle and end joints of the fingers are hinge joints.
The ankle joint at the foot works like a hinge.
The knee is a pivot hinge joint.
The shoulder joint is not a hinge joint but a ball-and-socket joint.

abschnitte.text: In a hinge joint, a roller-shaped end of bone fits into a hollow of the other bone. This allows only one movement around **one axis**: **bending** and **straightening**. Sideways or turning movements are hardly possible. Strong **ligaments** at the sides keep the joint stable.

In the fingers, the **middle and end joints** are hinge joints. In the elbow, the joint between the **upper arm bone and the ulna** works as a hinge. At the foot, the **ankle joint** moves the foot up and down. The **knee joint** is often called a pivot hinge joint: when the knee is bent, the lower leg can also be turned a little.

Muscles can only pull, not push. That is why every hinge joint needs two opposing muscles: a **flexor** and an **extensor**. At the elbow the biceps bends the arm, and the triceps straightens it again. When one works, the other gives way.

Some hinge joints have a bony stop. When you straighten the elbow fully, the **olecranon** of the ulna bumps against the upper arm bone. This means you cannot bend the arm further backwards. You can feel the olecranon as the point of the elbow.

Not all joints are hinges. The **shoulder joint** and the hip joint are **ball-and-socket joints**: they allow movements in all directions. That is why you can circle your arm, but not your finger. There are also saddle joints, like at the base of the thumb, and pivot joints.

gewusst: You can bend and straighten your finger joints many thousands of times a day without them getting tired.
In the thumb, the joint at the base is a saddle joint, which is why it is so mobile.

teile.einleitung: A cut arises when something sharp slices open the skin, for example a knife or a piece of broken glass. Small cuts you can treat yourself. For deep wounds you need a doctor.
wichtigste: A dirty wound is first rinsed with clean water.
With heavy bleeding, you press a clean cloth firmly on the wound.
Deep, gaping cuts are often stitched or glued.
You always cut away from the body.
Broken glass is cleared away with a brush and dustpan.
The tetanus vaccination is important for dirty wounds.
Plasters and bandages belong in every home first-aid kit.

abschnitte.text: With a small cut, you first wash your own hands. Then you rinse dirt out of the wound with **clean water**. Then you can treat it with a **disinfectant**, which kills germs. Finally a **plaster** or a small bandage goes on. In every **home first-aid kit** there should therefore be plasters, bandaging material and disinfectant.

If a wound bleeds heavily, you press a **clean cloth** or a compress firmly on it. The pressure slows the bleeding. You can hold the injured arm or leg up meanwhile. With heavy bleeding you get help at once. In Switzerland you reach the ambulance service on the emergency number **144**.

If a cut is deep and the edges of the wound stand wide open, it is called a **gaping wound**. Then you should go to the doctor. There the wound is often **stitched**, stapled or closed with a special glue. This way the edges grow together well and a smaller scar remains. A visit to the doctor is also needed if a foreign object is stuck in the wound.

In the soil live bacteria that can cause **tetanus**. They get into the body through dirty wounds. A **vaccination**, which has to be refreshed regularly, protects against this dangerous disease. A wound can also become **inflamed**. Then it turns red, hot and swollen and hurts. In this case you should have it looked at by a doctor.

Many cuts happen in the kitchen or when doing crafts. With a knife you always cut **away from the body** and keep your fingers behind the blade. A sharp knife is often safer than a blunt one, because you have to press less. Broken glass is cleared away with a **brush and dustpan** and not with bare hands. Before throwing shards away, you wrap them in newspaper.

gewusst: The skin can close small cuts again by itself within a few days.
The bacteria that cause tetanus can survive for a long time in the soil as resistant spores.

teile.einleitung: Flat bones are broad, flat bones. They protect important organs such as the brain, heart and lungs and give many muscles a large surface to attach to.
wichtigste: Flat bones are flat and broad.
These include the shoulder blade, breastbone, ribs and the bones of the skull vault.
The skull vault protects the brain.
The frontal bone forms the forehead and the roof of the eye sockets.
Ribs and breastbone form the rib cage together with the spine.
The heel bone is not a flat bone, but a short bone.

abschnitte.text: Bones have different shapes. There are **long bones** such as the thigh bone and **short bones** such as the bones of the ankle and wrist area. These include the **heel bone**. A further group are the **flat bones**. They are **flat** and **broad**. Examples are the shoulder blade, the breastbone, the ribs and the bones of the skull vault.

The curved plates of the **skull vault** form a firm capsule around the delicate **brain**. At the front lies the **frontal bone**. It forms the forehead and also the roof of the eye sockets. At the top at the sides lie the two **parietal bones**. The bones are built of **two firm layers**, between which lies a layer of **spongy bone**. This construction is light and yet stable.

The **shoulder blade** is a triangular flat bone on the back. On its broad surface many shoulder and back muscles attach. They move and steady the **arm**. The **ilium** too has a large, broad **blade**. It forms the upper part of the pelvis. The **iliac crest** can be felt well at the side of the hip.

The **ribs** and the **breastbone** are also flat bones. Together with the thoracic spine they form the **rib cage**. It encloses and protects the **heart** and **lungs**. In breathing the rib cage rises and falls. The ribs are joined to the breastbone by cartilage, which makes the rib cage somewhat flexible.

In many flat bones of the adult there is **red bone marrow**. There new **blood cells** are constantly made. Especially much of it is found in the **breastbone** and the **iliac crest**. That is why doctors sometimes take a sample of bone marrow at these places, to investigate blood diseases.

gewusst: In newborns the skull bones are not yet firmly joined, and between them lie soft places, the fontanelles.
A human being normally has twelve pairs of ribs.

teile.einleitung: Spots (in German Pickel) are small inflammations in the skin. Almost everyone has them at some time, especially often teenagers. Mostly they heal by themselves after a few days.
wichtigste: Spots arise when sebum blocks a pore.
Sebum is a fat that the skin makes itself.
An inflamed spot often contains pus.
Spots arise especially often on the face.
Teenagers have spots especially often.
Squeezing can lead to inflammation and scars.
With very many spots people speak of acne.

abschnitte.text: In the skin there are many small **pores**. Into them open **sebaceous glands**, which make a skin fat of their own, the **sebum**. Sebum protects the skin and keeps it supple. But if the skin makes too much of it, it can **block** a pore together with dead flakes of skin. First a **blackhead** forms. If bacteria are added, the place becomes inflamed, and a spot arises.

An inflamed spot is often red and somewhat swollen. It often has a whitish dot in the middle. This is **pus**. Pus arises when the body fights germs. It consists, among other things, of white blood cells. Most spots disappear by themselves after **a few days**, the body heals them itself.

On the **face** the skin has especially many sebaceous glands. That is why spots often arise there, but also on the back and chest. In **teenagers** the body changes, and the skin makes especially much sebum. That is why many have spots at this age. This is quite normal and no sign of poor care.

It is tempting to squeeze a spot. But in doing so **germs** are pressed deeper into the skin. The inflammation can get worse and leave **scars**. It is better to **wash the skin gently**, morning and evening. This removes excess fat and dirt. Scratching and strong rubbing only irritate the skin.

If someone has very many spots, often on the face and back, this is called **acne**. Acne is a common **skin disease**. A skin doctor, the **dermatologist**, can help well here. There are creams and medicines that calm the skin. Early treatment can prevent scars.

gewusst: Blackheads are often dark on the surface because the sebum becomes darker in the air, not because of dirt.
Acne is among the most common skin diseases of all.

teile.einleitung: Proprioception is the perception of the position and movement of your own body. Thanks to it, you know where your arms and legs are even with your eyes closed. In German it is also called Tiefensensibilität (deep sensitivity).
wichtigste: Proprioception means perceiving the position and movement of your own body.
In German it is also called Tiefensensibilität.
It includes the sense of position, the sense of movement and the sense of force.
Muscle spindles report how far a muscle is stretched.
Golgi tendon organs in the tendons measure how hard a muscle is pulling.
Exercises on a wobbly surface train proprioception.

abschnitte.text: Besides sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, we have other senses. One of them is **proprioception**. It constantly tells the brain how the joints are positioned and how the body is moving. Because the sense organs lie deep in muscles, tendons and joints, it is also called **deep sensitivity**. We hardly notice this sense because it always works in the background.

Proprioception is counted as three partial senses. The **sense of position** tells you how your joints are positioned at the moment, for example whether your arm is bent. The **sense of movement** reports whether and how fast a part of the body is moving. The **sense of force** helps you to judge how much force you need, for example to lift a glass or a heavy bag.

The information comes from special sense organs. **Muscle spindles** lie in the muscle and report how far it is stretched. **Golgi tendon organs** sit in the tendons and measure how hard the muscle is pulling. There are also sensors in the joint capsules. The brain combines all these reports with what the eyes and the sense of balance supply.

A doctor can test proprioception easily: you close your eyes and bring your **index finger to your nose**. If this works well, the sense is working properly. If a leg has “gone to sleep”, the feedback about its position is missing, which is why you stumble easily. After a **ligament injury to the foot**, people often train with exercises on a **wobbly surface**, such as a cushion or a balance board. That way the foot learns again to adjust safely.

gewusst: The term proprioception comes from the Latin “proprius”, which means “own”.
Without proprioception you would have to keep looking at your own feet when walking.

teile.einleitung: Snoring is the loud, humming sound that some people make when breathing in their sleep. It arises when parts in the throat flutter. Often it disturbs mainly the others in the room.
wichtigste: Snoring arises because parts in the throat flutter.
Often the uvula at the back of the mouth flutters too.
Many people snore most when lying on their back.
A blocked nose makes snoring more frequent.
Men snore more often on average.
Animals such as dogs can snore too.

abschnitte.text: In sleep, the muscles in the throat relax. The throat becomes narrower as a result. When the breathing air streams through, soft parts begin to **flutter**, much like a flag in the wind. Especially often the **uvula** at the back of the mouth flutters too, and so does the soft palate.

Lying **on your back**, many people snore most. Then the tongue slips back a little and narrows the throat. A **blocked nose**, for example with a cold, also makes snoring more frequent. Being overweight and alcohol in the evening strengthen it as well.
**Men** snore more often than women on average, and snoring increases with age. Children also snore sometimes, for example with large tonsils. And not only people: **dogs** and cats can snore too.

Usually **the others in the room** notice the snoring, while the snoring person sleeps on. Ordinary snoring is usually harmless. But if pauses in breathing and great tiredness by day are added, **sleep apnoea** may be behind it. Then you should seek medical advice.

gewusst: Snoring can become so loud that you can hear it in the next room.
Often it helps just to sleep on your side.

teile.einleitung: The resting pulse shows how often the heart beats in one minute when you are completely calm. It tells you something about how fit you are. You can easily measure it yourself.
wichtigste: The **resting pulse** is the pulse when you are completely calm.
It is best measured **in the morning after waking up**.
In healthy adults it is about **60 to 80 beats per minute**.
**Babies** usually have the fastest resting pulse.
Well-trained athletes often have a low resting pulse because their heart pumps more blood with each beat.
A **mouse** has a much faster pulse, an **elephant** a slower one than humans.

abschnitte.text: With every heartbeat, the heart pumps blood into the vessels. You can feel this pressure wave in some places, for example at the **wrist** or at the side of the **neck**. This is the **pulse**. It says how often the heart beats per minute. The **resting pulse** is the pulse when you are not exerting yourself and are completely calm.

It is best to measure the resting pulse **in the morning after waking up**, before you get up. You lay two fingers on your wrist and count the beats for 15 seconds. You multiply the number by 4 and get the beats per minute. Just before measuring, you should not **run around**, because exercise makes the pulse faster. Excitement can also raise it.

In healthy adults the resting pulse is about **60 to 80 beats per minute**. Children have a faster pulse than adults. The heart beats fastest in **babies**, often over 100 times a minute. As you grow, the heart becomes bigger and stronger. Then it has to beat less often.

The heart is a muscle and becomes stronger through endurance sport. A trained heart **pumps more blood with every beat**. That is why it has to beat less often to supply the body. Well-trained endurance athletes therefore often have a very low resting pulse. If you do sport regularly, you can sometimes see your resting pulse slowly falling.

In animals the rule is often: the smaller the animal, the faster the heart beats. A **mouse** has a much faster pulse than a human, several hundred beats per minute. An **elephant**, on the other hand, has a slower resting pulse than we do. Small animals lose heat faster and therefore need a fast metabolism.

gewusst: An adult’s heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
Many sports watches measure the pulse with light directly at the wrist.

teile.einleitung: The prefrontal cortex is the front part of the cerebral cortex, right behind the forehead. It helps us to plan, make decisions and control impulses. It is one of the areas of the brain that take the longest to mature.
wichtigste: The prefrontal cortex lies in the frontal lobe, behind the forehead.
It is important for planning, deciding and controlling impulses.
Working memory depends heavily on it.
According to what we know today, it matures until about the mid-twenties.
The messenger substance dopamine is especially important for it.
The case of Phineas Gage showed in 1848 how important this area is for personality.

abschnitte.text: The cerebrum is divided into lobes. At the very front lies the **frontal lobe**, and its foremost part is the **prefrontal cortex**. The word cortex means bark or rind. One part of it lies directly above the eye sockets and is called the **orbitofrontal cortex**. It helps to judge whether something is worth it, for example a reward.

The prefrontal cortex is often described as a control centre. It helps with **planning**, **deciding** and **impulse control**. If you sit down to do your homework even though you would rather play games, it is working especially hard. **Working memory** also depends heavily on it. It lets you keep information ready for a short time, such as a telephone number while you type it in.

The brain does not develop all at once. The prefrontal cortex is one of the areas that take the longest. According to what we know today, it is fully mature only at **about the mid-twenties**. This partly explains why teenagers sometimes act more spontaneously and judge risks differently from adults. Over time, the connections in this area get better and better.

Nerve cells pass on signals using messenger substances. For the prefrontal cortex, **dopamine** is especially important. It influences attention and motivation. In **ADHD**, medicines such as **methylphenidate** are used, which strengthen the effect of dopamine. They can help people to concentrate better.

In 1848 the American railway worker **Phineas Gage** had an accident: an iron rod went through the front of his brain. He survived, but his personality changed greatly. The case showed how important this part of the brain is. Later the Portuguese doctor **Egas Moniz** developed the **prefrontal leucotomy**, an operation on the frontal brain, and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1949. The operation often had serious consequences and is seen today as a wrong path.

gewusst: The skull of Phineas Gage and the iron rod are still kept today in a museum of Harvard University.
In humans the frontal lobe is larger in proportion to the brain than in most other animals.

teile.einleitung: The sarcomere is the smallest unit that can contract in a muscle. Thousands of sarcomeres lie one behind the other in a muscle fibre. When they all shorten at the same time, the muscle moves.
wichtigste: A sarcomere is bounded at both ends by **Z discs**.
The light **I band** contains only thin actin filaments.
In the **H zone** there are only myosin filaments with no overlap with actin.
The **A band** stays the same length during contraction.
A resting sarcomere is about **2 to 3 micrometres** long.
**Titin** is regarded as the largest known protein in humans.

abschnitte.text: A sarcomere is bounded at both ends by a **Z disc**. Thin threads of **actin** are attached to the Z discs. In the middle lie thicker threads of **myosin**. They are anchored at the **M line** in the middle of the sarcomere. Actin and myosin filaments interlock like the fingers of two hands. A resting sarcomere is only about **2 to 3 micrometres** long.

Under the microscope the sarcomere shows different regions. The **A band** is dark. It corresponds to the length of the myosin filaments. The **I band** is light, because here lie only the thin **actin filaments**. In the middle of the A band lies the **H zone**. There is only **myosin** there, with no overlap with actin. Because the sarcomeres lie next to each other so regularly, skeletal muscle looks **striated**.

During contraction, the heads of the myosin filaments pull the actin filaments towards the middle. For this they need energy from **ATP** and a signal from **calcium**. The filaments themselves do not become shorter in the process, they only slide past each other. This is called the **sliding filament model**. The Z discs move closer together, and the I band and H zone become narrower. The **A band**, on the other hand, stays **the same length**.

In the sarcomere there is one more special protein: **titin**. It reaches from the Z disc to the M line and acts like an elastic spring. Titin holds the myosin in the middle and makes sure that the muscle springs back after being stretched. It is regarded as the **largest known protein in humans**.

How much force a muscle can produce depends on the length of the sarcomeres. The greatest force arises at **medium length with optimal overlap**. Then especially many myosin heads can pull on the actin. If the muscle is stretched a lot, the filaments overlap too little. If it is greatly shortened, the filaments bump into each other. In both cases the force falls.

gewusst: In a single muscle fibre, thousands of sarcomeres can lie one behind the other.
The heart muscle is also striated and consists of sarcomeres.

teile.einleitung: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a fine network of tubes and chambers in every muscle fibre. It stores calcium and releases it when the muscle is meant to contract. Afterwards it pumps the calcium back, and the muscle relaxes.
wichtigste: Its main job is to **store and release calcium**.
The calcium is released through the **ryanodine receptor**.
The pump **SERCA** carries calcium back using ATP.
Inside, the protein **calsequestrin** binds the calcium.
One T tubule and two cisternae together form a **triad**.
A mutation in the ryanodine receptor RYR1 can trigger **malignant hyperthermia**.

abschnitte.titel: A network in the muscle fibre
abschnitte.text: The word **sarcoplasm** means the inside of a muscle fibre. **Reticulum** means “little net”. The sarcoplasmic reticulum is therefore a network of membrane tubes that wraps around the myofibrils. In some places it is widened into larger chambers, the **cisternae**. There the **calcium** is stored. Inside, the protein **calsequestrin** binds a lot of calcium so that there is enough in reserve.

A nerve signal triggers an **action potential** at the muscle membrane. It runs deep into the fibre along tube-shaped infoldings, the **T tubules**. A T tubule and two adjoining cisternae together form a **triad**. The whole process in which the electrical signal becomes a contraction is called **excitation-contraction coupling**.

In the T tubule sits the **dihydropyridine receptor**. It acts as a **voltage sensor**. When the voltage changes, it moves and mechanically opens the calcium channel of the reticulum, the **ryanodine receptor**. Now calcium streams into the cytosol. It binds to proteins of the muscle filaments and so gives the starting signal for contraction. In a resting fibre, by contrast, the free calcium concentration is very low, only about **100 nanomoles per litre**.

For the muscle to relax again, the calcium has to go back into the reticulum. This work is done by the pump **SERCA**. It needs energy from **ATP** for this. As soon as the calcium concentration in the cytosol is low again, the filaments release each other. The muscle goes slack and is ready for the next contraction.

In some people the ryanodine receptor **RYR1** is altered by a **mutation**. If they are given certain anaesthetics, too much calcium can stream out. The muscles then work uncontrollably, and body temperature rises sharply. This dangerous anaesthetic complication is called **malignant hyperthermia**. Anaesthetists therefore ask before operations about such cases in the family and keep an antidote ready.

gewusst: The ryanodine receptor is named after the plant substance ryanodine, which binds to it.
At rest, much more calcium is dissolved in the sarcoplasmic reticulum than in the cytosol of the muscle fibre.

teile.einleitung: Each hand has five fingers, and each has its own name. The fourth finger, counted from the thumb, is called the **ring finger**. It has its name because many people wear a ring on it.
wichtigste: The ring finger lies between the middle finger and the little finger.
Many married people wear their wedding ring on the ring finger.
The ring finger is the hardest to move completely on its own.
In many people it is about the same length as the index finger.

abschnitte.text: The **ring finger** is the fourth finger when you begin counting at the thumb. It lies between the **middle finger** and the **little finger**. Many married people wear their **wedding ring** on it. Depending on the country and custom, it is worn on the left or on the right hand. The finger has its name from this custom.

abschnitte.titel: Hard to move on its own
abschnitte.text: Try it out: the ring finger is **the hardest to move completely on its own**. This is because its tendons are linked to those of the neighbouring fingers. In addition, the same muscles control several fingers at once. When you raise the ring finger, the middle finger or little finger often moves along with it. Musicians therefore practise for a long time until every finger works independently.

In most people the middle finger is the longest finger. In many people the ring finger is **about the same length as the index finger**. In some it is a little longer, in others a little shorter. Like every finger except the thumb, it has three finger bones. These bones are called phalanges.

gewusst: In ancient Rome people believed that a special vein led from the ring finger straight to the heart.
The thumb is the only finger with just two finger bones.

teile.einleitung: After training, the body needs time to recover. This recovery phase is called **regeneration**. It is only during this time that the body really becomes stronger and more capable.
wichtigste: Regeneration is the recovery of the body after strain.
In active regeneration you move gently, for example by easy cycling.
Sauna, massage and sleep count as passive regeneration.
Gentle cooling down helps to break down lactate faster.
Carbohydrates refill the glycogen stores in the muscles.
Muscle soreness is usually strongest one to three days after training.

abschnitte.text: There are two kinds of recovery. In **active regeneration** you move gently, for example by easy cycling, walking or calm swimming. The strain is so low that the body does not tire. In **passive regeneration** the body rests, for example when sleeping, in the sauna or during a massage. The two forms complement each other well.

With very intense strain, more **lactate** is formed in the muscles, a substance from the breakdown of sugar without enough oxygen. Many athletes jog gently for a few more minutes after a race. The light movement keeps the blood flow high, and so lactate is broken down faster than in complete rest. Even after the strain has ended, you go on breathing faster for a while. This increased oxygen uptake is called **EPOC**.

When you sweat, the body loses water and **electrolytes**, above all sodium, which is a component of table salt. After a lot of sweating, a drink with a little salt therefore helps. In the muscles, energy is stored as **glycogen**, a storage form of glucose. After training, **carbohydrates** such as bread, rice or pasta refill these stores. A little protein also supports the repair of the muscles.

**Muscle soreness** is caused by tiny injuries in the muscle fibres. It occurs especially easily with braking, so-called **eccentric** work, in which the muscle gets longer under tension, for example when running downhill. The pain comes with a delay and is usually strongest 24 to 72 hours after the strain. In English it is therefore called DOMS, which means delayed onset muscle soreness. After a few days it disappears by itself.

Some athletes step into an ice bath after training. This **cold water immersion** makes the blood vessels narrower and can dull pain. Whether it helps the body in the long term is disputed among experts. Undisputedly important, on the other hand, is enough **sleep**. In sleep the whole body recovers especially well.

gewusst: A muscle does not become stronger during training but in the recovery time afterwards.
If you train too much and recover too little, you can even become weaker in time.

teile.einleitung: We swallow many hundreds of times a day, mostly without thinking about it. In doing so, the tongue, throat and larynx work together exactly, so that food gets into the gullet and not into the windpipe.
wichtigste: The tongue pushes the mouthful backwards into the throat.
When swallowing you cannot breathe in at the same time.
If food gets into the windpipe, you choke and cough.
You also swallow without food, saliva all day long.
When swallowing, the larynx hops up at the neck.

abschnitte.text: First the food is chewed and mixed with **saliva**. Then the **tongue** pushes the mouthful backwards into the throat. From there everything runs automatically: muscles push the mouthful into the **gullet** and on to the stomach. If a mouthful is very dry, **a sip of water** helps.

In the throat, the food route and the air route cross. When swallowing, the **larynx** rises, and the **epiglottis** closes off the windpipe. That is why you **cannot swallow and breathe in at the same time**. You can see the raising of the larynx at the neck: it hops briefly upwards.

If something does get into the windpipe, you say you have **choked**. The body reacts at once with **coughing**. This carries the food out again. That is why you should not laugh loudly or run around while eating.

Small children like to put everything in their mouth. Small, round things such as **marbles**, buttons or coins can be swallowed or breathed in by them. Such objects should therefore be kept out of reach.
Even without eating, you swallow **saliva all day long**. The mouth constantly makes new saliva, which protects the teeth and keeps the mouth moist. In sleep you swallow clearly less often.

gewusst: A person swallows about 1000 to 2000 times a day.
The gullet pushes food so strongly that you can even swallow standing on your head.

teile.einleitung: Sleep architecture describes how sleep is built up in a night: which sleep stages there are, in which order they come and how long they last. It is measured in the sleep laboratory with the EEG.
wichtigste: A distinction is made between non-REM sleep and REM sleep.
Today non-REM sleep is divided into 3 stages.
In the falling-asleep stage N1, theta waves dominate.
In REM sleep, sawtooth waves appear.
The REM latency is the time from falling asleep to the first REM phase.
Sleep efficiency is the share of time in bed in which you are really asleep.

abschnitte.text: Sleep consists of **non-REM sleep** and **REM sleep**. REM means “rapid eye movement”. The division in use today, from the **American Academy of Sleep Medicine**, has **three** non-REM stages: N1, N2 and N3. The older division by **Rechtschaffen and Kales** from 1968 still distinguished four non-REM stages.

The **EEG** records the brain’s electrical activity. In the falling-asleep stage **N1**, **theta waves** dominate. In stage N2, **K complexes** and sleep spindles appear. A K complex can be triggered, for example, by a **noise**. In REM sleep you see typical **sawtooth waves**.

The **REM latency** is the time from falling asleep to the start of the first REM phase. **WASO** stands for “wake after sleep onset”, that is, the time awake after first falling asleep. Such values help specialists to recognise sleep disorders.

The **sleep efficiency** says what percentage of the time in bed you are actually asleep. If someone lies in bed for 8 hours and sleeps 6 hours, you work out 6 divided by 8. That gives **75 per cent**. In healthy sleep the value is usually clearly higher.

Straight after waking up, you are often still groggy and less able to perform. This is called **sleep inertia**. It is stronger if you are woken from deep sleep, and usually passes after a few minutes.

gewusst: Over the course of the night, the REM phases become longer and deep sleep shorter.
The display of the stages over the night is called a hypnogram.

teile.einleitung: **Retroviruses** are special viruses that build their genetic material into the genetic material of the infected cell. To do so they take an unusual route: they rewrite RNA into DNA. The best-known retrovirus is HIV.
wichtigste: Retroviruses carry single-stranded RNA in the virus particle.
The enzyme reverse transcriptase rewrites this RNA into DNA.
Integrase builds the virus DNA into the genetic material of the host cell.
The built-in virus DNA is called a **provirus**.
HIV is the best-known retrovirus that makes humans ill.
About 8 per cent of human genetic material consists of remains of old retroviruses.

abschnitte.text: In cells, genetic information is normally copied from **DNA** into **RNA**. Retroviruses do it the other way round, hence the name: “retro” is Latin and means backwards. Their genetic material consists of **single-stranded RNA**. In the host cell, the enzyme **reverse transcriptase** rewrites this RNA into DNA. An enzyme is a protein that carries out chemical processes.

The newly formed virus DNA travels into the cell nucleus. There the enzyme **integrase** builds it into the genetic material of the host cell. The built-in virus DNA is called a **provirus**. The cell now reads it like its own genes and makes new viruses. Because the provirus is firmly lodged in the genetic material, it is very hard to get rid of a retrovirus completely.

The best-known retrovirus that makes humans ill is **HIV**, the human immunodeficiency virus. It infects mainly the **T helper cells**, important cells of the immune system. Over time more and more of these cells are lost, and the defences become weaker. Without treatment this can lead to the disease **AIDS**. Today there are medicines that suppress the virus strongly, and many of them inhibit precisely the reverse transcriptase.

Reverse transcriptase was discovered in **1970**. Two researchers found it independently of each other: **Howard Temin** and **David Baltimore**. Before that people thought that genetic information always flows only from DNA to RNA. For their discovery the two received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1975, together with Renato Dulbecco. Today reverse transcriptase is also an important tool in research laboratories.

In the course of evolution, retroviruses have left traces in the genetic material again and again. Such remains are called **endogenous retroviruses**. About **8 per cent** of human genetic material consists of them. Most of them have long been broken and can no longer make viruses. Some of these old virus genes even do useful jobs in the body today.

gewusst: The human genetic material contains more remains of old viruses than genes that carry the instructions for proteins.
Retroviruses also exist in animals such as cats, chickens and mice.

teile.einleitung: The pleura, in German Brustfell, is a thin, smooth membrane that wraps the lung and lines the rib cage from inside. Thanks to it the lung can glide without friction in the rib cage when breathing. It also makes sure that the lung expands with the rib cage when breathing in.
wichtigste: The pleura is a thin membrane that wraps the lung.
In German it is called Brustfell.
It consists of two layers: the visceral pleura (Lungenfell) and the parietal pleura (Rippenfell).
Between them lies a narrow gap with a little fluid.
The fluid lets the lung glide when breathing.
Through negative pressure in the gap the lung follows the movements of the rib cage.
An inflammation of the pleura is called pleurisy.

abschnitte.text: The **pleura** is a very thin, smooth membrane in the rib cage. The word comes from Greek and means side or rib. In German it is called **Brustfell**. Each half of the lung has its own pleura, so that the right and left lungs are protected separately.

The pleura consists of two layers. The **visceral pleura** (Lungenfell) lies directly on the lung. The **parietal pleura** (Rippenfell) lines the inside of the rib cage and the diaphragm. Between the two lies a wafer-thin gap, the pleural space.

In the pleural space there are only a few millilitres of fluid. It acts like a lubricant, so that the lung glides without friction with every breath. In addition the two layers stick to each other because of it, rather like two wet panes of glass. When the rib cage rises on breathing in, the lung is therefore pulled along and fills with air.

If air gets into the pleural space, for example through an injury or a burst air sac, the lung collapses. This is called a **pneumothorax**. People affected have sudden chest pain and shortness of breath. In hospital the air is often sucked off with a tube.

An inflammation of the pleura is called **pleurisy**. It causes stabbing pains on breathing, because the irritated layers rub against each other. Sometimes too much fluid collects in the gap, a pleural effusion. Then the fluid presses on the lung and breathing becomes hard.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin skin or layer in the body.
The narrow space between the visceral and parietal pleura.
The collapse of the lung when air gets into the pleural space.
An inflammation of the pleura.

gewusst: The lung itself has no muscles, it is moved only by the diaphragm and the rib cage.
The parietal pleura is very sensitive to pain, the visceral pleura hardly at all.
Without the adhesion in the pleural space the elastic lung would contract like a balloon let go.

teile.einleitung: The shoulder joint connects the upper arm to the shoulder blade. It is the most mobile joint in the body. But for that reason it is also less stable than other joints.
wichtigste: The round head of the upper arm bone sits in the socket of the shoulder blade.
The socket is small and shallow, which is why the shoulder is so mobile.
Mainly muscles and tendons hold the upper arm bone in place.
Of all the large joints, the shoulder joint most often jumps out of its socket.
Then it is said that the shoulder is dislocated.
The deltoid muscle lies like a cap over the shoulder.
With arm circles you warm up the shoulders well.

abschnitte.text: The shoulder joint is a **ball-and-socket joint**. The round head of the **upper arm bone** lies in a **socket** formed by the **shoulder blade**. The socket is **small and shallow**, roughly like a plate under a ball. That is why the upper arm can turn and circle in almost all directions. When you put your hand up at school, you are moving mainly this joint.

Because the socket is so shallow, the joint needs a lot of support from outside. This is given mainly by **muscles and tendons**. An important group is the **rotator cuff**, which pulls the head of the upper arm into the socket. Over the shoulder lies the triangular **deltoid muscle** like a cap. It raises the arm sideways and gives the shoulder its round shape.

The great mobility has a disadvantage: of all the large joints, the shoulder joint **jumps out of its socket most often**. Then it is said that the shoulder is **dislocated**, the technical term being luxation. This often happens in falls, for example when skiing or cycling. A dislocated shoulder hurts a great deal, and the arm can hardly be moved. A doctor has to put the bone back in.

Before sport you should **warm up** the shoulders, for example with **arm circles** forwards and backwards. Strong muscles protect the joint. Swimming, climbing and gymnastics train the shoulder well. Anyone who sits at a screen a lot should now and then let the shoulders circle loosely and sit upright.

gewusst: With the shoulder joint you can move the arm in an almost complete circle.
After a dislocated shoulder, in some people the joint jumps out again more easily later.

teile.einleitung: Penicillin was the first antibiotic that was used in large amounts as a medicine. It works against many bacteria and since the 1940s has saved the lives of countless people.
wichtigste: Alexander Fleming discovered in 1928 the effect of a mould on bacteria.
Howard Florey and Ernst Chain made penicillin into a medicine around 1940.
All three received the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 1945.
Penicillin inhibits the building of the cell wall of bacteria.
Decisive for the effect is the beta-lactam ring in the molecule.
The best-known side effect is an allergic reaction.
Today penicillin is made mainly with the fungus Penicillium chrysogenum.

abschnitte.text: In 1928 the Scottish researcher **Alexander Fleming** noticed something strange in London. On a dish with bacteria a **mould** had grown. Around the mould no more bacteria were growing. Fleming called the substance that the mould gave off **penicillin**. He could not yet obtain it in pure form.

Around 1940 **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Chain** in Oxford succeeded in purifying penicillin. They showed that it can cure sick animals and people. During the Second World War its production was greatly expanded. Fleming, Florey and Chain received together in 1945 the **Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine**. Today penicillin comes mainly from high-yield strains of **Penicillium chrysogenum**.

Many bacteria have a firm **cell wall**. Penicillin inhibits enzymes that build and strengthen this wall. Growing bacteria thereby become unstable and burst. Important here is the **beta-lactam ring**, a small, strained ring in the molecule. Penicillin G works mainly against **Gram-positive bacteria**, which have a thick, easily reached cell wall.

**Penicillin G** is destroyed by stomach acid and is therefore mostly injected. **Penicillin V** is more stable to acid and can be swallowed as a tablet. **Amoxicillin** works against more kinds of bacteria and is often prescribed, for example, for a middle ear infection. Antibiotics work only against bacteria, not against viruses such as cold viruses.

Some people react **allergically** to penicillin. This ranges from a skin rash to a dangerous shock reaction. That is why the doctor asks about allergies before treatment. A further problem is **resistance**: some bacteria make enzymes that destroy the beta-lactam ring. That is why you should take antibiotics only when they are needed, and exactly as directed.

gewusst: Fleming’s discovery is regarded as one of the most important chance discoveries in medicine.
The cephalosporins, another group of antibiotics, also have a beta-lactam ring.

teile.einleitung: The skull is the bony framework of the head. It protects the brain from knocks and gives the face its shape. It consists of many bones that are firmly fused together.
wichtigste: The skull protects the brain from knocks.
It consists of the cranium and the facial skeleton.
An adult’s skull consists of more than 20 bones.
The bones are joined by firm sutures.
Only the lower jaw is movable.
Babies have soft spots, the fontanelles.
A helmet protects the skull additionally.

abschnitte.text: The skull consists of two parts. The **cranium** encloses the brain like a hard capsule. The **facial skeleton** forms the forehead, eye sockets, nose, cheeks and jaws. Together there are about 22 bones in an adult, not counting the tiny ossicles of the ear.

Most skull bones are joined firmly to each other by jagged connections, the **cranial sutures**. They look like jigsaw pieces that interlock. The only movable bone is the **lower jaw**. Without it we could neither chew nor speak.

In newborns the skull bones are not yet firmly fused. In between lie soft spots, the **fontanelles**. This allows the head to change shape a little during birth, and the brain has room to grow. The large fontanelle usually closes by the age of about two years.

The skull protects the delicate brain from knocks. In addition, the meninges and a fluid cushion the brain. With a violent blow, a **concussion** can still happen. That is why a helmet is so important when cycling, skiing or skating.

The skull has many openings for eyes, nose, ears and nerves. The spinal cord leaves through the large foramen magnum. Researchers can read a lot from skulls, for example a person’s age or what our ancestors looked like. Famous finds of early humans are often skulls.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the skull that encloses the brain.
The bones that shape the face.
A firm connection between two skull bones.
A soft spot on a baby’s head.

gewusst: At birth, a baby has more separate bone parts in the skull than an adult, because some grow together later.
The lower jaw is the largest and strongest bone of the face.
The brain itself feels no pain, so the protection by the skull is all the more important.

teile.einleitung: **Robert Koch** was a German doctor and one of the founders of bacteriology, the study of bacteria. He showed that tiny living things cause serious diseases. His discoveries have helped millions of people.
wichtigste: Robert Koch came from Germany and lived from 1843 to 1910.
A microscope, a present from his wife, made it possible for him to begin his research.
In 1876 he proved that the agent of anthrax is the cause of a disease.
On 24 March 1882 he presented the agent of tuberculosis, which World Tuberculosis Day commemorates.
In 1883 and 1884 he found the agent of cholera.
In 1905 he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

abschnitte.titel: A country doctor with a microscope
abschnitte.text: Robert Koch was born in **1843** in Clausthal in the Harz mountains, so he came from **Germany**. At first he worked as a country doctor. His wife Emmy gave him a **microscope**. With it he began to do research alongside his work. In a small room in his home he examined disease-causing agents.

In **1876** Koch proved that a bacterium causes **anthrax**, a disease mainly of cattle and sheep. For the first time, an agent had thus been proved to be the cause of a disease. He became famous through the discovery of the agent of **tuberculosis**. He presented this in Berlin on **24 March 1882**. Every year **World Tuberculosis Day** commemorates this.

In **1883 and 1884** Koch travelled to **Egypt** and **India**. There he searched for the agent of **cholera**, a severe diarrhoeal disease. He found the bacterium and showed that it spreads through polluted water. This finding helped to prevent many illnesses with clean drinking water. In **1905** Koch received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine** for his research on tuberculosis.

Koch set up rules with which you can test whether an agent causes a disease. They are called **Koch’s postulates**. The agent must be found in the sick. It must be possible to grow it pure outside the body. And the cultured agent must cause the same disease again.

Important aids were invented in Koch’s laboratory. His assistant **Julius Richard Petri** invented the flat glass dish for bacterial cultures, the **Petri dish**. It is still used today in laboratories all over the world. In Berlin the national health institute is named after him, the **Robert Koch Institute**. Koch died in **1910** in Baden-Baden.

gewusst: The Petri dish is today usually made of plastic and used only once.
Koch stained bacteria with dyes so that they could be seen better under the microscope.

teile.einleitung: Long bones are long bones with a hollow shaft, rather like a tube. They include, for example, the thigh bone and the shinbone. Their construction makes them light and yet very stable.
wichtigste: A typical long bone is the **shinbone**.
The shaft is called the **diaphysis** in technical language.
The thickened ends are called **epiphyses**.
Inside the shaft lies the **medullary cavity**.
On the outside is the hard **compact bone**, in the ends the spongy **cancellous bone**.
The **finger bones** count as short long bones.

abschnitte.text: Long bones are found mainly in the arms and legs. Examples are the **thigh bone**, the **shinbone**, the **upper arm bone** and the bones of the forearm. The thigh bone is the longest bone of the human body. In the hands and feet there are also small long bones, for example the **finger bones** and the metacarpal bones. They are called **short long bones**.

A long bone has a long middle part, the **shaft**. In technical language it is called the **diaphysis**. On both sides lie the thickened ends, the **epiphyses**. Together with other bones they form the **joints** and are covered with smooth cartilage. In children and teenagers, a **growth plate** lies between the shaft and the end. That is where the bone grows in length.

The outer layer of the bone is very dense and hard. It is called the **compact bone**. In the shaft it is especially thick. In the ends, on the other hand, there is a spongy tissue of many fine bony struts, the **cancellous bone**. The struts are arranged so that they take up forces well. On the outside, a thin **periosteum** surrounds the bone.

Inside the shaft there is a hollow space, the **medullary cavity**. It is filled with **bone marrow**. In children it is often still red, blood-forming bone marrow. In adults, the medullary cavity of the long bones usually contains yellow bone marrow, which consists mainly of fat.

Being built as a **hollow tube** has a great advantage: the bone is **light and yet resistant to bending**. A hollow tube is almost as stable as a solid rod but much lighter. Engineers also use this principle, for example in bicycle frames or scaffolding. In this way we can move quickly without carrying too much weight.

gewusst: Bird bones are also hollow and so especially light, which helps in flying.
The thigh bone makes up about a quarter of body height.

teile.einleitung: A stroke is an emergency in which a part of the brain gets too little blood. In Switzerland it is mostly called a “Hirnschlag”. The faster help is given, the better the chances.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the stroke is mostly called a “Hirnschlag”.
Most strokes arise from a blocked vessel.
If a vessel in the brain bursts, it is called a haemorrhagic stroke.
In the FAST test, T stands for the time until the emergency call.
Thrombolysis is usually possible up to about 4.5 hours.
Atrial fibrillation is a common cause of blood clots.

abschnitte.text: The brain constantly needs oxygen from the blood. In a **stroke**, a part of it is no longer supplied properly, and nerve cells die. Most strokes arise from a **blocked vessel**, and they are called **ischaemic**. More rarely **a vessel in the brain bursts**, which is a **haemorrhagic stroke**.

With the **FAST test** you recognise a stroke. **F** stands for Face: does a corner of the mouth droop? **A** stands for Arms: can you raise both arms? **S** stands for Speech: is the speech slurred? **T** stands for Time, the **time until the emergency call**. In Switzerland you dial **144** immediately.

In an ischaemic stroke, the blood clot can be dissolved with medicines. This is called **thrombolysis** and is usually possible up to about **4.5 hours** after the symptoms begin. In **mechanical thrombectomy**, the clot is pulled out of the vessel with a thin **catheter**. In Switzerland there are specialised centres for this, the **stroke units**.

One risk is **high blood pressure**. A common cause of clots is the heart rhythm disorder **atrial fibrillation**. Here the atria beat irregularly, and clots can form in the heart. These are carried to the brain. Smoking and lack of exercise also raise the risk.

A **transient ischaemic attack**, **TIA** for short, is a brief stroke whose symptoms quickly disappear again. It is an important warning sign. Even then you must go to hospital immediately, because a real stroke can soon follow.

gewusst: In a stroke the saying is “time is brain”, every minute counts.
Young people and even children can rarely suffer a stroke too.

teile.einleitung: The quadriceps is the large muscle at the front of the thigh. It is one of the strongest muscles in the body. Without it we could neither stand up nor climb stairs or jump.
wichtigste: The quadriceps lies at the front of the thigh.
It has four heads, hence its name.
Its main job is to straighten the knee.
The kneecap is embedded in its tendon.
The rectus femoris also spans the hip joint.
Its opposing muscle is the muscle group at the back of the thigh.

abschnitte.text: The name **quadriceps** comes from Latin and means “four-headed”. The muscle really does consist of **four heads**, that is, four partial muscles. They lie **at the front of the thigh** and join at the bottom into one shared, strong tendon. This tendon runs over the knee and attaches to the shinbone. The quadriceps is one of the largest muscles of the human body.

The **main job** of the quadriceps is to **straighten the knee**. You need this when standing up, walking, running and jumping. It works especially hard when **climbing stairs**, cycling and in a knee bend. One of its heads, the **rectus femoris**, also spans the **hip joint**. That is why it also helps to lift the leg forwards at the hip.

A special bone is embedded in the tendon of the quadriceps: the **kneecap**. It acts like a pulley. This allows the muscle to pull on the knee with more leverage. The kneecap also protects the knee joint from the front. Below the kneecap, the tendon continues to the shinbone.

Muscles often work in pairs. The opposing muscle of the quadriceps is the **muscle group at the back of the thigh**, which bends the knee. Doctors test the quadriceps with a well-known test: a light tap with a small hammer on the tendon **below the kneecap** triggers a reflex. The **lower leg shoots forwards**. This shows whether nerves and muscle work well together.

gewusst: The quadriceps is the muscle that is often especially strongly developed in footballers and cyclists.
The kneecap is the largest sesamoid bone of the human body, which is what bones lying inside a tendon are called.

teile.einleitung: The **emergency blanket** is a thin, shiny foil that belongs in every first aid kit. It is folded up tiny but can cover an injured person completely. In this way it protects them from the cold.
wichtigste: An emergency blanket is usually gold on one side and silver on the other.
It consists of a very thin plastic foil.
It protects injured people above all from the cold.
You find it in the first aid kit, also in the car.
Because it is light and small, it belongs in the rucksack on mountain hikes.
Rescuers can see the shiny blanket from far away.

abschnitte.text: An emergency blanket is usually **gold** on one side and **silver** on the other. It consists of a **very thin plastic foil** coated with a wafer-thin layer of metal, mostly aluminium. The foil is thinner than a sheet of paper. Folded up, it fits into a trouser pocket. Spread out, though, it is about as big as a duvet.

An injured person cools down quickly, especially if they lie still. The emergency blanket **protects against the cold**. It reflects body heat back and keeps out wind and rain. You **cover the injured person with it** and wrap it as closely as possible around the body. It is also important that the injured person does not lie directly on the cold ground.

The emergency blanket is in every **first aid kit**, for example in the car first aid kit, at school or in the sports club. Because it is **light and small**, it also belongs in the rucksack on every **mountain hike**. In the mountains the weather can change quickly. If you are injured and have to wait for help, you will be glad of the protection.

The shiny foil helps in another way too. It reflects light and so is **visible from far away**. This makes it easier for rescuers to find an injured person, for example from a helicopter. In Switzerland, after an accident in the mountains, you call Rega on the number **1414**. In any emergency, though, the first rule is: stay calm and get help.

gewusst: The foil of the emergency blanket was originally developed for space travel.
An emergency blanket weighs only about as much as a letter, around 50 grams.

teile.einleitung: Rega is the Swiss Air Rescue. With its red and white helicopters it helps people in need, especially in the mountains. In Switzerland you can alert it on the number 1414.
wichtigste: Rega stands for the Swiss Air Rescue service (Rettungsflugwacht).
You alert Rega on the telephone number 1414.
Rega was founded in 1952.
It mostly comes by helicopter, especially often in the mountains.
Its helicopters are red and white.
On a mission a doctor goes along.
Supporters back Rega with an annual contribution.

abschnitte.text: **Rega**, the **Swiss Air Rescue**, rescues people from the air. Mostly it comes by **helicopter**. This matters above all where an ambulance cannot get to, or only slowly. It helps especially often **in the mountains**, for example after accidents while hiking, climbing or skiing. But it also flies patients quickly to a hospital, for example after serious road accidents.

In Switzerland you alert Rega on the number **1414**. On the telephone you say who you are, where you are and what has happened. The operations centre then decides what help is needed. On a mission a **doctor** goes along, together with a pilot and a paramedic. This means that treatment can begin at the scene of the accident. It is worth knowing the number 1414 by heart.

Rega’s helicopters are **red and white**, like the Swiss flag. This means you can recognise them from far away. Rega has bases spread across the whole of Switzerland so that a helicopter can be anywhere as quickly as possible. For flights at night the crews use **night vision goggles**. With these they can see obstacles such as cables or rocks even in the dark. With its own aircraft, the ambulance jets, Rega also brings sick or injured people back from abroad.

Rega was founded in **1952**. Since then it has rescued many thousands of people. At the beginning it also flew with small aeroplanes and dropped rescuers by parachute. Soon the helicopter became the most important means of rescue in the mountains. Today Rega is a **charitable foundation**.

To a large extent Rega is supported by **patrons**. These are people who pay it an **annual contribution** every year. Millions of people in Switzerland take part, often whole families. Thanks to this support, Rega can be ready around the clock. Under certain conditions, patrons have the costs of a mission waived.

gewusst: Rega is ready for action around the clock on every day of the year.
More than a third of the people in Switzerland support Rega as patrons.

teile.einleitung: Pain is unpleasant but very useful: it warns us of danger and shows that something in the body is not right. Nerves report pain to the brain, where we then feel it.
wichtigste: Pain warns the body of danger.
On a scale from 0 to 10, 0 means no pain at all.
Painkillers ease pain.
After a knock, a bruise often forms.
In Switzerland people mostly say “Kopfweh” for a headache.
If a pain lasts a long time, you go to the doctor.

abschnitte.text: Pain **warns of danger**. If you touch something hot, you pull your hand back in a flash. Special nerve endings in the skin and body report the danger along the nerves to the **brain**. Only there does the feeling of pain arise.

You cannot see pain directly. Doctors therefore often ask about a **pain scale** from 0 to 10. The **0** means **no pain at all**, the 10 the strongest imaginable. In this way you can compare whether it is getting better or worse.

After a knock, a **bruise** often forms, a blue patch. Here small blood vessels under the skin have burst. With a **wasp sting** the skin swells and hurts. If you hit your **funny bone** at the elbow, you feel a **tingle like electricity**: there a nerve lies directly under the skin.
In Switzerland a headache is mostly called **Kopfweh**. It can come from drinking too little, little sleep or tension. Often rest, fresh air and a glass of water help.

A **painkiller** can ease pain. Children should take one only after speaking to adults. Cooling often helps with knocks and stings. If a pain **does not go away for a long time** or is very strong, you should **go to the doctor**.

gewusst: The brain itself has no pain sensors.
The funny bone is not a bone at all but a nerve that lies unprotected there.

teile.einleitung: In a pollen allergy, also called hay fever, the immune system reacts excessively to pollen. In Switzerland about one person in five is affected.
wichtigste: A substance that triggers an allergy is called an allergen.
Typical are sneezing, a runny nose and itchy eyes.
Often an allergic conjunctivitis arises.
Hay fever is triggered mainly by wind-pollinated plants such as grasses and trees.
Hyposensitisation slowly accustoms the body to the allergen.
Untreated, asthma can develop, which is called a “change of floor”.
About 20 per cent of the Swiss population have a pollen allergy.

abschnitte.text: The **immune system** is meant to protect the body from disease germs. In an **allergy**, however, it reacts to substances that are actually harmless. Such a substance is called an **allergen**. Mostly it is a protein-containing substance, for example from a **pollen grain** or a food. According to the **Swiss Allergy Centre (aha!)**, about **20 per cent** of the population suffer from a pollen allergy.

Pollen irritates mainly the **mucous membranes** of the nose and eyes. People affected often **sneeze**, and the nose runs or is blocked. If pollen lands on the **conjunctiva** of the eyes, it becomes inflamed. The eyes become red, **itch** and water. This is called an **allergic conjunctivitis**. Many also feel tired in the pollen season.

Hay fever is triggered mainly by **wind-pollinated** plants. These include **grasses** and many **trees** such as birch, hazel and ash. Their pollen is light and flies far. Plants with large, colourful flowers such as **roses**, on the other hand, are **insect-pollinated**. Their pollen is heavy and sticky and is carried by insects. It hardly gets into the air.

Whoever knows what they are allergic to can partly **avoid** pollen. When **cycling**, a close-fitting **pair of sunglasses** keeps pollen away from the eyes. Washing your hair in the evening and not undressing in the bedroom also helps. Medicines such as **antihistamines** relieve the complaints. The **pollen forecast** from MeteoSwiss shows when many pollen are flying.

In **hyposensitisation**, also called specific immunotherapy, you receive small amounts of the allergen regularly over several years. The immune system thus learns to react **less violently**. This is important, because without treatment the complaints can move from the nose into the **bronchi**. This is called the **“Etagenwechsel”** (change of floor), and **allergic asthma** can arise.

gewusst: Some people allergic to birch pollen feel a tingling in the mouth when eating raw apples, which is called a cross-allergy.
The name hay fever comes from the time when people believed that fresh hay triggered the complaints.

teile.einleitung: Plaque is a soft, sticky coating on the teeth that consists of bacteria. If it is not brushed away regularly, it can cause tooth decay and gum inflammation.
wichtigste: Plaque, also called dental plaque, is a film of bacteria.
In biology plaque is called a biofilm.
Bacteria make acids from sugar that demineralise the enamel.
Streptococcus mutans is regarded as an important cause of tooth decay.
Saliva neutralises acids and supplies minerals.
Disclosing tablets make plaque visible.
Water gives the bacteria no sugar.

abschnitte.text: **Plaque**, also called **dental plaque**, is a sticky film on the teeth. It consists of **bacteria**, their waste products and food remains. Plaque forms **anew every day**. In biology such a thing is called a **biofilm**: a community of micro-organisms in a slimy layer on a surface. Such biofilms also exist on stones in a stream.

The bacteria in the coating use **sugar** from food. In doing so they give off **acids**. These acids dissolve minerals from the **enamel**. In time a hole forms, the **cavity**. An important cause is the bacterium **Streptococcus mutans**. It sticks well to the teeth and makes a lot of acid from sugar.

After every intake of sugar the bacteria make acid for a time. Whoever **snacks constantly** during the day sets off ever new **acid attacks**. The saliva then has no time to neutralise the acid. Sweet drinks such as squash, fruit juice or iced tea contain a lot of sugar. **Water** or unsweetened tea, on the other hand, give the bacteria no sugar.

**Saliva** buffers acids. It also contains **calcium** and **phosphate**. With these it can partly repair attacked enamel. In **sleep**, however, only little saliva flows. Acids from the coating then act undisturbed on the teeth for a long time. That is why **brushing your teeth before sleeping** is especially important.

Thorough **tooth brushing** with fluoride toothpaste removes the coating. Between the teeth **dental floss** helps. With **disclosing tablets** you can make plaque visible. They colour the coating red or blue, and you see exactly where you have not yet brushed well. In many Swiss schools there is **school dental care** (Schulzahnpflege), in which children practise brushing properly.

gewusst: If plaque is not removed, it can turn into hard tartar through minerals from the saliva.
In Switzerland the little tooth figure with an umbrella shows that a sweet is kind to teeth.

teile.einleitung: Rolf Zinkernagel is a Swiss doctor and immunologist. Together with the Australian Peter Doherty, he found out how the immune system recognises cells infected by viruses. For this the two received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1996.
wichtigste: Rolf Zinkernagel was born in 1944 in **Riehen** near Basel.
He made his most important discovery in **Australia**, together with Peter Doherty.
They studied mainly **cytotoxic T cells**.
T cells recognise viruses only together with the body’s own **MHC molecules**.
For the experiments they used mice and the virus **LCMV**.
Later he headed the Institute of Experimental Immunology at the **University of Zurich**.

abschnitte.text: Rolf Zinkernagel was born in 1944 in **Riehen**, a municipality in the canton of Basel-Stadt. He studied medicine at the University of Basel. Early on he was interested in research and especially in the **immune system**, that is, the body’s defence against disease-causing agents. To continue his research, he went abroad.

In the 1970s Zinkernagel worked in **Canberra** in Australia. There he did research together with the vet **Peter Doherty**. The two infected mice with the virus **LCMV**, which can cause meningitis. Then they observed how certain defence cells attack the infected cells. In doing so they made a surprising discovery.

**Cytotoxic T cells** are defence cells that destroy diseased body cells. Zinkernagel and Doherty showed that these T cells recognise a virus only if it is displayed on the cell surface together with one of the body’s own **MHC molecules**. This is called **MHC restriction**. In humans the MHC molecules are called **HLA**. This finding was very important for understanding the immune system, vaccinations and transplants better.

After Australia, at the end of the 1970s Zinkernagel did research at the **Scripps Clinic in La Jolla** in California. After that he returned to Switzerland, to the **University of Zurich**. There he later headed the **Institute of Experimental Immunology**. He went on studying how the body protects itself against viruses and how vaccinations work.

In 1996 Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty together received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine**. It was awarded for their discovery of how the immune system recognises cells infected by viruses. This makes Zinkernagel one of the Swiss Nobel prizewinners in medicine. His work is still explained today in textbooks of immunology.

gewusst: Zinkernagel and Doherty made the prizewinning discovery as early as the 1970s, and received the Nobel Prize only about 20 years later.
HLA features also play a role when a matching donor is sought for an organ or stem cell donation.

teile.einleitung: The cartwheel is a popular gymnastics exercise in which you turn sideways over your hands. Arms and legs move like the spokes of a wheel. With a little practice, many children manage it in the garden or on the meadow.
wichtigste: In a cartwheel, hand, hand, foot, foot touch the ground one after the other.
You move sideways.
In the air the legs are straight and spread apart.
For a short moment the arms carry the whole weight.
The exercise is called a wheel because arms and legs turn like spokes.
A line on the ground helps to do the cartwheel straight.

abschnitte.titel: Why it is called a wheel
abschnitte.text: In German the gymnastics exercise is called **Rad**, a wheel, because **arms and legs turn like spokes** around the middle of the body. Seen from the side, you see a star that turns round once. You also say “turning a cartwheel”. You move **sideways**, not forwards. The cartwheel is an important basic exercise in floor gymnastics.

You take a run-up and hold your **arms high above your head**. Then you place the first hand on the ground, and straight after it the second. The legs swing one after the other over the body. For a short moment **the arms carry the whole weight**. After that one foot lands first, then the other. The order is therefore **hand, hand, foot, foot**. In the air the legs are **straight and spread apart**.

At the beginning the cartwheel is often still crooked. A **line on the ground** helps a lot: hands and feet should all land on this line. It can be a piece of tape in the gym or a line drawn in chalk. Strong arms and good body tension are also important. It is best to practise on a mat or on soft grass.

If you can do the cartwheel well, you can make it harder. For example, you can do it **with one hand only**. An important further development is the **round-off**: here you make a quarter turn and land on **both feet at the same time**. In artistic gymnastics the round-off is often done before somersaults to build up momentum.

gewusst: Practised gymnasts can even do the cartwheel completely without hands, which is called an aerial cartwheel.
Many children first learn the cartwheel on the meadow before they practise it in the gym.

teile.einleitung: Salmonella are bacteria that can cause diarrhoeal illnesses in humans. You usually catch them through food. With hygiene in the kitchen and thorough heating, you can protect yourself well.
wichtigste: Salmonella are **bacteria**.
They usually cause a **diarrhoeal illness**.
They are found especially often in **raw eggs and poultry**.
**Thorough heating** makes them harmless.
They are named after the vet **Daniel Elmer Salmon**.
One particular kind of salmonella causes **typhoid**.

abschnitte.text: Salmonella are **bacteria**, that is, tiny living things that you can only see under the microscope. There are very many different kinds of them. They often live in the gut of animals. They are named after the American vet **Daniel Elmer Salmon**. They were discovered in his research team in the 19th century.

Salmonella usually cause a **diarrhoeal illness**. Typical are stomach ache, diarrhoea, nausea and sometimes fever. The first complaints usually come **a few hours to about 3 days** after the infection. In healthy people the illness usually passes by itself after a few days. It is important to drink a lot, because the body loses water through the diarrhoea.

Salmonella are found especially often in **raw eggs** and **poultry** such as chicken. Raw meat and dishes made with raw eggs, such as tiramisu or mayonnaise, can also be affected. In warmth the bacteria multiply quickly. **Reptiles such as tortoises** also often carry salmonella without seeming ill. After touching such animals you should wash your hands.

**Thorough heating** reliably makes salmonella in food harmless. Meat and eggs should therefore be well cooked. Raw poultry is cut on a board of its own, and afterwards you wash your hands, knife and board. Food should quickly go into the fridge, because cold slows the bacteria. If you follow these rules, you are well protected.

One particular kind of salmonella causes **typhoid**. This is a severe disease with a high fever that can be dangerous without treatment. It spreads mainly where drinking water is polluted. In Switzerland, typhoid is very rare thanks to clean water. Before travelling to some countries, though, you can have a vaccination against it.

gewusst: Salmonella are not killed by freezing, only by enough heat.
There are far more than a thousand different types of salmonella.

teile.einleitung: An **ambulance** brings help to sick and injured people and drives them to hospital. In Switzerland it is also called the **Sanität**. With blue lights and siren it gets quickly through the traffic.
wichtigste: In Switzerland an ambulance is often called an **Ambulanz**.
