The emergency number for the ambulance service in Switzerland is **144**.
Trained paramedics work in the ambulance.
The vehicle is equipped like a small mobile treatment room.
When blue lights and siren are on, other vehicles must make way.

abschnitte.text: In Germany people mostly say Rettungswagen. In Switzerland it is often called **Ambulanz** or simply **Sanität**. The emergency number for the ambulance service is **144** all over Switzerland. In the emergency call centre, experts decide which vehicle sets off. In serious emergencies, an emergency doctor sometimes goes along as well.

Inside the vehicle there is a **stretcher** on which the patient lies. There are also devices for measuring pulse and blood pressure, oxygen and a **defibrillator**, which can get a stopped heart going again. Bandages and medicines are also on board. The **paramedics** are specially trained for this. They can already help a great deal on the way.

In an emergency, the ambulance drives with **blue lights** and **siren**. Then all other vehicles must make way and form a lane. If you are on foot, you wait at the side of the road. Cyclists are also best off stopping. This way the help reaches its destination quickly.

gewusst: The word “ambulance” comes from the Latin “ambulare”, which means to walk about.
For accidents in the mountains or far from the nearest hospital, Switzerland also has rescue helicopters.

teile.einleitung: An X-ray image shows what it looks like inside the body without having to open it. Bones in particular can be seen very well on it. That is why it helps doctors, for example, to recognise a broken bone.
wichtigste: With an **X-ray image** you can see whether a bone is broken.
**Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen** discovered X-rays in **1895**.
On one of the first famous X-ray images you see a **hand with a ring**.
Bones appear **light to white** in the image.
X-rays are **invisible**.
A heavy **apron** protects parts of the body that are not being X-rayed.

abschnitte.text: In **1895** the physicist **Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen** was experimenting in Würzburg with a glass tube and electric current. He noticed that a screen nearby began to glow. It had to be invisible rays that even passed through paper and wood. He called them **X-rays**. In German they are now named after him, **Röntgenstrahlen**. Incidentally, Röntgen had studied in **Zurich**.

Soon after his discovery, Röntgen made one of the first famous X-ray images. It shows his wife’s **hand**. You can clearly see the bones of the fingers and a **ring**. People marvelled that you could suddenly see inside the body. In **1901** Röntgen was the very first person to receive the **Nobel Prize in Physics**.

X-rays pass through the body with different ease. **Bones** stop many rays. That is why they appear **light to white** in the image. Soft tissue lets more rays through and looks grey. Air lets almost all rays through, which is why the lungs, for example, are dark. Metal stops the rays completely and is very bright in the image.

Before an X-ray you often have to take off **metal jewellery**, because it would get in the way of the image. Then you lay the part of the body on a plate or stand in front of it. You have to keep completely still for a moment. Sometimes you are given a heavy **apron** to wear. It protects the other parts of the body from the rays. The picture itself does not hurt and takes only a moment.

abschnitte.titel: What X-ray images are used for
abschnitte.text: X-ray images are most often taken to recognise a **broken bone**. You can also see whether a broken bone is growing together well. Dentists X-ray teeth to find hidden holes. The lungs can also be examined in this way. Because X-rays in large amounts can do harm, an X-ray is only taken when it is necessary.

gewusst: Röntgen did not patent his discovery so that all people could benefit from it.
You can neither see nor feel X-rays.

teile.einleitung: X-radiation is an invisible radiation that passes through many substances. In medicine it is used to make images of the inside of the body. But it is also used in technology and in security checks.
wichtigste: X-rays belong to **electromagnetic radiation**, like light.
They arise in an **X-ray tube** when fast electrons hit metal.
The lungs appear dark because their **air** hardly stops the rays.
The effect of a radiation dose on humans is measured in **sieverts**.
X-rays are also used in **luggage checks at the airport**.
In a high dose the radiation can **damage cells**, which is why X-rays are taken only when necessary.

abschnitte.text: Like visible light, radio waves and UV rays, X-rays belong to **electromagnetic radiation**. But they have much more energy than visible light. That is why they can pass through substances that are opaque to our eyes. X-rays cannot be seen. They were discovered in 1895 by the physicist **Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen**.

An X-ray machine contains an **X-ray tube**. In it, **electrons** are strongly accelerated by a high electrical voltage. When these fast electrons hit a piece of **metal**, they are slowed down abruptly. This produces X-radiation. A large part of the energy, however, turns into heat, so the tube has to be cooled.

abschnitte.titel: Images of the inside of the body
abschnitte.text: Different tissues stop the rays to different degrees. Bones swallow a lot of radiation and appear light. The **lungs** contain a lot of **air**, which hardly stops the rays. That is why they are dark in the image. Very often an X-ray image is used to check for a **broken bone**. The **dentist** regularly X-rays teeth to find decay between the teeth.

X-rays are also used in technology. In **luggage checks at the airport**, suitcases and bags are scanned without being opened. In industry they are used to check whether welds or components have cracks. Researchers use X-rays to study the structure of crystals. Works of art are also X-rayed to discover hidden layers of paint.

In a high dose, X-radiation can **damage cells**. That is why an X-ray is only taken when it is really necessary. How strongly a radiation dose affects humans is given in the unit **sievert**. In an X-ray image the dose is usually very small. Lead aprons and protective walls stop rays. In Switzerland the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) monitors radiation protection.

gewusst: The unit sievert is named after the Swedish researcher Rolf Sievert.
In English, X-rays are still called “X-rays” today, after Röntgen’s name for them.

teile.einleitung: The shoe size says how long the foot is for which a shoe was made. Children’s feet grow fast, which is why children often need new shoes. Well-fitting shoes are important so that the feet develop healthily.
wichtigste: The shoe size shows how long the foot is.
Children often need new shoes because their feet are growing.
At the front there should be about a thumb’s width of room.
If the toes touch the front, the shoe is too small.
It is best to try on new shoes in the afternoon.
The left and the right foot are often not the same length.

abschnitte.text: The **shoe size** is a number that matches the length of the foot. In Switzerland and the rest of Europe, the **European shoe size** usually applies. The longer the foot, the bigger the number. From one size to the next, the shoe becomes only a little longer, less than a centimetre. Someone who wears size 30 needs **size 31** next. In Great Britain and the USA there are different numbers for the same foot length.

Children’s feet grow very fast in the first years of life. A kindergarten child often wears a shoe size around **28**. Children often do not notice when a shoe pinches, because their feet are still soft. That is why it is worth measuring the feet regularly. Many shoe shops have a measuring device for this.

A shoe fits if there is about a **thumb’s width** of free space in front of the big toe. When walking, the foot slips forward a little. If the **toes touch the front**, the shoe is too small. Shoes that are too big are not good either, because you lose support in them and can trip. It is also important that the shoe is wide enough.

It is best to try on new shoes in the **afternoon**. During the day, the feet become a little thicker from standing and walking. You always try on **both shoes**, because the left and the right foot are often not exactly the same length. The larger foot is what counts. It is best to walk a few steps in the shop before you decide.

gewusst: The European shoe size is based on an old unit of measure, the “Paris point”.
In the first years of life, children’s feet often grow by more than one shoe size a year.

teile.einleitung: If you put your hands on the sides of your chest, you feel hard arches under the skin. These are the **ribs**. Together they form a cage that protects the heart and lungs.
wichtigste: The ribs are attached at the back to the spine.
They protect above all the lungs and the heart.
Ribs, breastbone and thoracic vertebrae together form the rib cage.
The front ends of many ribs are made of flexible cartilage.
In a deep breath in, the rib cage becomes wider.
The lowest ribs are not attached at the front and are called floating ribs.

abschnitte.text: The ribs are **curved like a bow**. A human usually has **12 pairs of ribs**, that is, 24 ribs. At the back all the ribs are attached **to the spine**, more exactly to the thoracic vertebrae. From there they run in an arc to the front. Most of them are joined at the front to the **breastbone**, a flat bone in the middle of the chest.

**Ribs, breastbone and thoracic vertebrae** together form the **rib cage**. It is like a **protective cage** around important organs. Inside it lie the **lungs** and the **heart**. The lowest ribs also protect part of the liver, stomach and kidneys. In this way the rib cage is a kind of built-in armour.

The rib cage is not rigid. When you **breathe in deeply**, muscles between the ribs lift the rib cage, and it **becomes wider**. This gives the lungs more room, and air flows in. When you breathe out, it becomes narrower again. So that this works, the **front ends of many ribs are made of cartilage**, which is flexible.

The upper seven pairs of ribs are directly joined to the breastbone and are called **true ribs**. The next three pairs are attached by cartilage to the ribs above them and are called **false ribs**. The two lowest pairs end freely in the abdomen. They are not attached to the breastbone at the front and are therefore called **floating ribs**. Sometimes a person has one rib more or fewer.

gewusst: A broken rib usually heals by itself, because the rib cage holds it in place like a splint.
Men and women have the same number of ribs.

teile.einleitung: Saltatory conduction is a particularly fast way in which nerve fibres pass on signals. The signal jumps from gap to gap in the insulating myelin sheath. This is how nerve fibres in humans reach very high speeds.
wichtigste: “Saltatory” comes from the Latin word **saltare**, which means **to jump**.
The **myelin sheath** insulates the axon electrically.
Fast myelinated fibres conduct **up to about 100 m/s**.
Fibres without myelin conduct **continuously** and more slowly, thin C fibres at about **1 m/s**.
**Fewer ions have to be pumped back**, which saves energy.
Squid reach high speed through a **very large axon diameter**.

abschnitte.text: A nerve cell passes on signals along a long extension, the **axon**. Many axons are surrounded by a fatty layer, the **myelin**. This **myelin sheath** is not continuous. At regular intervals there are small gaps, the **nodes of Ranvier**. The myelin **insulates** the axon electrically, much like the plastic coating on an electric cable.

At the insulated places no action potential can arise. It forms only at the **nodes**, where there are many sodium channels. The electrical excitation spreads very fast under the sheath to the next node and triggers a new action potential there. So the signal seems to **jump** from node to node. That is where the name comes from: the Latin word **saltare** means to jump.

Fast myelinated nerve fibres in humans conduct **up to about 100 metres per second**. A signal then needs only **10 milliseconds** for a fibre 1 m long. In axons without myelin, the excitation runs bit by bit along the whole fibre. This is called **continuous conduction**. Thin unmyelinated **C fibres** conduct only about **1 m/s**. Because ions flow only at the nodes, in saltatory conduction **fewer ions have to be pumped back** as well. That saves energy.

Squid have no myelin. Even so, they have to flee very fast when in danger. They solve the problem with a **very large axon diameter**. The thicker an axon is, the faster it conducts even without insulation. These giant axons are so thick that researchers were able to study the basics of nerve conduction on them. Vertebrates, on the other hand, save a lot of space thanks to myelin.

If the myelin sheath is damaged, nerves conduct signals more slowly or no longer properly at all. This happens, for example, in the disease **multiple sclerosis**. In it, the body’s own immune system attacks the myelin in the brain and spinal cord. Depending on which nerves are affected, there are problems with seeing, feeling or moving.

gewusst: The nodes of Ranvier are named after the French researcher Louis-Antoine Ranvier.
When you knock your hand, you often feel a sharp pain first and a dull one only later, because different nerve fibres conduct at different speeds.

teile.einleitung: Every scent that we smell is first recognised by **olfactory cells**. These special nerve cells sit in the nose. They have an astonishing ability: they are renewed throughout life.
wichtigste: Olfactory cells are nerve cells in the olfactory mucous membrane.
They are constantly replaced by new ones.
A human has several million olfactory cells.
There are about 350 different kinds of olfactory receptors.
A single olfactory cell usually carries only one kind of receptor.
Richard Axel and Linda Buck received the Nobel Prize in 2004 for the discovery of the olfactory receptors.

abschnitte.text: Olfactory cells are **nerve cells**. They sit in the olfactory mucous membrane right at the top of the nose. A human has **several million** of them. At their end, which projects into the nasal mucus, they carry **fine olfactory hairs**. On these sit the receptors that recognise the scent substances.

Most nerve cells stay the same for life. Olfactory cells are an exception: they are **constantly replaced by new ones**. An olfactory cell lives only a few weeks. Then a new one grows from precursor cells. This is necessary because the cells come into direct contact with the outside air and some harmful substances.

Humans have **about 350** different kinds of **olfactory receptors**. A single olfactory cell usually carries **only one kind** of them. A scent substance fits certain receptors like a key fits locks. Every scent stimulates its own mixture of receptors. The brain recognises the scent by this pattern.

How the olfactory receptors work was studied by the two American researchers **Richard Axel** and **Linda Buck**. They discovered the large family of genes that contain the instructions for the olfactory receptors. For this they received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine** in **2004**. Their work showed how the sense of smell is built up.

The signals of the olfactory cells travel along the **olfactory nerve** to the brain. They go **directly to parts of the brain** responsible for **feelings and memory**. That is why smells often awaken especially strong memories. The scent of cake can suddenly remind you of your grandmother. With other senses this route is less direct.

gewusst: The olfactory nerve is the first of the twelve cranial nerves.
Humans can tell apart many more smells than there are kinds of olfactory receptors.

teile.einleitung: Some people recover especially well after hard times. This inner strength is called **resilience**. The good news: you can practise and strengthen it.
wichtigste: Resilience is the ability to cope well with crises.
The word comes from the Latin “resilire”, to spring back.
Emmy Werner researched resilience in a long-term study on the island of Kauai.
A stable person to rely on strengthens children’s resilience especially.
Resilience is not inborn and unchangeable, it can be strengthened throughout life.
Resilience is often compared to a tumbler toy that always springs upright again.

abschnitte.text: In psychology, **resilience** means the ability to cope well with crises and difficult experiences. The word comes from the Latin **“resilire”**, which means to spring back or bounce off. Resilient people also experience grief and stress. But after a while they find their balance again. In a picture, it is compared to a **tumbler toy**, which stands up again after every knock.

The subject became well known through the psychologist **Emmy Werner**. She followed children on the Hawaiian island of **Kauai** who were born in 1955 over decades. Many of them grew up under difficult conditions. Some of these children nevertheless developed well and became contented adults. Werner studied what had helped these children.

Such helpful circumstances are called **protective factors**. Especially important is a **stable person to rely on**, that is, someone who is reliably there. This can be a parent, but also grandparents, a teacher or a coach. Other protective factors are good friendships and the feeling of being able to do something. Someone who can ask for help is also better equipped.

Resilience includes a particular way of looking at problems. Resilient people mostly see problems as **solvable**. They concentrate on what they themselves can influence. They take feelings seriously but do not let themselves be steered entirely by them. And they believe that difficult times pass again.

Resilience is **not inborn and unchangeable**. You can strengthen it throughout life. A simple exercise is to write down **three good things** from the day every evening. This directs your attention to what has gone well. Enough sleep, exercise and good conversations with people you trust also help.

gewusst: In engineering, resilience describes how well a material returns to its old shape after being deformed.
The Kauai study followed about 700 children for about 40 years.

teile.einleitung: The body has to regulate its blood pressure and amount of water well. A chain of hormones and enzymes helps with this: the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system**, or **RAAS** for short. Many blood pressure medicines act at exactly this point.
wichtigste: The enzyme renin is made in the kidney.
Renin is released mainly when the blood pressure in the kidney falls.
Renin splits the protein angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.
The angiotensin-converting enzyme, ACE for short, turns this into angiotensin II.
Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex makes the kidney take back more sodium.
ACE inhibitors and sartans are important blood pressure medicines.

abschnitte.text: The kidney constantly measures how much blood arrives at it. If the blood pressure in the kidney falls, it releases the enzyme **renin**. An **enzyme** is a protein that speeds up chemical processes. In the blood, renin splits the protein **angiotensinogen**, which comes from the liver. This produces **angiotensin I**.

Angiotensin I itself has hardly any effect. The **angiotensin-converting enzyme**, or **ACE** for short, changes it into **angiotensin II**. Angiotensin II narrows the blood vessels, and the blood pressure rises. It also stimulates the adrenal gland to make another hormone. In this way several substances work together like the links of a chain.

**Aldosterone** is made in the **adrenal cortex**. In the kidney tubules it makes sure that **more sodium** is taken back into the blood. With the salt, more water also stays in the body. This increases the amount of blood and so the blood pressure. In this way the whole system helps to make up for blood pressure that is too low.

With high blood pressure, the RAAS can be slowed with medicines. **ACE inhibitors** block the enzyme ACE so that less angiotensin II is formed. A typical side effect is a dry **irritating cough**. The **sartans**, on the other hand, block the angiotensin II receptor, the docking point of the hormone. Both groups are among the most common blood pressure medicines.

gewusst: The first ACE inhibitor, captopril, was developed on the model of a substance from the venom of a South American pit viper.
Renin was discovered as early as 1898, long before the whole system was understood.

teile.einleitung: The school playground (in German Pausenplatz) is the place where children play, run and recover between lessons. Many games there are already very old and are passed on from older to younger children.
wichtigste: On the playground children move about and top up their energy for lessons.
In “Himmel und Hölle” (hopscotch) you hop on one leg through painted squares.
With pavement chalk you draw playing areas on the tarmac.
In hide and seek one child counts and then looks for the others.
In skipping and in elastics you jump according to rules.
The slide and the seesaw, often called “Gigampfi” in Switzerland, are popular play equipment.

abschnitte.text: With **pavement chalk** you can draw colourful playing areas on the ground. The chalk is thick, and the rain later washes it away again. A well-known hopping game is **“Himmel und Hölle”**, which is German for “heaven and hell” and is the same as hopscotch. You throw a stone into a square and then hop on one leg through the squares. The square with the stone is jumped over.

In **hide and seek** (“Versteckis” in Swiss German) one child closes their eyes and counts out loud. The others hide in this time. Then the child looks for all the others. **Tag** (“Fangis”) is also popular on many playgrounds: one child tries to touch the others. Such games need only space and good humour.

In **skipping** a rope swings over the head and under the feet. Each time you have to jump at the right moment. In **elastics** (“Gummitwist” in German) two children hold a long elastic band stretched around their legs. A third child jumps in and out according to fixed rules. With each round the band gets higher, and it gets harder. Both games train **stamina** and **skill**.

Many playgrounds have play equipment. On the **slide** you climb a ladder and then slide down the smooth track sitting. On the **seesaw** a child sits at each end, and it goes up and down in turn. In Switzerland people often call it a **“Gigampfi”**. Often there are also climbing frames, swings and sandpits.

In break time the body moves, and the head recovers from learning. Afterwards you can often concentrate better again in lessons. In playing you also learn to keep to **rules**, to take turns and to be fair. Teachers often have **break duty** and help when there is a quarrel. In the long break many children also eat their **“Znüni”**, the Swiss word for the mid-morning snack.

gewusst: Hopping games with painted squares exist in many countries of the world, each with different names and rules.
Skipping is not only a playground game, but is also used by athletes as training.

teile.einleitung: In sleepwalking, someone gets up in their sleep and walks around without being awake. It happens mainly in children and is usually harmless.
wichtigste: Sleepwalking happens in deep sleep.
Children sleepwalk most often.
The eyes are often open in the process.
In the morning you usually do not remember it.
In children it usually stops by itself.
Too little sleep can make sleepwalking more frequent.

abschnitte.text: In **sleepwalking**, someone gets out of bed and walks around although they are asleep. The **eyes** are often **open**, but the gaze looks empty. Some talk, open doors or tidy things about. It happens in **deep sleep**, usually in the first hours of the night.

**Children** sleepwalk much more often than adults. In them it **usually stops by itself** as they get older. In the morning, sleepwalkers **usually do not** remember their outing. Sleepwalking becomes more frequent with **too little sleep**, with fever or with a lot of excitement.
You should not shout at a sleepwalker or shake them. They could be startled and confused. It is best to lead them **calmly back to bed**. Usually they are easy to guide.

When sleepwalking you can stumble or fall. That is why it is important to **secure stairs and windows**, for example with a gate or a window lock. Objects on the floor are cleared away. In frequent sleepwalking you can seek medical advice.

gewusst: The technical term for sleepwalking is “somnambulism”.
Often several people in the same family sleepwalk.

teile.einleitung: With red-green colour vision deficiency, you find it harder to tell red and green shades apart. It is the most common form of colour vision deficiency and is usually inborn. Men are affected much more often than women.
wichtigste: Around **8 per cent** of men in Central Europe have a red-green colour vision deficiency.
It is inherited in an **X-linked recessive** way.
In **deuteranopia** the green cone (M cone) is missing.
In **protanomaly** the red cone (L cone) is altered.
Testing is often done with **Ishihara plates**, and exact classification with the **anomaloscope**.
Colour blindness is also called **Daltonism**, after John Dalton.

abschnitte.text: In the retina of the eye there are sense cells, the **cones**. There are three kinds: the **L cones** react mainly to red light, the **M cones** to green and the **S cones** to blue. The brain compares their signals and creates all colours from them. If one kind of cone does not work properly, some colours look similar.

If the red cone is altered, it is called **protanomaly**. If it is missing completely, it is **protanopia**. For the green cone, it is correspondingly **deuteranomaly** and **deuteranopia** if the M cone is missing. The milder forms with altered cones are more common. Many of those affected do not notice for a long time that they see colours differently.

The gene for red-green colour vision deficiency lies on the **X chromosome** and is inherited **recessively**. Men have only one X chromosome. If the gene is altered there, the deficiency shows. Women have two X chromosomes, and a healthy one can usually compensate for the other. That is why about 8 per cent of men are affected, but only about half a per cent of women.

The **Ishihara plates** are well known. They show circles made of many coloured dots in which a number is hidden. Someone with a red-green colour vision deficiency does not recognise the number or sees a different one. The **anomaloscope** is more exact. With it you have to adjust two colour fields so that they look the same. This allows the kind of deficiency to be determined exactly.

abschnitte.titel: In everyday life and at work
abschnitte.text: In everyday life most of those affected cope well. For some jobs, though, normal colour vision is a requirement, for example **airline pilot**. For train drivers or electricians, too, good colour vision can be important. The English natural philosopher **John Dalton** described his own colour vision deficiency in the 18th century. That is why it is also called **Daltonism**.

gewusst: Red-green colour vision deficiency cannot be cured, but special apps and colour markings help in everyday life.
Many dogs see colours similarly to people with a red-green colour vision deficiency, because they have only two kinds of cones.

teile.einleitung: The sweet pepper (in Swiss German Peperoni) is a crunchy vegetable that comes in red, yellow, orange and green. It is mild, slightly sweet and contains a lot of vitamin C.
wichtigste: The sweet pepper originally comes from Central and South America.
It belongs to the nightshade family, like the tomato and the potato.
Green peppers are often unripe, ripe ones turn yellow or red.
Red peppers contain especially much vitamin C.
Eaten raw, the most vitamin C is kept.
In Germany people mostly say Paprika.

abschnitte.text: The sweet pepper comes from **Central and South America**. There people grew it long before the arrival of the Europeans. Sailors brought it to Europe over **500 years** ago. In Switzerland people say **Peperoni**, in Germany mostly **Paprika**. The same vegetable is meant.

The sweet pepper belongs to the **nightshade family**. This plant family also includes tomatoes, potatoes and aubergines. The plant needs a lot of warmth and sun. In Switzerland it therefore often grows in **greenhouses**. Inside, a pepper is hollow. In the middle sit many small, pale **seeds** from which new plants can grow.

Many **green peppers** are simply not yet ripe. If you leave them longer on the plant, they turn yellow, orange or red. Ripe peppers taste sweeter. But there are also varieties that have a different colour from the start. So the colour often shows how ripe a pepper is.

Peppers are healthy. **Red peppers** contain especially much **vitamin C**, often more than a lemon. Green ones contain markedly less. Vitamin C is partly lost through heat. Most is kept if you eat peppers **raw**, for example as vegetable sticks for the “Znüni”, the mid-morning snack.

Ordinary peppers do not burn in the mouth, they are **mild**. Their hot relatives are called **chilli** or **peperoncini**. The heat comes from a substance called **capsaicin**. Sweet peppers contain hardly any of it. That is why children can eat them well too.

gewusst: Botanically the pepper is a fruit, more exactly a berry, although we eat it as a vegetable.
Sweet peppers and hot chillies belong to the same plant genus, called Capsicum.

teile.einleitung: The acid-base balance makes sure that the blood always stays equally acidic. Even small departures from the normal pH disturb many processes in the body. That is why buffers, lungs and kidneys work together constantly.
wichtigste: The normal pH of arterial blood is 7.35 to 7.45.
A pH that is too low is called acidosis, one that is too high alkalosis.
The most important buffer in plasma is the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer.
The lungs regulate the CO2, the kidney the bicarbonate.
The kidney excretes a lot of acid as ammonium.
The enzyme carbonic anhydrase speeds up the formation of carbonic acid.

abschnitte.text: The **pH** shows how acidic or basic a liquid is. In arterial blood it is kept tightly around 7.4, between **7.35 and 7.45**. The blood is therefore slightly basic. Values below this are called **acidosis**, over-acidification. Values above it are called **alkalosis**. If the cause comes from the metabolism, it is called metabolic, if it comes from breathing, respiratory.

**Buffers** catch acids and bases before they change the pH much. The most important one in blood plasma is the **carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer**. It is especially effective because the lungs can regulate CO2 and the kidney can regulate bicarbonate independently of each other. It is therefore called an open buffer system. The enzyme **carbonic anhydrase** in red blood cells and kidney cells speeds up the formation of carbonic acid from CO2 and water many times over.

The **lungs** react quickly. In a metabolic acidosis, you breathe deeper and faster and blow off more CO2. This makes the pH rise again. This deep breathing is called **Kussmaul breathing**. The **kidney** works more slowly, but thoroughly. Its tubule cells make ammonia from glutamine, which binds acid in the urine. In this way a lot of acid is excreted as **ammonium**, and another part is bound to phosphate.

With the **Henderson-Hasselbalch equation** you calculate the pH: pH equals 6.1 plus the log of bicarbonate divided by dissolved CO2. At 24 mmol/l of bicarbonate and a CO2 partial pressure of 40 mmHg, times 0.03 that is 1.2 mmol/l, this gives 6.1 plus log 20. That is 6.1 plus 1.3, so **7.4**.

In a **diabetic ketoacidosis**, a lack of insulin produces many ketone bodies, which are acids. This is a **metabolic acidosis**. Someone who **hyperventilates** strongly in a panic, on the other hand, breathes out too much CO2. The blood becomes more basic, and a **respiratory alkalosis** results. It can cause tingling and muscle cramps.

gewusst: A pH difference of 1 means a difference of ten times in the amount of acid.
The lungs can influence the pH within minutes, the kidney needs hours to days for it.

teile.einleitung: In physiotherapy people learn to move well again after an injury, operation or illness. Physiotherapists work with targeted exercises and with their hands.
wichtigste: Physiotherapy helps people to move well again.
Physiotherapists show, for example, how to walk properly with crutches.
Important parts are exercises, massage and warmth or cold.
Many exercises you carry on with yourself at home.
In Switzerland a doctor usually prescribes physiotherapy.

abschnitte.text: After a broken leg, an operation or an accident the muscles are often weak and the joints stiff. This is where **physiotherapy** helps. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “treatment with natural means”. The aim is that a person can **move** again as well as possible and without pain.

Whoever may not put weight on a leg often gets **crutches**. The **physiotherapist** shows how to walk properly with them. You learn how much weight you may put on the injured leg. **Climbing stairs** with crutches is also practised. In this way you move safely and prevent falls.

In physiotherapy you do targeted **exercises** to strengthen muscles and make joints more mobile. The therapist also moves joints with her hands or **massages** tense muscles. Sometimes **warmth**, **cold** or equipment are added. It is important that you also keep doing many exercises regularly **at home**.

Physiotherapy exists for all age groups. **Athletes** get back in shape after injuries. Older people practise **balance**, so that they fall less. **Children** can also get physiotherapy, for example if they have difficulty with posture or movement. For breathing problems there is a special **breathing therapy**.

In Switzerland a **doctor** usually prescribes physiotherapy. With this **prescription** the health insurer pays part of the costs from basic insurance. Physiotherapists study at a **university of applied sciences**. They work in their own practices, in hospitals, rehabilitation clinics or with sports clubs.

gewusst: Even in antiquity doctors used exercise, massage and water to treat the sick.
Regular small exercises at home are often more effective than a single long treatment.

teile.einleitung: Sleep deprivation is when someone sleeps too little over a longer time. It affects concentration, mood, hunger and health. Teenagers in particular often sleep too little.
wichtigste: Teenagers aged 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.
Sleep deprivation weakens above all concentration.
Anyone who sleeps too little often gets hungrier.
Constant sleep deprivation weakens the immune system.
Microsleep is dangerous when driving.
Accumulated lack of sleep is called sleep debt.

abschnitte.text: Specialists recommend **8 to 10 hours** of sleep for teenagers between 13 and 18. Many sleep clearly less. **Concentration** suffers most. You remember new things less well, make more mistakes and become irritable more quickly. In sleep, the brain firms up what has been learned.
Sleep deprivation muddles the signals for hunger and fullness. You get **hungrier**, often for sweet or fatty things. That is why constant sleep deprivation can also affect body weight.
Anyone who constantly sleeps too little weakens their **immune system**. You fall ill more easily, for example catch a cold. In the long term the risk of other illnesses also rises.

The brief, unintended nodding off is called **microsleep**. When driving it is very dangerous, because even a few seconds are enough for an accident. Studies compare performance after about **17 hours without sleep** with about **0.5 per mille of alcohol** in the blood.

Several nights that are too short add up to a **sleep debt**. A single long lie-in at the weekend makes up for it only partly. Better are regular nights of enough length. In 1964 the pupil **Randy Gardner** stayed awake without a break for about **11 days** for a school project. Specialists today strongly advise against such experiments.

gewusst: After his experiment, Randy Gardner first slept about 14 hours in a row.
In many teenagers the inner clock shifts, and they become tired later in the evening.

teile.einleitung: Rickets is a disease in which children’s bones stay soft and become deformed. The most common cause is a lack of vitamin D. Today rickets is rare in Switzerland, because it can be prevented well.
wichtigste: The most common cause of rickets is vitamin D deficiency.
The body makes vitamin D itself when sunlight falls on the skin.
Vitamin D helps to absorb calcium from the gut.
Typical signs are bowed legs and thickenings on the ribs.
In Switzerland, babies are given vitamin D drops daily to prevent it.
In adults the softening of the bones is called osteomalacia.

abschnitte.text: For strong bones, the body needs **calcium**. So that it can absorb calcium from the gut, it needs **vitamin D**. The special thing is that the body makes most of its vitamin D itself when **sunlight falls on the skin**. Only a few foods, such as oily fish, contain a lot of it. If vitamin D is missing, the bones do not become properly hard. In children this disease is called **rickets**.

Because the bones are soft, they can bend under the body’s weight. Children with marked rickets often have **bowed legs**. On the ribs there are knobbly thickenings called the **rachitic rosary**, because they look like the beads of a rosary. The children often grow more slowly and are weaker. In adults a similar softening of the bones is called **osteomalacia**.

In the **19th century** rickets was very common in the industrial cities of Europe. **Smoke** from factories and **narrow alleys** kept out the sunlight. Many children also worked in dark rooms. As a remedy they were given **cod liver oil**, an oil from the liver of fish that contains a lot of vitamin D. Many children, however, found its taste horrible.

Today we know exactly how to prevent rickets. In Switzerland it is recommended to give **babies** in their first year of life **vitamin D drops every day**. Later, exercise outdoors and a balanced diet help. Because of this prevention, rickets has become rare here. In some countries of the world, however, it is still widespread.

gewusst: Vitamin D is really more of a hormone, because the body can make it itself.
In winter the sun in Switzerland is often too weak for the skin to make enough vitamin D.

teile.einleitung: In sleep apnoea, breathing stops again and again during sleep. Sleep is disturbed as a result, and those affected are often very tired during the day. There are good treatments.
wichtigste: An apnoea is a pause in breathing of at least 10 seconds.
A hypopnoea is a clear flattening of breathing.
The AHI counts pauses and flattenings of breathing per hour of sleep.
From 5 per hour, with symptoms, it is called mild sleep apnoea.
Typical is marked daytime sleepiness.
Untreated, sleep apnoea promotes high blood pressure.

abschnitte.text: An **apnoea** is a pause in breathing during sleep of **at least 10 seconds**. In a **hypopnoea**, breathing does not stop completely, but it flattens clearly. In the process the oxygen in the blood falls, or the brain reacts with a short **arousal**. The person usually does not really wake up, but sleep is interrupted again and again.

In **obstructive sleep apnoea**, the upper airways in the throat collapse. The body tries to breathe, but the air does not get through. Often those affected snore loudly. In **central sleep apnoea**, the brain sends too few breathing signals. In people with heart failure, **Cheyne-Stokes breathing** often occurs, a change between swelling and fading breathing with pauses.

In the sleep laboratory, the pauses and flattenings of breathing are counted. From this comes the **apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI)**: the number per hour of sleep. From **5 per hour**, with matching symptoms, it is called mild sleep apnoea. Higher values mean a moderate or severe form.

The leading symptom by day is **marked daytime sleepiness**. Those affected nod off easily, even when driving. Untreated, obstructive sleep apnoea promotes **high blood pressure** and other cardiovascular diseases.

Often you wear a **breathing mask** at night, which keeps the airways open with slight positive pressure. In mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnoea, a **mandibular advancement splint** often helps. It pushes the lower jaw forward a little, so the throat stays more open. Losing weight and sleeping on your side can also help.

gewusst: “Apnoea” comes from Greek and means “without breath”.
Many of those affected know nothing of their pauses in breathing, often the person in the same room notices first.

teile.einleitung: In everyday speech people say “I’ve had a shock” when they have been frightened. In medicine, though, shock means something much more serious: a life-threatening disturbance of the circulation. Then the organs get too little blood and oxygen.
wichtigste: A medical shock is a life-threatening circulatory disturbance.
Typical are pale, cold, sweaty skin and a fast pulse.
A great loss of blood or fluid leads to hypovolaemic shock.
A severe allergic shock is called anaphylactic shock.
You call the emergency number 144, cover the person and stay with them.
A person in shock should not eat or drink anything.

abschnitte.text: The heart pumps blood through the vessels to all the organs. This circuit is called the **blood circulation**. In a **shock**, too little blood arrives at the organs. They then receive too little oxygen and can be damaged. A shock is therefore always an **emergency** in which help is needed quickly.

A person in shock is often **pale**, and their skin feels **cold** and **sweaty**. The body tries to direct the little blood to the most important organs. That is why the heart beats faster, and the **pulse** is quick and often weak. Many of those affected feel cold, tremble, are restless or anxious. Later they can become confused or unconscious.

There are several kinds of shock. If someone loses a lot of blood or fluid, for example in a severe injury or heavy diarrhoea, it is called **hypovolaemic shock**. An **anaphylactic shock** is a very violent allergic reaction, for example after a wasp sting or to certain foods. People with such an allergy often carry an emergency pen with the medicine **adrenaline**. A shock can also arise when the heart pumps too weakly.

First you call the **emergency number 144**. If the person has lost a lot of blood and no injury speaks against it, you lay them **flat on their back** and raise the legs slightly. This way more blood flows back to the heart. With a **broken leg**, though, you do not raise the legs. You **cover** the person so that they do not get cold, speak calmly to them and **do not leave them alone**.

Even if the person is thirsty, you give them **nothing to eat or drink**. They may have to be operated on in hospital soon, and the stomach should be empty for that. In addition, a person in shock may feel sick, so that they vomit. In a **first aid course** you learn how to act correctly in such situations.

gewusst: A shock can develop slowly, which is why you go on watching injured people even if they feel well at first.
Positioning with raised legs is also called the shock position.

teile.einleitung: Plasmodia are tiny single-celled organisms that cause malaria. They are passed on by mosquitoes and in humans first attack the liver and then the red blood cells.
wichtigste: Plasmodia are single-celled organisms and cause malaria.
They are passed on by the bite of Anopheles mosquitoes.
After the bite they first travel to the liver.
After that they attack the red blood cells.
Plasmodium falciparum causes the most dangerous form, tropical malaria.
Alphonse Laveran discovered the germs in 1880.
Tu Youyou received the Nobel Prize in 2015 for the malaria drug artemisinin.

abschnitte.text: Plasmodia are **single-celled organisms**, that is, living things made of only one cell. They are passed on by the bite of **Anopheles mosquitoes**. In the mosquito a stage called the **sporozoite** arises. The sporozoites collect in the salivary glands of the mosquito. In the bite they get with the saliva into the skin of the person.

After the bite the germs first travel to the **liver**. There they multiply unnoticed in the liver cells. After that **merozoites** arise, which get into the blood and attack the **red blood cells**. In these they multiply further and make the cells **burst**. When many cells burst at the same time, **bouts of fever** occur.

There are several Plasmodium species that attack humans. **Plasmodium falciparum** causes **tropical malaria**, the most dangerous form. Affected blood cells can stick together in small vessels, for example in the brain. **Plasmodium vivax** and **Plasmodium ovale** cause **tertian malaria**, with bouts of fever about every 48 hours. In **quartan malaria** there are about 72 hours in between.

The French army doctor **Alphonse Laveran** observed the germs in **1880** in Algeria in the blood of sick people. For this he received the Nobel Prize in 1907. The Chinese researcher **Tu Youyou** obtained the drug **artemisinin** from sweet wormwood. For this she received the Nobel Prize in **2015**. Combination therapies with artemisinin are today standard against tropical malaria. The **Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute** in Basel also researches malaria.

**Sickle cell anaemia** is an inherited blood disease. People who have inherited the sickle cell gene from only one parent are mostly hardly ill. But they fall seriously ill with tropical malaria less often. That is why this gene is common in **malaria regions of Africa**. Travellers to such regions protect themselves with mosquito repellent, mosquito nets and sometimes with medicines.

gewusst: Only the female Anopheles mosquitoes bite and can therefore pass on malaria.
Malaria is still among the most common infectious diseases in the world, above all in Africa.

teile.einleitung: After a fall, a dark, hard layer soon forms on a wound: the scab. It is a natural plaster that the body makes itself. Under it, the skin heals in peace.
wichtigste: A scab is formed from dried blood.
Another word for a scab is a crust.
It protects the wound from dirt and germs.
New skin grows under the scab.
A scab is mostly dark red to brown.
When the wound has healed, it falls off by itself.
Anyone who keeps picking it off risks a scar.

abschnitte.text: When the skin is injured, blood comes out. In the blood swim tiny **platelets**. They stick together at the wound and, together with the protein **fibrin**, form a fine net. Blood cells get caught in it, and the blood **clots**. When this layer dries in the air, it becomes hard. This is how the **scab** arises, also called a **crust**.

The scab closes the wound like a lid. It **protects** it from dirt and germs that could cause an inflammation. Underneath, the body can work undisturbed. Its colour is mostly **dark red to brown**, because it consists of dried blood. The bigger the wound, the bigger the scab usually becomes.

Under the scab, new cells form. From the edges of the wound, **new skin** slowly grows over the injured spot. Depending on the size of the wound, this can take a few days to a few weeks. When the skin underneath is finished, the scab loosens and **falls off by itself**. The new skin is often pink and a little sensitive at first.

A scab can itch, and many people want to pick it off. It is best, though, to leave it **in peace**. If you tear it off, the wound opens again, and germs can get in. Healing then starts again from the beginning and takes longer. Anyone who does this again and again risks a **scar**. It helps to keep the spot clean and to have short fingernails.

gewusst: Animals such as dogs and cats also form scabs on wounds.
The itching during healing is a sign that the skin underneath is working.

teile.einleitung: A reflex is a fast, automatic reaction of the body to a stimulus. You do not have to think about it, the body reacts by itself. The path that the signal takes is called the reflex arc.
wichtigste: At the start of every reflex arc is a sensory receptor that picks up a stimulus.
Many reflexes are fast because they are switched over in the spinal cord.
Motor nerve cells pass the signal from the spinal cord to the muscle.
In the knee-jerk reflex the lower leg shoots forwards.
In the knee-jerk reflex only one synapse in the spinal cord is passed through.
The blink reflex protects the eye.

abschnitte.text: A **reflex arc** has several stations. At the start is a **sensory receptor** that picks up a stimulus, for example pressure or stretching. A sensory nerve cell passes the message to the **spinal cord**. There the signal is switched over. **Motor nerve cells** then pass the command to the **muscle**, which contracts. The brain often only learns afterwards what has happened.

Many reflexes happen very fast because they are **switched over in the spinal cord**. The signal does not first have to take the long route to the brain and back. This is important for protection: if you touch a hot hob, you pull your hand back in a flash. Only a moment later do you feel the pain consciously.

The best-known reflex is the **knee-jerk reflex**. The doctor strikes the tendon below the kneecap with a small hammer. This briefly stretches the thigh muscle, and the **lower leg shoots forwards**. In this, only **one synapse** in the spinal cord is passed through, that is, one connecting point between nerve cells. Because stimulus and reaction take place in the **same muscle**, it is called a **monosynaptic stretch reflex**.

Many reflexes protect us. The **blink reflex** closes the eyes when something suddenly approaches fast. Coughing and sneezing are also reflexes: they carry dust and foreign bodies out of the airways. The swallowing reflex makes sure that food goes into the gullet and not into the windpipe.

Besides inborn reflexes there are also learned ones. The Russian researcher **Ivan Pavlov** studied them using **dogs**. He noticed that dogs produce saliva as soon as they expect food. If a signal always sounded before feeding, the dogs soon produced saliva at the signal alone. Pavlov called this a **conditioned reflex**. He received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1904, but for his research on digestion.

gewusst: With the small hammer, doctors check whether nerves and spinal cord work properly.
The knee-jerk reflex is also called the patellar reflex, after the Latin word for kneecap.

teile.einleitung: Plasma cells are cells of the immune system that make antibodies. They arise from B lymphocytes and work like small factories that release large amounts of defensive substances into the blood.
wichtigste: Plasma cells develop from activated B lymphocytes.
Their main job is to release large amounts of antibodies.
They have a strongly developed rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Their cell nucleus looks like the spokes of a wheel and usually lies at the edge.
Long-lived plasma cells sit mainly in the bone marrow.
Multiple myeloma is a cancer of degenerated plasma cells.

abschnitte.text: The **immune system** protects the body from disease germs. An important part is played by the **B lymphocytes**, a kind of white blood cell. If a B cell recognises a germ, it is **activated**. It divides and develops further into **plasma cells**. These are entirely specialised in making **antibodies**.

Plasma cells are real **antibody factories**. They release antibodies into the blood and into tissue fluids. Antibodies are **proteins** that attach to germs. In this way they mark the germs for other defence cells or make them harmless. Each plasma cell makes only a single kind of antibody, which fits exactly one germ.

Because antibodies are proteins, the cell needs many **ribosomes**. These sit on the **rough endoplasmic reticulum**, a network of membranes that is especially large in plasma cells. The **Golgi apparatus** is also large. The **cell nucleus** usually lies at the edge of the cell. Its genetic material is arranged in clumps, which recalls the spokes of a **cartwheel**.

abschnitte.titel: At home in the bone marrow
abschnitte.text: Many plasma cells live only briefly. **Long-lived plasma cells**, however, find special niches with survival signals in the **bone marrow**. From there they release antibodies into the blood permanently. This is one reason why you are protected for a long time after some illnesses or vaccinations. In healthy adults, however, plasma cells make up **less than 5 per cent** of the cells in the bone marrow.

In **multiple myeloma** a single group of plasma cells multiplies without control in the bone marrow. It often makes large amounts of a uniform antibody and can damage the **bones**. To detect plasma cells in tissue samples, experts use features on the cell surface. A frequently used marker is called **CD138**, also called syndecan-1.

gewusst: A single plasma cell can make thousands of antibodies per second.
The name plasma cell comes from the 19th century, when the cells were described under the microscope because of their striking cytoplasm.

teile.einleitung: The shinbone is the large, strong bone at the front of the lower leg. It carries most of our body weight and is part of the knee and ankle.
wichtigste: The shinbone is called the tibia in technical language.
It carries most of the body weight in the lower leg.
With the thigh bone it forms the knee joint.
The inner ankle bone belongs to the shinbone.
A knock hurts because the bone lies directly under the skin.
In football, shin pads are compulsory.

abschnitte.text: In the lower leg there are two bones: the **shinbone** at the inner front and the thinner **fibula** on the outside. The shinbone, in Latin **tibia**, is much thicker. It carries most of the **body weight**. After the thigh bone, it is one of the longest bones in the body.

At the top, the shinbone forms the **knee joint** together with the **thigh bone**. At the bottom it is part of the ankle joint. The **inner ankle bone**, which you can feel on the inside of the foot, is the lower end of the shinbone. The outer ankle bone belongs to the fibula.

abschnitte.titel: Why a knock hurts so much
abschnitte.text: At its front edge, the shinbone lies **directly under the skin**. There, neither muscles nor fat cushion it. The periosteum is very sensitive. That is why even a light knock, for example against the edge of a bed, hurts especially badly.
In football there are often kicks against the shin. That is why the rules of the game require **shin pads**. In ice hockey and in combat sports too, the shin is protected.

Below the knee, the shinbone has a small **bump**. The ligament of the **kneecap** attaches there, which transfers the force of the thigh muscle. In sporty young people who are growing, this bump can hurt. This condition is called **Osgood-Schlatter disease**. It usually heals by itself once growth is finished.

gewusst: The name “tibia” also means “flute” in Latin, because in the past flutes were carved from such bones.
Shin pads have existed in football since the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: The school bag accompanies children to school every day. In Switzerland it is often called a “Thek”. To keep the back healthy, weight, packing and carrying matter.
wichtigste: A packed school bag should weigh at most about 10 per cent of body weight.
At 35 kg of body weight, that is 3.5 kg.
You carry it with both straps on your back.
Heavy books are packed close to the back.
Bright colours and reflectors make children visible in traffic.
A chest or hip strap spreads the load.

abschnitte.text: The **school bag** is a firm bag that you carry on your back. In Switzerland it is colloquially often called a **Thek**. It has a sturdy base and a firm back panel so that exercise books and books do not get bent. Children in kindergarten often have a smaller little bag for their mid-morning snack. Older pupils often take a rucksack.

Specialists recommend that a packed school bag should weigh at most **about 10 per cent of body weight**. A child of 35 kg should therefore carry no more than **3.5 kg**. You can easily add up the weight: an empty bag of 1.2 kg, books of 2.5 kg and a snack of 0.3 kg together make **4 kg**. That would already be a little too much for this child. So it is worth packing only what is needed.

Heavy things such as books belong **close to the back**. That way the bag pulls less backwards. You always carry it with **both straps** and not just over one shoulder. You adjust the straps so that the bag sits well on the back and does not hang too low. A **chest or hip strap** holds it firm and spreads the load better.

Many children walk to school. That is why school bags have **bright colours** and **reflectors**. Reflectors throw back the light of car headlights and light up brightly at dusk. This way drivers see the children sooner. Especially in winter, when it is still dark in the morning, this is important.

gewusst: Even small children can learn to pack their bag themselves in the evening.
Reflectors can be seen from far away in headlight beams.

teile.einleitung: The oxygen dissociation curve shows how much oxygen the haemoglobin in the blood has bound at a given oxygen pressure. It explains why the blood takes up a lot of oxygen in the lungs and gives it up again in the tissue.
wichtigste: Haemoglobin is the red blood pigment and transports oxygen.
The binding curve of haemoglobin is S-shaped.
The S shape arises because the four subunits work together.
At about 27 mmHg, adult haemoglobin is half saturated (P50).
Heat and the substance 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shift the curve to the right.
Myoglobin in muscle has a hyperbolic curve.
Healthy arterial blood is about 97 per cent saturated at sea level.

abschnitte.text: On the horizontal axis is the **partial pressure of oxygen**, that is, how much oxygen is currently present. On the vertical axis is the **saturation**: what share of the haemoglobin is carrying oxygen. The curve of haemoglobin is **S-shaped**, also called sigmoid. In the middle range it rises steeply, at high pressure it flattens off. In the lungs the pressure is high, and the blood is loaded almost fully. Healthy arterial blood is about **97 per cent** saturated at sea level.

A haemoglobin molecule consists of **four subunits**, and each can carry one oxygen molecule. When the first subunit binds oxygen, the shape of the whole molecule changes. As a result the others bind more easily. This is called **cooperative binding**. It produces the steep middle part: even small differences in pressure in the tissue release a lot of oxygen.

The **P50** is the pressure at which half of the haemoglobin is loaded. In adults it is about **27 mmHg**. If the P50 is higher, haemoglobin gives up oxygen more easily. If it is lower, it holds on to the oxygen more firmly.

A **rise in temperature**, more acid and more carbon dioxide shift the curve to the right. That fits well: working muscles are warm and acidic and so get more oxygen. The substance **2,3-bisphosphoglycerate** in the red blood cells also shifts the curve to the right. It increases when you live at high altitude for a longer time. **Myoglobin**, the oxygen store in muscle, has only one subunit. Its curve is therefore hyperbolic and lies far to the left.

**Carbon monoxide** is a poisonous gas with no smell that is produced by incomplete combustion. Haemoglobin binds it about **200 to 300 times** more strongly than oxygen. Then there is less room for oxygen, and the bound oxygen is given up less well. That is why detectors for carbon monoxide make sense in some homes.

gewusst: The S shape of the curve was already measured at the start of the 20th century.
The shift to the right caused by acid and carbon dioxide is called the **Bohr effect**.

teile.einleitung: Salty is one of the basic tastes that our tongue can recognise. We taste it mainly when there is table salt in food. Our body needs a little salt, but too much of it is not healthy.
wichtigste: **Crisps** mostly taste salty.
Salty is one of the **basic tastes**, alongside sweet, sour, bitter and umami.
In Switzerland salt is obtained at the **saltworks on the Rhine** and in **Bex**.
The body needs a little salt so that **nerves and muscles** work well.
**Tears** and sweat taste salty.
Anyone who eats a lot of salty food often gets **thirsty**.

abschnitte.text: Our tongue can recognise five **basic tastes**: sweet, sour, **salty**, bitter and umami. We taste salty mainly because of **table salt**. Chemically it is called **sodium chloride**. Many foods taste salty, for example **crisps**, pretzels or cheese. On the breakfast egg you sprinkle a little **salt**.

In Switzerland, salt is obtained from the ground. Deep underground lie old layers of salt. Water is pumped down, the salt dissolves in it, and the salt water is brought up again. Then the water is evaporated, and the salt is left. This happens at the **saltworks on the Rhine** and in **Bex** in the canton of Vaud. In Bex you can even visit an old salt mine.

Our body needs a little salt so that **nerves and muscles** work well. Salt also helps to regulate the water balance in the body. That is why **tears** and **sweat** are salty too. Anyone who eats a lot of salty food often gets **thirsty**. In this way the body fetches water to balance out the salt. Too much salt over a long time is not healthy, though, and can raise blood pressure.

Salt is not needed only in the kitchen. In winter, **salt is spread on the road**. Salt water freezes only at lower temperatures than pure water. That is why **the ice melts** and the roads become less slippery. A large part of the salt from the Swiss saltworks is used as road salt.

gewusst: In the past, salt was so valuable that it was called “white gold”.
Sea water is salty because a great deal of salt is dissolved in it.

teile.einleitung: Mucous membranes line the inside of many hollow spaces in the body, such as the nose, mouth, airways and stomach. They are moist and form an important protective layer against dust and disease-causing agents.
wichtigste: Mucous membrane lines, for example, the inside of the nasal cavity.
The mucus holds on to dust and germs.
Cilia move the mucus towards the throat.
Sneezing and coughing clear the nose and bronchi.
On mucous membranes, immunoglobulin A is especially common.
The conjunctiva covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelid.

abschnitte.text: Mucous membranes are found in the **nasal cavity**, in the mouth, in the throat, in the bronchi, in the stomach and in the gut. The eye has one too: the **conjunctiva**. It covers the white part of the eye and the inside of the eyelids. Mucous membranes are moist because they constantly make **mucus**.

abschnitte.titel: The cleaning crew of the airways
abschnitte.text: In the airways, the mucus holds on to **dust and germs** like a sticky trap. Tiny **cilia** move in waves and carry the mucus towards the throat. There it is swallowed or coughed up. This keeps the lungs clean.

If irritants get into the nose, the **sneeze reflex** hurls them out at high speed. The **cough reflex** frees the **bronchi** of mucus. If the lining of the nose is inflamed, it is called **rhinitis**. This is the case, for example, with a cold.
On mucous membranes, the antibody **immunoglobulin A**, IgA for short, is especially common. It catches germs before they enter the body. Together with the mucus, it forms a first line of defence.

In the stomach there is very strong **acid** that breaks down food. A **thick layer of mucus** protects the stomach lining from being attacked by this very acid. In addition, the stomach lining renews itself continually.

gewusst: A person makes a considerable amount of mucus every day, which they mostly swallow without noticing.
When you sneeze, the air shoots out of the nose and mouth at high speed.

teile.einleitung: The thyroid gland is a small hormone gland at the front of the neck, shaped like a butterfly. It regulates the body’s metabolism through hormones. For this it needs iodine, which we take in with food.
wichtigste: The thyroid gland lies at the front of the neck below the larynx.
It regulates the body’s metabolism through hormones.
Its most important hormones are called thyroxine and triiodothyronine.
For the hormones it needs iodine.
In Switzerland, table salt has been enriched with iodine since 1922.
A lack of iodine can lead to an enlargement of the thyroid gland, the goitre.
The thyroid gland is controlled by the pituitary gland.

abschnitte.text: The **thyroid gland** lies at the front of the neck, below the larynx and in front of the windpipe. It has two lobes that are joined by a narrow bridge. That is why it looks like a butterfly. In adults it weighs about 20 to 25 grams.

The thyroid gland makes the hormones **thyroxine** and triiodothyronine, abbreviated T4 and T3. They determine how fast the body uses energy, that is, the **metabolism**. They influence heartbeat, body temperature and digestion. In children they are also important for growth and the development of the brain.

For its hormones, the thyroid gland needs **iodine**. In the Alpine countries, soils and drinking water contain little iodine. That is why in the past many people in Switzerland had a **goitre**, that is, a greatly enlarged thyroid gland. Since 1922, table salt in Switzerland has been enriched with iodine, and goitre has become rare since then.

If the thyroid gland makes too few hormones, it is called an **underactive thyroid**. Those affected are often tired, feel the cold easily and put on weight. With an overactive thyroid, the heart beats fast, you sweat, are restless and lose weight. Both disorders can be treated well with medicines.

The thyroid gland does not work alone. The **pituitary gland** in the head constantly measures how much thyroid hormone is in the blood. If there is too little, it sends a signal hormone that drives the thyroid gland. This creates a control loop like a thermostat.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the chemical processes by which the body gains energy and converts substances.
A trace element that the thyroid gland needs for its hormones.
A strong enlargement of the thyroid gland.
The most important hormone of the thyroid gland.

gewusst: The Bernese surgeon Theodor Kocher received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1909 as the first Swiss, for his research on the thyroid gland.
In newborns in Switzerland, thyroid function is checked with a small blood test from the heel.
Sea fish and algae are among the foods richest in iodine.

teile.einleitung: Poliomyelitis, polio for short or infantile paralysis, is a viral disease that can cause paralysis. Thanks to vaccinations it has today almost disappeared from the whole world.
wichtigste: Polio is caused by the poliovirus, an enterovirus.
It is passed on faecal-orally through dirty hands, water or food.
Fewer than 1 per cent of infections lead to paralysis.
The virus can destroy motor nerve cells in the spinal cord.
Jonas Salk developed the first successful inactivated vaccine, licensed in 1955.
The WHO European Region has been polio-free since 2002.
In 2025 wild polio was endemic only in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

abschnitte.text: The **poliovirus** belongs to the **enteroviruses**. It multiplies in the **gut** and is passed out in the stool. It is passed on **faecal-orally**, that is, through dirty hands, contaminated water or food. The great majority of infections run without complaints or with mild ones. That is why the virus can spread unnoticed.

In **fewer than one per cent** of infections the virus gets into the nervous system. It can then destroy the **motor nerve cells** in the spinal cord, which send commands to the muscles. The muscles concerned fail, and **flaccid paralysis** results, often in the legs. If the breathing muscles are paralysed, it becomes life-threatening. In the 1950s the **iron lung** kept such patients alive. It produced negative pressure in a tank, so that the rib cage rose.

**Jonas Salk** developed a vaccine with killed, **inactivated** viruses. It was licensed in **1955** and is injected (IPV). This vaccine is used today in **Switzerland** too. **Albert Sabin** developed an **oral vaccine** with weakened viruses. It is easy to give, but has a rare risk: in poorly vaccinated areas the vaccine viruses can change and themselves cause paralysis.

Since 1988 a **global polio initiative** has been fighting the disease. Of the three types of the wild virus, **type 2** was declared eradicated in 2015 and **type 3** in 2019. Only **type 1** still circulates. As of 2025 the wild virus was endemic, that is, permanently widespread, only in **Pakistan** and **Afghanistan**.

The **WHO European Region**, to which Switzerland also belongs, was declared free of wild polio in June **2002**. All the same the virus can be brought in from other countries. That is why the **Swiss vaccination schedule** continues to recommend polio vaccination for all children. Only if almost everyone is vaccinated does the disease stay away.

gewusst: The word poliomyelitis means roughly “inflammation of the grey matter of the spinal cord”.
After smallpox, polio could be the second human disease to be eradicated worldwide.

teile.einleitung: Smallpox was a dangerous viral disease that killed many people over centuries. Thanks to worldwide vaccinations it is today eradicated, the first human disease ever to be so.
wichtigste: Smallpox is caused by the variola virus.
In the severe form, variola major, about one in three people who fell ill died.
Many survivors kept scars on the skin.
Edward Jenner vaccinated for the first time with cowpox in 1796.
The word vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, cow.
The disease is eradicated, which is why people in Switzerland no longer vaccinate against it.
Samples are kept only in two high-security laboratories in the USA and Russia.

abschnitte.text: Smallpox is caused by the **variola virus**. The name comes from the Latin word **“varius”**, meaning coloured or spotted. The virus is passed on **from person to person**. On the skin **blisters** filled with fluid form. In the severe form, **variola major**, about **one in three** people who fell ill died. Many survivors kept deep **scars**, and some went blind.

Long before modern vaccination people looked for protection. In **variolation** healthy people were deliberately infected with material from real smallpox blisters. Mostly they then fell ill more mildly and were protected afterwards. But the method was dangerous, because some became seriously ill. It was later replaced by the safer **vaccination**.

The English country doctor **Edward Jenner** observed that milkmaids were often protected from real smallpox after harmless **cowpox**. In **1796** he vaccinated the boy **James Phipps** with cowpox material. After that the boy was protected. The word **vaccine** comes from the Latin **“vacca”**, cow. Cowpox was then called “vaccinia”.

The World Health Organization **WHO** started a great programme against smallpox. The success was possible because the virus attacks **only humans** and cannot hide in animals. If all the people around a case were vaccinated, the chain of infection broke. In **1980** the WHO declared smallpox **eradicated**. That is why vaccination is no longer necessary in **Switzerland** either.

After the end of smallpox almost all virus samples were destroyed. Only two strictly guarded **high-security laboratories**, one in the **USA** and one in **Russia**, may still keep samples. Whether they should be kept for research or destroyed has long been discussed. Experts have different opinions on this.

gewusst: To this day smallpox is the only human disease that has been eradicated worldwide.
The last natural case of smallpox occurred in 1977 in Somalia.

teile.einleitung: In the brain there is a small control centre, the **hypothalamus**. It sends messenger substances to the pituitary gland and in this way gives it orders. These messenger substances are called **releasing hormones**.
wichtigste: Releasing hormones are made in the hypothalamus.
They make the pituitary gland release its own hormones.
TRH makes the pituitary release TSH, and CRH makes it release ACTH.
GHRH promotes the release of growth hormone, and somatostatin inhibits it.
Most releasing hormones are peptides, that is, short chains of protein.
TRH consists of only 3 amino acids.

abschnitte.text: The **hypothalamus** is a small part of the diencephalon. Directly beneath it hangs the **pituitary gland**. The hypothalamus makes hormones that reach the pituitary through fine blood vessels. These **releasing hormones** order it to release certain hormones of its own into the blood. The hormones of the pituitary then control other glands in the body in turn.

**TRH** (thyrotropin-releasing hormone) makes the pituitary release **TSH**. TSH stimulates the thyroid gland. **CRH** is also called **corticoliberin** and leads to the release of **ACTH**. ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce the stress hormone cortisol. **GHRH** promotes the release of **growth hormone**.

The hypothalamus can not only drive but also brake. Such substances are called inhibiting hormones. **Somatostatin** inhibits the release of growth hormone. The messenger substance **dopamine** inhibits the release of **prolactin** from the pituitary. In this way the body keeps the amounts of hormones in balance.

Most releasing hormones belong to the **peptides**. These are short chains of **amino acids**, the building blocks of proteins. TRH is especially small and consists of only **three amino acids**. Other releasing hormones are much longer. Because they work in very small amounts, researching them was difficult.

gewusst: For discovering hormones of the hypothalamus, Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1977.
Releasing hormones work even in tiny amounts, far less than a millionth of a gram.

teile.einleitung: Rubella is a contagious disease caused by a virus. Typical are small light red spots on the skin. In children the disease is mostly mild.
wichtigste: Rubella is caused by the **rubella virus**.
Typical are **small light red spots** on the skin.
The rash usually begins **on the face**.
The **lymph nodes in the neck** often swell.
The rash usually lasts only **1 to 3 days**.
Some children hardly notice the disease.

abschnitte.text: Rubella is an **infectious disease**. It is caused by the **rubella virus**. The virus is passed on through fine droplets when coughing, sneezing or speaking. In German, rubella is called Röteln, from the **red spots** on the skin. Between catching the infection and the first signs, usually two to three weeks pass.

Typical are **small light red spots**. The rash usually begins **on the face** and then spreads over the body. It usually lasts only **1 to 3 days**. Often the **lymph nodes in the neck** and behind the ears swell. Some children also have a slight fever or feel a bit tired.

In children, rubella is **mostly mild**. Many hardly notice it or have only a few spots. That is why not every child knows that they had rubella. If you are ill, you should rest and drink plenty. If you have had rubella once, you are usually protected for life afterwards.

There is a **vaccination** against rubella. In Switzerland it is usually given together with the vaccination against measles and mumps, as the **MMR vaccination**. Two doses are recommended in early childhood. The vaccination protects not only the vaccinated child but also helps the virus to spread less. In this way it also protects people for whom an infection would be more dangerous.

gewusst: Because many people are vaccinated, rubella has become rare in Switzerland today.
Rubella is usually much more harmless than measles, although both cause red spots.

teile.einleitung: A power nap is a short sleep in the day that is meant to give new energy. Done properly, it makes you more awake without your being tired and groggy afterwards.
wichtigste: A power nap ideally lasts about 10 to 20 minutes.
If you sleep much longer, you get into deep sleep and feel groggy afterwards.
The early afternoon is best suited.
An alarm clock helps so that the sleep does not last too long.
In Spain the traditional midday rest is called the siesta.
In 1995 NASA investigated in pilots the effect of a short sleep of about 26 minutes.

abschnitte.text: The secret of a power nap is its shortness. About **10 to 20 minutes** are ideal. In this time you stay in light sleep. If the sleep lasts much longer than 20 to 30 minutes, you get into **deep sleep**. If you are then woken, you often feel heavy and groggy. That is why it is worth setting an **alarm clock**.

Many people become tired in the **early afternoon**, often after lunch. This is called the afternoon dip. Just then a power nap suits especially well. If you sleep in the late afternoon or in the evening, on the other hand, this can disturb your sleep at night. A power nap also does not replace good sleep at night.

In many countries a break at midday is part of tradition. In Spain there is the **siesta**, a rest in the hot midday hours. In Japan there is **inemuri**: there it is often accepted to doze off briefly in a meeting or on the train. In German a short sleep in the day is simply called a **Nickerchen** (nap).

The American space agency **NASA** investigated in 1995 the effect of short sleep in **pilots** on long flights. The pilots were allowed to rest in the cockpit for about 26 minutes while their colleagues flew. Afterwards they were more alert and reacted better. Such studies made the term power nap known. Pupils too can profit from a short break, for example before homework.

gewusst: Even a few minutes of rest with closed eyes can be restful, even if you do not really fall asleep.
The English word “power” means strength, and “nap” means a short sleep.

teile.einleitung: The shoulder blade is a flat, triangular bone at the back of the upper body. It belongs to the shoulder girdle and forms the socket of the shoulder joint. In Latin it is called the scapula.
wichtigste: The Latin technical term for the shoulder blade is scapula.
It lies at about the level of the 2nd to 7th rib.
At the acromion it is joined to the collarbone by a small joint.
On the trunk it is attached mainly by muscles.
The spine of the scapula is a ridge of bone on the back.
The rotator cuff holds the head of the upper arm in the socket.
If the shoulder blade stands out clearly, it is called a winged scapula.

abschnitte.text: The **shoulder blade**, in Latin **scapula**, is a flat, roughly triangular bone. It lies on each side at the back of the rib cage, at about the level of the **2nd to 7th rib**. The tip of the triangle points downwards. You can feel the shoulder blade easily under the skin, especially when you move the arm backwards.

On the back runs a strong ridge of bone, the **spine of the scapula**. It ends on the outside in the **acromion**, the highest point of the shoulder. There the shoulder blade is joined to the **collarbone** by a small joint. At the front, below the collarbone, the **coracoid process** juts out, where muscles and ligaments attach. At the side lies the shallow **socket** for the head of the upper arm.
