Unlike most bones, the shoulder blade is not joined to the trunk by a large joint. It is attached to the rib cage mainly by **muscles**. That is why it can glide on the back, rise, sink and turn. This mobility makes it possible to raise the arm very high. From the shoulder blade also comes the **rotator cuff**, a group of muscles that holds the head of the upper arm in the socket.

Normally the shoulder blade lies flat against the back. If it stands out clearly from the back, it is called a **winged scapula**. This can happen if a certain muscle on the rib cage is too weak or its nerve has been injured. It often shows when you support yourself with your hands against a wall. Targeted training and physiotherapy can help.

gewusst: The name coracoid process comes from the fact that this part of the bone resembles a curved bird’s beak.
Because it hangs mainly on muscles, the shoulder blade can turn clearly when the arm is raised.

teile.einleitung: After digestion, the food building blocks are small enough to get into the blood. This uptake through the gut wall is called **absorption**. It takes place mainly in the small intestine.
wichtigste: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
Tiny bulges, the microvilli, form the brush border and enlarge the surface.
Glucose gets into the gut cell together with sodium.
For vitamin B12, the intrinsic factor from the stomach is needed.
Fats and the vitamins A, D, E and K first go into the lymphatic system.
The portal vein brings sugar and amino acids first to the liver.

abschnitte.text: The **small intestine** is the most important place of absorption. Its inner wall is strongly folded and covered with finger-shaped **villi**. The gut cells themselves carry even tinier bulges, the **microvilli**. Together they form the **brush border**. This creates a very large surface through which nutrients are taken up.

**Glucose**, that is, grape sugar, gets into the gut cell by **secondary active transport**. That means it is carried through a transporter together with **sodium**. **Fructose**, fruit sugar, takes a different route via the transporter **GLUT5**. Proteins are broken down into amino acids and small pieces. Di- and tripeptides, that is, chains of two or three amino acids, get into the cell together with protons via **PepT1**.

Fats do not dissolve in water. With the help of bile, they form tiny droplets, the **micelles**. The fat-soluble **vitamins A, D, E and K** also need these micelles to be absorbed. In the gut cell, the fats are packed into transport packages, the **chylomicrons**. These first get into the **lymphatic system** and only later into the blood.

Sugar and amino acids go straight into the blood. The **portal vein** collects this blood from the gut and brings it first to the **liver**. The liver checks the substances, stores some of them and makes harmful substances harmless. Only after that does the blood reach the rest of the body. In this way the liver is a kind of checkpoint.

**Vitamin B12** needs a helper to be absorbed. The parietal cells of the stomach make the **intrinsic factor** for this. Vitamin B12 binds to it and is only absorbed in the last section of the small intestine. If the intrinsic factor is missing, a deficiency of B12 can arise. Such a deficiency can lead to anaemia.

gewusst: The inner surface of the small intestine is about as large as a small flat, around 30 to 40 square metres.
A large part of the water is only taken back from the food pulp in the large intestine.

teile.einleitung: Pollen flight (in German Pollenflug) is the name for the pollen that flies through the air. How much pollen is on the move depends on the season, the weather and the place.
wichtigste: The pollen concentration is given in pollen grains per cubic metre of air.
A pollen trap sucks in air and collects the pollen on an adhesive strip.
Grass pollen fly in Switzerland mainly from May to July.
The introduced ragweed (Ambrosia) flowers in late summer and is controlled.
Rain washes pollen out of the air.
In the mountains the load is mostly lower.
Because of climate change the pollen season begins earlier and lasts longer.

abschnitte.text: A classic measuring device is the **pollen trap**. It sucks in air continuously. The pollen stick to an **adhesive strip**. Experts then identify and count them under the **microscope**. The amount is given in **pollen grains per cubic metre of air**. In Switzerland **MeteoSwiss** runs a measuring network and publishes pollen forecasts.

Different plants flower at different times. **Hazel** and **alder** can flower as early as January or February. In spring trees such as the **birch** follow. **Grasses** flower mainly in late spring and early summer, in Switzerland chiefly from **May to July**. In this time most pollen allergy sufferers are affected most strongly.

**Ragweed** (Ambrosia) comes from **North America** and was brought into Europe. It flowers from about **August to October**. Its pollen is very **allergenic**, and even a few can trigger complaints. That is why the plant is consistently **controlled** in Switzerland. Whoever discovers it can report it to the authorities of the municipality or the canton.

A longer-lasting **rain** binds the pollen and brings it to the ground. Afterwards the air is often markedly lower in pollen. It is different at the start of a **thunderstorm**: moisture makes pollen grains **burst**, and gusts of wind spread the tiny fragments. These get deep into the airways and can trigger **thunderstorm asthma**. In the **mountains** fewer plants flower and only later, which is why the load there is mostly lower.

Warmer temperatures make many plants **flower earlier**. Measurements by MeteoSwiss show that the pollen season begins earlier in several species. In some it also lasts **longer**. For allergy sufferers this means a longer time with complaints. New plants such as ragweed can also spread more easily.

gewusst: Pollen grains are so small that you can recognise them properly only under the microscope, and every plant species has its own shape.
A single ragweed plant can make very large amounts of pollen.

teile.einleitung: Prions are special disease-causing agents. They are neither bacteria nor viruses, but consist only of protein. They can cause serious diseases of the brain, in animals and in humans.
wichtigste: Prions consist of misfolded protein.
They multiply by making normal proteins fold incorrectly as well.
Stanley Prusiner coined the term prion and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1997.
BSE in cattle also concerned Switzerland in the 1990s.
In humans, prions cause for example Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
Prions survive many common sterilisation methods.

abschnitte.titel: A protein in the wrong shape
abschnitte.text: Proteins are long chains that fold into a particular shape. Only in the right shape can they do their job. A **prion** is a protein that is folded wrongly. The special thing is this: when it meets a normal protein of the same kind, it makes that protein fold wrongly too. This creates a chain reaction. The misfolded proteins clump together and little by little damage the **brain**.

For a long time people believed that every disease-causing agent needs genetic material. The American researcher **Stanley Prusiner** put forward the idea that a protein alone can be infectious. He coined the word **prion**, a short form of the English for proteinaceous infectious particle. At first his idea was very controversial. In 1997 he received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine** for it.

The best-known prion disease in animals is **BSE**, popularly called mad cow disease. In the 1990s there were cases of BSE in Great Britain and also in **Switzerland**. The authorities took strict measures, for example they banned feeding meat-and-bone meal to cattle. In sheep and goats there has been a prion disease called **scrapie** for a very long time.

In humans, **Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease** is the best-known prion disease. It is very rare but takes a severe course. One form of it was linked to BSE. In **Papua New Guinea**, a disease called **kuru** appeared among one people. It was passed on through certain mourning rituals and disappeared when these customs were given up.

Prions are surprisingly resistant. They survive many common **sterilisation methods** that are otherwise used to kill bacteria and viruses. That is why surgical instruments must be treated in a special way, or even thrown away, if prions are suspected. In hospitals strict rules apply for this.

gewusst: Prions have no genetic material of their own and can still spread in the body.
For his research on kuru, the American Carleton Gajdusek received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1976.

teile.einleitung: How does the body notice that it is bright, that something smells nice or that someone touches us? For this there are **receptors**. These sense cells pick up stimuli and translate them into nerve signals.
wichtigste: A sensory receptor changes a stimulus into an electrical nerve signal.
The adequate stimulus is the stimulus to which a receptor reacts most sensitively.
The sense cells for smell and taste are chemoreceptors.
With an unchanging stimulus, receptors get used to it.
Actual perception arises in the brain.
Sharks use electroreceptors to sense weak electric fields.

abschnitte.text: A **sensory receptor** is a cell or part of a cell that picks up stimuli. It **changes the stimulus into an electrical nerve signal**. This signal is sent along nerves to the brain. Every receptor reacts especially sensitively to a certain kind of stimulus. This is called the **adequate stimulus**, for the eyes for example light.

Receptors are classified by their stimuli. **Chemoreceptors** react to substances, and the sense cells for **smell and taste** belong to them. **Photoreceptors** in the eye react to light. **Mechanoreceptors** sense pressure, touch or sound. There are also receptors for warmth, cold and pain.

In the morning you can still feel your socks, but after a while you no longer can. This is because many receptors **get used to an unchanging stimulus**. They then send fewer signals. This getting used to it is called **adaptation**. That way the brain stays free for new and important stimuli.

The actual perception, for example of a smell, only arises **in the brain**. The receptors just deliver signals. The brain interprets them depending on which sense organ they come from. If you press hard on your closed eyes, the pressure stimulates the **retina**. The brain interprets the signal as light, and you see patches of light.

Some animals have receptors that we lack. **Sharks** use **electroreceptors** to sense the weak electric fields of their prey, even when it is hidden in the sand. The **mantis shrimp** has especially many kinds of light receptors. It can even see **UV light**, which is invisible to humans. Bees also perceive UV light.

gewusst: Humans have three kinds of cones for colour vision, while the mantis shrimp has many more kinds of light receptors.
In a human eye there are over 100 million light receptors.

teile.einleitung: School sport is PE lessons at school. In Switzerland people often simply say “Turnen”. In it, children move, play together and get to know many sports.
wichtigste: The federal government requires at least 3 sport lessons a week in compulsory school, excluding kindergarten.
When it rains, the lesson takes place in the gym.
In the gym you wear trainers with light soles.
In basketball you throw the ball into a basket, in dodgeball you hit opponents.
On sports day the whole school holds competitions outdoors.
A sprint is a short, fast run.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, PE is regulated in a **federal law**, the Sports Promotion Act. For compulsory school it requires at least **three sport lessons a week**, with kindergarten excepted. Sport is thus a compulsory subject like German or mathematics. Regular exercise strengthens muscles, bones and heart. It also helps you to concentrate better afterwards.

In fine weather the class often goes to the **sports field**, when it rains into the **gym**. There you wear **trainers with light soles**, because dark soles leave black marks on the floor. In the hall there is equipment such as rings, parallel bars, horizontal bar, vaulting buck and mats. With them you practise climbing, swinging, jumping and rolling. Before sport you warm up so that muscles and joints are ready.

Ball games are very popular in school sport. In **basketball** you try to throw the ball into a basket hanging high up. In **dodgeball**, two teams play against each other and try to hit opponents with the ball. Football, floorball and volleyball are also often played. In team games you learn to be fair and to work together.

**Athletics** includes running, jumping and throwing. A **sprint** is a short, fast run, for example over 60 or 80 metres. In the **long jump** you take a run-up, take off from the board and land in the **sandpit**. The sand cushions the landing, and you can measure the distance well. In ball throwing or shot put, what counts is how far you throw.

Once a year at many schools there is a **sports day**. Then the whole school holds competitions outdoors, often in relays and groups. Some schools organise a **ski camp** in winter. For sport outside lessons, Switzerland has the programme **Youth+Sport** (Jugend+Sport), which the federal government supports. There children and young people can try out many sports in courses and camps.

gewusst: The Federal Sports School is in Magglingen above Biel.
In some regions dodgeball is also called Abwerfen or Jägerball.

teile.einleitung: Insomnia means that you fall asleep badly, often wake up at night or wake too early. Almost everyone knows this occasionally, but some people suffer from it for a long time.
wichtigste: The technical term for sleeplessness is insomnia.
It is chronic at three nights a week over three months.
Adenosine builds up sleep pressure while awake.
Brooding over worries keeps many people awake.
The first choice for long-lasting insomnia is cognitive behavioural therapy.
Many sleeping pills can lead to dependence if taken for longer.

abschnitte.text: In **insomnia** you fall asleep badly, wake up often or are awake too early in the morning. By day you then feel tired and irritable. It is called **chronic insomnia** when the problems occur on at least **three nights a week** over **three months**.

While we are awake, the substance **adenosine** builds up in the brain. It creates the **sleep pressure**: the longer you are awake, the more tired you become. In sleep, adenosine is broken down again. Caffeine blocks the effect of adenosine, which is why coffee keeps you awake.

Many people with insomnia lie awake and **brood over worries**. The more you get annoyed that you are not sleeping, the more awake you become. If you cannot fall asleep after about **20 minutes**, specialists advise: **get up** and do something calm until you are tired.

Rules and habits that promote good sleep are called **sleep hygiene**. These include fixed sleep times, a cool, dark room and little screen time before sleeping. You should also avoid caffeine in the evening.

For long-lasting insomnia, **cognitive behavioural therapy** is the first choice. Here you learn to change thoughts and habits around sleep. **Sleeping pills** help in the short term, but many can **lead to dependence** if taken for longer. That is why you take them only briefly and after medical advice.

gewusst: The word “insomnia” comes from the Latin “somnus”, which means sleep.
Many people sleep worse on the first night in an unfamiliar place.

teile.einleitung: How long we have to sleep depends mainly on age. Babies sleep a great deal, adults clearly less. Enough sleep is important for health, growth and learning.
wichtigste: Newborns sleep the most.
Teenagers aged 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours.
Adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep.
People sleep through about a third of their lives.
Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day.

abschnitte.text: **Newborns** sleep the most, often around 14 to 17 hours a day, spread over many short naps. School children usually need about 9 to 12 hours. **Teenagers** aged 13 to 18 need **8 to 10 hours**. **Adults** manage with **7 to 9 hours**.

You can calculate well with sleep times. Someone who sleeps **from 8 pm to 7 am** sleeps **11 hours**. Someone who gets up at 7 am and wants to sleep 10 hours has to go to bed at **9 pm**. If someone sleeps 10 hours every night, that is 7 times 10, so **70 hours**, in a week.

People sleep through about **a third** of their lives. That is not lost time. In sleep the body recovers, the brain sorts what has been learned and the immune system is strengthened. Children grow mainly in sleep.

abschnitte.titel: Long sleepers in the animal kingdom
abschnitte.text: The **koala** sleeps up to **20 hours** a day. Its food, eucalyptus leaves, gives very little energy. Sloths and bats also sleep very long. Giraffes and elephants, on the other hand, sleep only a few hours.

gewusst: A regular sleep rhythm, even at the weekend, helps with falling asleep.
A person who lives to 75 sleeps about 25 years in total.

teile.einleitung: Samaritans give first aid and look after people at accidents or at large events. In Switzerland they are organised in Samaritan societies in many municipalities. Most of them work as volunteers.
wichtigste: The word goes back to the **parable of the Good Samaritan** in the Bible.
Since 2022 the umbrella organisation has been called **Samariter Schweiz**.
The first societies joined together in an association in **1888**.
The association has its seat in **Olten**.
Samaritans often provide **medical cover and first aid** at fairs and sporting events.
The youth groups are called **Help**.

abschnitte.text: The word **Samaritan** comes from the Bible. In the **parable of the Good Samaritan**, Jesus tells of a man who lies injured by the wayside. Several people walk past him. Only a man from Samaria stops, tends his wounds and takes him to an inn. Since then the word Samaritan has stood for a person who helps others in need.

In **1888** the first Samaritan societies of Switzerland joined together in a common association. For a long time it was called the Swiss Samaritan Federation. Since **2022** the umbrella organisation has been called **Samariter Schweiz**. Its seat is in **Olten** in the canton of Solothurn. It is linked to the **Swiss Red Cross** and is one of its rescue organisations.

At **folk festivals**, concerts and **sporting events**, Samaritans often take over the **medical cover**. They give **first aid** when someone gets hurt or feels unwell. They also help with blood donation drives. Many societies offer courses, for example the **emergency aid course** that you need in Switzerland for the learner driver’s permit.

Most Samaritans work **voluntarily and unpaid**. That means they receive no wages for their work. They practise regularly so that they act correctly in an emergency. For children and young people there are special groups called **Help**. There they learn in a playful way how to give first aid.

gewusst: Many municipalities in Switzerland have their own Samaritan society.
Anyone who knows first aid can bridge the time in an emergency until the ambulance service arrives.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland every person must have health insurance for basic cover. For many households the premiums are a heavy burden. With the individual premium reduction, the Confederation and the cantons help people with lower incomes.
wichtigste: IPV stands for individual premium reduction.
The premium reduction is paid for by the Confederation and the cantons.
The cantons decide who is entitled to it and how much they get.
Premiums for children from households with low and middle incomes are reduced by at least 80 per cent.
For young adults in training it is at least 50 per cent.
The Confederation pays 7.5 per cent of the gross costs of basic insurance towards the premium reduction.
In 2024 the voters rejected the Premium Relief Initiative.

abschnitte.text: Since 1996 the Health Insurance Act, or **KVG** for short, has applied in Switzerland. Since then **basic insurance** has been compulsory for everyone. The premium does not depend on income: a person with a small wage pays the same as a person with a large wage with the same insurer and the same plan. So that premiums stay affordable for households with little money, there is the **individual premium reduction**, or **IPV** for short.

The premium reduction is paid for jointly by the **Confederation and the cantons**. The Confederation pays a fixed contribution of **7.5 per cent** of the gross costs of basic insurance. The cantons add money of their own. Because every canton has its own rules, the support can be very different depending on where you live.

The **cantons** decide who is entitled to a premium reduction and how high it is. Mostly they look at taxable income and assets. In some cantons the reduction is paid out automatically, in others you have to make an application. The money usually goes straight to the health insurer, which then sends a lower bill.

For families there are rules set by the Confederation. For households with low and middle incomes, the cantons must reduce the premiums of **children** by at least **80 per cent**. For **young adults in training** it is at least **50 per cent**. This is meant to make sure that families with children are not burdened too heavily.

How much premiums should be reduced is a matter of political dispute. In 2024 Switzerland voted on the **Premium Relief Initiative**. It wanted to make sure that nobody has to pay more than **10 per cent** of their disposable income on premiums. Supporters saw it as necessary relief, while opponents warned of high costs for the Confederation and the cantons. The voters rejected the initiative.

gewusst: A considerable share of the people in Switzerland receive a premium reduction.
The health insurance premium in Switzerland is a per-head premium: it is paid per person, not according to income.

teile.einleitung: Moulds are tiny fungi that are found almost everywhere. You see them as fluff on old bread or as patches on damp walls. Some are harmful, others very useful.
wichtigste: Mould belongs to the fungi.
It spreads through tiny spores in the air.
Mould grows especially well in damp and warmth.
Mouldy bread is thrown away completely.
The medicine penicillin comes from a mould.
Camembert deliberately has a white mould on the outside.

abschnitte.text: Mould belongs to the **fungi**. It consists of fine threads that you usually see only when they grow densely. Then a green, white, grey or black **fluff** appears. Mould feeds on things such as bread, fruit or wallpaper.

Moulds multiply through tiny **spores**. These are so light that they float through the air. They are almost everywhere. If they find a damp, warm place with food, they start to grow. That is why you should not sniff mouldy food: otherwise you breathe in spores.

On old **bread**, mould grows especially often. The fungal threads can run through the whole loaf, even where you see nothing. Some moulds produce toxins. That is why mouldy bread is thrown away **completely**, and you do not just cut off the patch.

In damp rooms such as the bathroom or bedroom, mould can grow on the walls. It can cause coughing or allergies. The best remedy is **regular airing**: several times a day, briefly open the windows wide. This lets the damp air escape.

In 1928, **Alexander Fleming** discovered that a mould kills bacteria. This led to the medicine **penicillin**, one of the first antibiotics. In the kitchen too, mould is wanted: **Camembert** has a white layer of mould on the outside, Roquefort blue veins inside.

gewusst: Fleming discovered penicillin because one of his bacteria dishes happened to go mouldy.
Single mould spores are so small that you can only see them under the microscope.

teile.einleitung: In the sleep laboratory, specialists examine how someone sleeps. The person spends a night there while many body values are measured at the same time. In this way sleep disorders can be recognised.
wichtigste: The examination in the sleep laboratory is called polysomnography.
The EEG records the brain’s electrical activity.
The EOG measures eye movements, the EMG muscle activity.
A pulse oximeter on the finger measures oxygen saturation.
Often examined are sleep apnoea and narcolepsy.

abschnitte.text: A sleep laboratory often looks like a quiet hotel room. In the evening, small **electrodes** and sensors are stuck onto the person. Then they sleep as normally as possible. Measuring many values at once is called **polysomnography**. In Switzerland there are sleep laboratories at various hospitals.

The **EEG** records the brain’s electrical activity, from which the sleep stages are recognised. The **electrooculogram (EOG)** measures the **eye movements**, important for REM sleep. The **electromyogram (EMG)** measures **muscle activity**. In addition there are breathing, heartbeat and a **pulse oximeter** on the finger, which measures the **oxygen saturation** in the blood. Often a camera runs too.

A common question in the sleep laboratory is **sleep apnoea**: here breathing stops again and again at night. It is often treated with a **breathing mask with slight positive pressure**. The mask keeps the airways open.

In **narcolepsy**, those affected suddenly and unintentionally fall asleep during the day. This rare disease is also examined in the sleep laboratory. For this, how quickly someone falls asleep on several occasions is often measured by day as well.

gewusst: The term “polysomnography” means roughly “recording many things in sleep”.
Some measurements can today also be made at home with small devices.

teile.einleitung: Red blood cells live for only a few months and have to be replaced constantly. Very young red blood cells are called **reticulocytes**. Their number in the blood shows how busy the bone marrow is.
wichtigste: A reticulocyte is a young red blood cell without a nucleus.
It still contains ribosomal RNA, which the mature erythrocyte lacks.
Classically, reticulocytes are made visible with brilliant cresyl blue.
In a healthy person, about 0.5 to 2 per cent of the red blood cells are reticulocytes.
After about 1 to 2 days in the blood, a reticulocyte becomes a mature erythrocyte.
In aplastic anaemia the reticulocyte count is greatly reduced.

abschnitte.text: In technical language, red blood cells are called **erythrocytes**. They arise in the **bone marrow** from precursors. One of these precursors is the **normoblast**. It expels its cell nucleus and thereby becomes a **reticulocyte**. This then gets into the blood.

The reticulocyte no longer has a nucleus but still contains **ribosomal RNA**. With the dye **brilliant cresyl blue**, this remaining substance becomes visible as a fine network. That is where the name comes from: “reticulum” is Latin and means little net. The reticulocyte circulates in the blood for about **1 to 2 days**. Then it loses the RNA and is a mature erythrocyte.

In a healthy person, about **0.5 to 2 per cent** of the red blood cells are reticulocytes. Doctors measure this value in a blood test. It shows how many new red blood cells are just being made. In this way you can tell whether the bone marrow is working well. Today measuring machines usually count the cells automatically.

After **blood loss**, the reticulocyte count rises markedly. This shows that the bone marrow is increasing blood production to make up for the loss. If the count is greatly reduced, on the other hand, the bone marrow is making too little blood. One example is **aplastic anaemia**, a rare disease in which the bone marrow hardly makes any blood cells any more. Anaemia is a shortage of red blood cells.

gewusst: Every second, the body of an adult makes about two million new red blood cells.
A mature red blood cell lives for about 120 days.

teile.einleitung: The trunk muscles include the muscles of the abdomen and back. They hold us upright and protect the spine. They work with almost every movement, whether sitting, walking or throwing.
wichtigste: The trunk muscles consist mainly of **abdominal and back muscles**.
Their main job: they **stabilise the spine**.
The **rectus abdominis** forms the visible “six-pack”.
The **transversus abdominis** lies deepest and acts like a belt.
The **erector spinae** straightens the back along the spine.
The **forearm plank** trains the trunk without any movement.

abschnitte.text: The **trunk** is the part of the body between the shoulders and the pelvis, without arms and legs. Its muscles lie at the front, at the sides and at the back. Together, the **abdominal and back muscles** form a kind of sheath around the spine. Their most important job is to **stabilise the spine**. They also make it possible for us to bend, stretch and turn.

The **rectus abdominis** runs at the front **between the rib cage and the pelvis**. It is divided into sections by strips of tendon. With very little belly fat, you can see these sections as a “six-pack”. At the sides lie the **oblique abdominal muscles**, which help with turning. Deepest lies the **transversus abdominis**. It surrounds the abdomen like a belt and holds it firm.

At the back, the **erector spinae** runs along the whole spine. It consists of many individual strands of muscle. It straightens the back and keeps us upright when we stand or sit. Abdominal and back muscles work together as opposing muscles. Only if both are strong does the trunk stay in balance.

A well-known exercise is the **forearm plank**. You support yourself on your forearms and toes and hold the body straight without moving. In this way many trunk muscles work at the same time. In a **sit-up** from lying down, the **rectus abdominis** and the **hip flexors** work together. It is important to train the abdomen and back equally well.

Anyone who sits a lot and moves little often has weak trunk muscles. This can lead to **poor posture** and **back pain**. Regular movement in everyday life, sport and small exercises help against this. That is why trunk strength is often trained in school PE too.

gewusst: When coughing and sneezing, the abdominal muscles tense strongly.
The trunk muscles already work before you raise an arm, so that the body stays stable.

teile.einleitung: A plaster protects small wounds from dirt and germs. Whoever knows how to stick it on properly can help well with small injuries.
wichtigste: A plaster protects a small wound from dirt and germs.
Before helping, you wash your hands.
A graze is first rinsed with clean water.
A disinfectant kills germs.
You do not touch the soft pad in the middle with your fingers.
With heavy bleeding a plaster is not enough, then adults are needed.

abschnitte.text: A plaster consists of an **adhesive strip** and a soft **pad** in the middle. The pad lies directly on the wound. The plaster **covers the wound**, so that less dirt and fewer germs get in. In this way the skin can heal in peace. Plasters come in many sizes and shapes, also with colourful patterns.

If you fall on your knee, the top layer of skin is often rubbed off. This is called a **graze**. It usually bleeds only a little, but can sting. First you wash the dirt out of the wound with **clean water**. After that you can treat the wound with a **disinfectant**, which kills germs. Then the plaster goes on.

Before you help someone, you **wash your hands**. Clean hands bring fewer germs to the wound. When sticking it on, you hold the plaster by the adhesive strip. You do not touch the **pad in the middle** with your fingers, so that it stays clean. If the plaster gets **wet or dirty**, it is changed for a new one.

Plasters belong in the **home first-aid kit**. There everything for **first aid** is in one place: plasters, bandages, disinfectant and scissors. So you find it quickly when something happens. It is worth checking the kit now and then and replacing what is missing.

A plaster is only for **small wounds**. If a wound bleeds **heavily**, it needs a firm **bandage** and the immediate help of adults. Deep wounds, bites or wounds with foreign bodies also belong with the doctor. In an emergency in Switzerland you dial the number **144** for the ambulance service.

gewusst: Small grazes usually heal within a few days to about two weeks.
Under the scab of a wound the skin makes new cells, so you should not scratch the scab off.

teile.einleitung: A polytrauma is a serious multiple injury, for example after a road accident or a fall from a great height. Several regions of the body are injured, and together this is life-threatening.
wichtigste: In a polytrauma several regions of the body are injured at the same time.
One injury or their combination is life-threatening.
From 16 points on the Injury Severity Score people usually speak of a polytrauma.
The lethal triad consists of hypothermia, acidosis and a clotting disorder.
The ABCDE scheme sets out what is treated first.
In damage control surgery only bleeding is controlled first.

abschnitte.text: In a **polytrauma** several **regions of the body** or organ systems are injured at the same time. What matters is that one of the injuries or their **combination** threatens life. To measure the severity there is the **Injury Severity Score (ISS)**. It sums up the injuries in the three most strongly affected regions of the body. The maximum value is **75 points**, and from **16 points** people usually speak of a polytrauma.

Rescue teams proceed by the **ABCDE scheme**. **A** stands for airway, **B** for breathing, **C** for circulation, **D** for the neurological state (disability) and **E** for examination of the whole, undressed body (exposure). What becomes life-threatening fastest is treated first. In Switzerland in serious accidents **Rega** often also comes out with the helicopter.

The term **“golden hour”** means the first hour after the accident. In this time quick treatment can achieve especially much. Seriously injured people should therefore get as fast as possible to a suitable hospital with a **trauma centre**. The exact length is more of a guiding idea than a fixed limit. What matters is help as fast as possible, in Switzerland through the emergency number **144**.

Great blood loss is especially dangerous. Doctors fear the **lethal triad**: **hypothermia**, **acidosis** of the blood and a **clotting disorder**. These three reinforce one another. If a **broken pelvis** is suspected, the rescue service applies a **pelvic binder**. It presses the bones together and so reduces the internal bleeding.

A long operation would overtax a badly weakened body. That is why there is **damage control surgery**. First, in a short operation, only bleeding and contamination are controlled. After that the patient is stabilised in the **intensive care unit** and operated on fully later. In a **tension pneumothorax** air collects under pressure in the rib cage and presses on the lung and heart. A **needle** lets the air escape as an emergency measure.

gewusst: In the resuscitation room of a hospital, in a polytrauma a whole team of different experts works at the same time.
Rega has helicopter bases all over Switzerland, so that it can be at any accident site quickly.

teile.einleitung: The collarbone is a long bone at the top of the chest. It connects the arm to the trunk and gives the shoulder support. You can feel it easily with your fingers.
wichtigste: Every person has two collarbones.
The collarbone lies between the breastbone and the shoulder.
It is slightly S-shaped.
It connects the arm to the trunk.
In technical language it is called the clavicle.
In children it breaks especially often.

abschnitte.text: Humans have **two collarbones**, one on each side. They lie **between the breastbone and the shoulder**. Seen from above, the bone is **slightly S-shaped**. You can easily feel it **under the skin at the top of the chest**, because it is hardly covered by muscles.

The collarbone **connects the arm to the trunk**. On the inside it is joined to the breastbone, on the outside to the shoulder blade. It holds the shoulder away from the rib cage, so you can move your arm freely. It is the only bony connection between arm and trunk.

In technical language the collarbone is called the **clavicle**. This comes from the Latin “clavicula”, a “little key”. Its shape reminded people of an old key. The German name, Schlüsselbein, or “key bone”, refers to this too.

In a fall onto the shoulder or the outstretched arm, the collarbone breaks easily. In **children** it is one of the bones that break **especially often**. Usually the break heals well. Often it is enough to rest the arm for a time.

gewusst: The collarbone is the bone that breaks most often in children.
There are animals, such as horses, that have no collarbone at all.

teile.einleitung: Pyjamas are the clothes that you put on to sleep in. They are comfortable and keep us pleasantly warm at night. In Germany people often say Schlafanzug (sleep suit).
wichtigste: Pyjamas are clothes for sleeping in.
They usually consist of a top and trousers.
Pyjamas originate in India.
Cotton is popular because it is soft and absorbs sweat.
In Germany people often say Schlafanzug.
A long shirt for sleeping in without trousers is called a nightshirt.

abschnitte.text: **Pyjamas** usually consist of two parts: a **top** and **trousers**. They come with long sleeves and legs for the winter or short for warm summer nights. You put them on because they are **comfortable and clean**. The clothes from the day stay outside, and you sleep more pleasantly.

Pyjamas originate in **India**. The word comes from Persian and means roughly “leg garment”. At first it meant wide, light trousers. British travellers brought these clothes to Europe in the 19th century. There they gradually became the sleepwear that we know today.

**Cotton** is very popular for pyjamas. It is **soft**, pleasant on the skin and **absorbs sweat**. In winter there are also pyjamas made of thicker, fluffy fabric. **Warm socks** help against **cold feet**. What matters is that you can move freely in them and neither freeze nor sweat.

In Switzerland people mostly say **Pyjama**, in Germany often **Schlafanzug**. If you prefer to wear a long shirt without trousers, you sleep in a **nightshirt**. In the past many people wore such nightshirts, often with a nightcap. Today there are pyjamas in all colours and with patterns, from stars to animals.

gewusst: The word pyjamas is spelt differently in different countries, in American English for example “pajamas”.
Some children and adults have pyjama parties, at which everyone stays the night together in their pyjamas.

teile.einleitung: A shadow arises when something blocks the light. Shadows show how high the sun stands, and they help us to protect ourselves from strong sun.
wichtigste: A shadow arises behind an object that blocks light.
At midday the shadow is shortest.
In the morning and evening, shadows are especially long.
Shadow rule: if your shadow is shorter than you, the sun is strong.
In the shade it is cooler, because the sun is not warming directly.
Shade protects only partly from UV rays.

abschnitte.text: Light travels in straight lines. If something stands in the way, no direct light arrives behind it. This darker area is the **shadow**. On a heavily cloudy day the light is scattered and comes from everywhere. Then you hardly see a clear shadow.

At **midday** the sun stands highest, so the shadow is shortest. In the **morning** and **evening** it stands low, and the shadows become very long. In the past, people read the time from the shadow of a rod on **sundials**.

With your own shadow you can check how strong the sun is. If the shadow is **shorter than you**, the sun stands high and burns strongly. Then sun cream, a hat and a place in the shade are important. In Switzerland the sun is strongest around midday in summer.

In the shade it is cooler, because the sun is not warming directly there. Trees give especially pleasant shade, since their leaves also evaporate water. On the terrace or at the beach, a large **parasol** helps.
Shade protects **only partly** from **UV rays**. Part of the rays is reflected by water, sand, snow or light walls and so still reaches us. That is why you can get sunburnt even in the shade.

gewusst: The moon casts a shadow too: when it falls on the Earth, there is a solar eclipse.
Snow reflects a large part of the UV rays.

teile.einleitung: With a cold, the nose runs, it is blocked and you have to sneeze often. An ordinary cold is annoying but mostly harmless. After about a week it is usually over.
wichtigste: An ordinary cold is mostly triggered by viruses.
It usually lasts about a week.
An antibiotic does not help against a cold.
Frequent hand washing protects others from infection.
Used tissues belong in the bin.
Hay fever is an allergy to pollen.
Warm tea and rest do you good.

abschnitte.text: In a cold, the **lining of the nose** is inflamed. This is the moist skin inside the nose. It swells, which is why the nose is blocked. At the same time it makes a lot of **mucus**, and the nose runs. The technical term for a cold is **rhinitis**. Often sneezing, a sore throat or a slight cough are added.

An ordinary cold is almost always triggered by **viruses**, often so-called rhinoviruses. They spread through tiny droplets when sneezing and coughing and through the hands. An **antibiotic** does not help against them, because antibiotics work only against bacteria. The body deals with the viruses itself. After about a week the cold is usually over.

Anyone with a cold can infect others. That is why it helps to **wash your hands often**, best with soap. You sneeze and cough into the crook of your elbow instead of your hand. A used **tissue** goes straight into the bin, and you take a new one next time. This way fewer viruses are left on door handles and tables.

There is no miracle cure for the cold itself, but you can make life easier for yourself. **Warm tea** and drinking enough keep the mucous membranes moist. **Rest** and sleep help the body. Salt water for rinsing or nose drops from the chemist can clear the nose. With a high fever, or if it does not get better for a long time, you ask a doctor.

**Hay fever** looks similar to an ordinary cold but has a different cause. It is an **allergy** to flower dust, also called **pollen**. The immune system wrongly takes the harmless pollen for dangerous. Typical are itchy, watering eyes and frequent sneezing. Hay fever is not contagious and occurs mainly when certain plants are in flower.

gewusst: When you sneeze, tiny droplets can fly several metres.
There are over a hundred different rhinoviruses, which is why you can catch a cold again and again.

teile.einleitung: A reflex is an automatic, unconscious reaction of the body to a stimulus. One example is pulling your hand away in a flash from something hot, which is controlled through the spinal cord. Reflexes protect us before we can even think.
wichtigste: A reflex is an automatic, unconscious reaction to a stimulus.
Many reflexes run through the spinal cord and not through the brain.
That is why they are especially fast.
The path of a reflex is called a reflex arc.
The knee-jerk reflex is often tested by the doctor with a small hammer.
Babies have special reflexes that disappear later.
Reflexes protect the body from injuries.

abschnitte.text: A **reflex** is a reaction that always happens in the same way and without thinking. If you touch a hot hob, you pull your hand away before you properly feel the pain. If something flies towards your eye, the eyelid closes by itself. Such reactions can hardly be suppressed by will.

The path of a reflex is called the **reflex arc**. A sensor in the skin reports the stimulus along a nerve to the **spinal cord**. There the signal is switched directly to a nerve that leads to the muscle. The brain only finds out afterwards, which is why the reflex is so fast.

In the **knee-jerk reflex**, the doctor taps with a small hammer just below the kneecap. The lower leg then shoots forwards. In this way she can check whether nerves and spinal cord work properly. The pupil reflex is also often tested with a small lamp.

Newborn babies have special **infant reflexes**. If you put a finger in their hand, they grasp it firmly, which is the grasp reflex. If you touch their cheek, they turn their head and search for the breast. These reflexes disappear again in the first months of life.

Besides inborn reflexes there are also learned ones, which are called **conditioned reflexes**. The Russian researcher Ivan Pavlov showed around 1900 that dogs produce saliva when they merely hear a tone that was previously always followed by food. In humans too, your mouth sometimes waters when you think of lemons. Such links are formed through experience.

begriffe.erklaerung: An automatic reaction without thinking.
The path from the sensor through the spinal cord to the muscle.
Something that a sense organ perceives, for example heat or light.
A reflex that has come about through learning.

gewusst: Coughing, sneezing, swallowing and yawning are also reflexes.
A blink reflex lasts only about a tenth of a second.
Ivan Pavlov received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1904, but for his research on digestion.

teile.einleitung: The Nursing Initiative (in German Pflegeinitiative) was a federal popular initiative for better conditions in nursing. The people and the cantons accepted it on 28 November 2021.
wichtigste: The official title is “Für eine starke Pflege” (“For strong nursing”).
The professional association SBK launched the initiative in 2017.
On 28 November 2021 it was accepted with about 61 per cent yes.
It aims to fight the shortage of nursing professionals.
The federal government and the cantons are to provide enough qualified nursing professionals.
The first stage of implementation is a training drive.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland citizens can demand a change to the **Federal Constitution** with a **popular initiative**. For this 100'000 valid signatures are needed. The federal popular initiative **“Für eine starke Pflege”** (“For strong nursing”) is called the **Nursing Initiative** for short. It was launched in **2017** by the **Swiss Association of Nursing Professionals (SBK)**.

On **28 November 2021** the people voted. Just over **61 per cent** of those voting and a clear majority of the cantons said yes. A popular initiative needs the **popular majority** and the **majority of the cantons**. Because most popular initiatives fail at the ballot box, this was a rare success. Parliament and the Federal Council had put forward an indirect counter-proposal that went less far.

Many nurses leave the job after only a few years. At the same time the need rises, because the population is getting **older**. The initiative aims to fight this **shortage of nursing professionals**. The new constitutional article obliges the **federal government and the cantons** to promote sufficient nursing care of high quality that is accessible to everyone. This includes enough qualified nursing professionals.

The implementation takes place in **stages**. At the centre of the first stage is a **training drive**. For several years the federal government and the cantons support training in nursing, for example with contributions to students and to firms that train. In addition, nursing professionals may bill certain services, for example the assessment of the need for care, directly through basic insurance **without a doctor’s order**.

In a further stage it is about **working conditions**, for example working hours and duty rosters. There are different opinions on this. The nursing associations want quick and binding improvements. Others point to the costs for hospitals, homes and cantons. Parliament decides on the exact laws.

gewusst: The Nursing Initiative was one of the few popular initiatives that were accepted by the people and the cantons.
The initiative was voted on during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the work of nursing was especially visible.

teile.einleitung: Core stability means that the muscles of the abdomen, back and pelvis hold the upper body firm and secure. A stable trunk protects the spine and helps in almost every sport. In training people often talk about the “core”.
wichtigste: The **transversus abdominis** acts like a natural corset around the trunk.
The deep back muscle **multifidus** stabilises the individual vertebrae.
The **diaphragm** also contributes to core stability.
A stable trunk **transfers force** between the legs and arms.
Typical exercises are the **plank** and the **side plank**.
Weak abdominal muscles and a pelvis tilted forwards encourage a **hollow back**.

abschnitte.text: In training, the trunk muscles are often called by the English word **core**. What is meant are the muscles around the abdomen, back and pelvis. They form the middle of the body. When they work well together, the trunk stays stable even in fast movements. This is called **core stability**.

Especially important are muscles that lie deep in the body. The **transversus abdominis** surrounds the abdomen like a **corset** and tightens it. On the back lies the **multifidus**. It consists of many small strands of muscle and holds the individual **vertebrae** stable against each other. At the top, the **diaphragm** bounds the abdominal cavity. This breathing muscle helps to build up a supporting pressure in the abdomen.

In many movements, force has to flow from the legs into the arms, for example in throwing, hitting or jumping. A stable trunk **transfers this force** like a firm bridge. If the trunk is wobbly, part of the force is lost. That is why footballers, skiers and climbers train their core stability specifically. A stable trunk can also help to prevent injuries.

In the **plank**, you hold the body straight like a board on your **forearms and toes**. It is a **static exercise**, so you do not move. In the **side plank**, you lie on your side and support yourself on one forearm. This exercise trains especially the **side trunk muscles**. A clean posture and calm continued breathing are important.

Weak abdominal muscles and a pelvis tilted forwards encourage a **hollow back**. Here the lower back is strongly curved inwards. This can strain the back. A well-trained trunk helps you to sit and stand upright. Just a few minutes of exercises a day and plenty of movement are good for the back.

gewusst: In the plank, the abdomen, back, shoulders and legs all work at the same time.
The transversus abdominis often tenses even before you move an arm or a leg.

teile.einleitung: The ribs are long, curved bones that together form the rib cage. An adult human normally has 24 ribs, that is, 12 pairs. They protect the heart and lungs like a cage and help with breathing.
wichtigste: An adult human normally has 24 ribs, that is, 12 pairs.
Together with the breastbone and spine, the ribs form the rib cage.
They protect the heart, lungs and other organs.
At the back, all the ribs are attached to the thoracic spine.
At the front, most are joined to the breastbone by cartilage.
The two lowest pairs of ribs end freely.
Between the ribs lie muscles that help with breathing.

abschnitte.text: Each **rib** is a flat, curved bone. At the back it is joined by a joint to a thoracic vertebra. At the front it passes into a piece of **costal cartilage**, which makes it elastic. Thanks to this elasticity, the rib cage can expand when breathing.

The upper seven pairs of ribs are directly joined to the **breastbone** and are called true ribs. The next three pairs are attached by cartilage to the rib above. The two lowest pairs end freely in the abdomen and are called floating ribs. Altogether there are 12 pairs, that is, 24 ribs.

Ribs, breastbone and thoracic spine form the **rib cage**. Like a cage, it protects the heart, the lungs and the large blood vessels. The lower ribs also protect part of the liver, spleen and kidneys. Even so, the rib cage is flexible and not rigid.

Between the ribs lie the **intercostal muscles**. When you breathe in, they pull the ribs upwards and outwards, and the rib cage becomes wider. Together with the diaphragm, this sucks air into the lungs. In quiet breathing out, the ribs sink back again.

In falls or accidents, a rib can break or be bruised. A **bruised rib** or a broken rib hurts especially when breathing, coughing and laughing. A simple broken rib usually heals by itself in a few weeks. It becomes dangerous if a broken piece injures the lung.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bony cage made of ribs, breastbone and spine.
A flat bone at the front in the middle of the chest.
Flexible tissue that joins the ribs to the breastbone.
Muscles between the ribs that help with breathing.

gewusst: Some people have an extra cervical rib, which usually causes no complaints.
Men and women have the same number of ribs.
In chest compressions you press on the breastbone, and it can happen that ribs break.

teile.einleitung: Feeling nervous before an exam is completely normal. A little excitement can even help you to concentrate. But when the fear becomes so great that it blocks you, it is called exam anxiety, and there is a lot you can do about it.
wichtigste: In a blackout, you suddenly cannot think of anything because of fear.
Typical signs are a pounding heart, damp hands or tummy ache.
Negative self-talk such as “I won’t manage it anyway” strengthens the fear.
A study plan with fixed stages helps weeks before the exam.
A practice exam at home makes the situation more familiar.
Belly breathing calms you before and during the exam.
If the fear is strong, your teacher or the school psychology service can help.

abschnitte.text: Fear is really a protection programme of the body. It switches to alarm, as if it had to flee from a danger. Then the **heart** beats faster, the hands become damp, and the tummy tingles or hurts. Sometimes your head is suddenly empty, which is called a **blackout**. The knowledge is not gone, it is just blocked for a moment.

Thoughts such as “I won’t manage it anyway” or “Everyone else is better” are called **negative self-talk**. They make the fear bigger. It helps to replace them deliberately with kinder sentences, for example: “I have studied and I am doing my best.” A single exam does not decide your whole life either.

You can do something about exam anxiety **weeks ahead**. A **study plan with fixed stages** spreads the material over many small portions. That way you do not have to learn everything at once the evening before. A **practice exam at home** is very helpful: you solve old questions with a clock running. This makes the situation more **familiar**, and the brain has less reason for alarm. Enough sleep and exercise help as well.

A simple help is **belly breathing**: you breathe in slowly through your nose so that your tummy rises, and out even more slowly through your mouth. This calms the heart. If a blackout happens in the exam, you can **breathe deeply** and first solve an **easier question**. Often the knowledge then comes back by itself.

If the fear becomes very strong, you should not be left alone with it. In Switzerland you can turn to your **teacher** or to the **school psychology service**. Parents and friends can help too. The 147 helpline of Pro Juventute can also be reached around the clock.

gewusst: A moderate amount of excitement can even improve your performance in an exam.
If you explain the material to someone, you quickly notice what you already know well, and that builds self-confidence.

teile.einleitung: The portal vein is a special blood vessel in the abdomen. It collects the blood from the stomach, gut and spleen and brings it first to the liver before it flows back to the heart.
wichtigste: The portal vein is called Vena portae in technical language.
It is about 8 centimetres long.
It collects blood from the stomach, gut, spleen and pancreas.
After eating, its blood contains many nutrients from the gut.
It supplies about three quarters of the blood that flows to the liver.
Cirrhosis of the liver often leads to high pressure in the portal vein.

abschnitte.text: In Latin the portal vein is called **Vena portae**. The word **“porta”** means gate or door. At the liver there is a place where vessels enter and leave, like a front gate. The portal vein is a short but wide vessel about **8 centimetres** long. It arises behind the **pancreas**, where several veins flow together.

Normal **veins** bring the blood back to the **heart**. The portal vein is different: it leads into an **organ**, namely the **liver**. It joins the fine network of capillaries in the gut to a second network of capillaries in the liver. Into the portal vein open veins from the **stomach**, **gut**, **spleen** and **pancreas**.

The gut takes **nutrients** such as sugar and amino acids into the blood. After a meal the blood of the portal vein is especially rich in them. Through the portal vein these substances get first to the liver. The liver **stores** nutrients, converts them and makes poisonous substances **harmless**. That is why it makes sense that the blood from the gut flows first through the liver.

The liver gets blood from two sources. The **hepatic artery** brings oxygen-rich blood from the heart. The **portal vein** supplies the greater part, about **three quarters** of the blood. After the blood has flowed through the liver, it reaches the heart by the hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava.

abschnitte.titel: High pressure in the portal vein
abschnitte.text: In **cirrhosis of the liver** the liver tissue becomes scarred and hard. The blood can then no longer flow well through the liver. It backs up in front of the liver in the portal vein, and the pressure rises. This is called **portal hypertension**. The blood then looks for detours, for example through veins of the gullet, which can widen greatly in the process.

gewusst: A vessel that joins two networks of capillaries one after the other is called a portal system, and there is a similar one at the pituitary gland.
The liver is the largest internal organ of the human being.

teile.einleitung: Sleep hygiene means: habits and conditions that promote good sleep. These include fixed sleep times, a quiet, cool bedroom and sensible choices about food and sport.
wichtigste: Regular times for going to bed and getting up are especially important, even at the weekend.
The bedroom should be rather cool, about 16 to 19 °C.
No heavy meals shortly before sleeping.
Alcohol helps with falling asleep but disturbs later sleep.
Regular exercise helps, intense sport right before sleeping rather does not.
If you do not fall asleep after about 20 minutes, get up briefly.

abschnitte.text: One of the most important rules is a **regular rhythm**. You go to bed at about the same time every day and get up at the same time, **even at the weekend**. This sets the inner clock well, and falling asleep becomes easier.

The bedroom should be quiet, dark and **rather cool**. Usually about **16 to 19 °C** is recommended. Bright screens shortly before sleeping can delay falling asleep. Many people therefore put their phone away beforehand.

Shortly before going to bed you should eat **no heavy meals**. Coffee, cola and energy drinks contain caffeine, which keeps you awake. **Alcohol** does make it easier to fall asleep, but **disturbs later sleep**. **Regular exercise** promotes good sleep, while **intense sport right before sleeping** rather does not.

In **stimulus control**, you use the bed only for sleeping. You leave out watching television or working in bed. In this way the brain links the bed with sleep again. If you cannot fall asleep after about **20 minutes**, you get up and do something calm until you are tired.

For insomnia, specialists sometimes use **sleep restriction**. Here you adjust the time in bed to the time you actually sleep. This raises the **sleep pressure**, and you fall asleep faster and more deeply. Later you lengthen the time in bed again step by step.

gewusst: Even a short walk in daylight in the morning helps the inner clock.
An afternoon nap should stay short, otherwise you are less tired in the evening.

teile.einleitung: The back is the rear side of our upper body. Down its middle runs the spine, which holds us upright. The back also plays an important role in animals and in many sayings.
wichtigste: Down the middle of the back runs the **spine**, a chain of bones.
All **vertebrates** have a spine, for example the fish too.
You carry a school bag correctly **on both shoulders**.
**Lots of exercise** is good for a healthy back.
The **tortoise** carries a hard shell on its back.
“Backing someone” (German: “jemandem den Rücken stärken”) means **supporting** them.

abschnitte.text: Down the middle of the back runs the **spine**. It is a chain of many small bones, the **vertebrae**. Between the vertebrae lie soft **discs** that cushion shocks. This lets you bend and turn. The spinal cord is also well protected in the spine, an important strand of nerves. Many muscles in the back hold the spine upright.

For a healthy back, **lots of exercise** is important, for example playing, cycling or swimming. If you sit for a long time, you should get up now and then and stretch. It is best to carry your **school bag** **on both shoulders**. That way the weight is spread evenly. Heavy things are packed close to the back.

In the **backstroke** you lie on your back in the water and look upwards. The arms swing alternately back over the head, and the legs kick. It is one of the four swimming strokes in competitions. In gymnastics, climbing and rowing, too, the back muscles work hard.

All **vertebrates** have a spine like us: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and also the **fish**. The **tortoise** carries a hard **shell** on its back, into which it can withdraw. Koala mothers carry their larger young **on their back**. And the camel stores fat as a reserve in its hump on its back.

The back appears in many sayings. Someone who **“strengthens someone’s back”** supports them and helps them. Someone who talks about a person **“behind their back”** does so secretly, when the person cannot hear. That is not nice. And someone who **“turns their back”** on something turns away from it.

gewusst: A human spine consists of over 30 vertebrae.
In spite of its long neck, a giraffe has the same number of neck vertebrae as a human, namely seven.

teile.einleitung: The spinal cord is a long strand of nerve tissue that runs inside the spine. It passes signals back and forth between the brain and the body and controls reflexes. Together with the brain it forms the central nervous system.
wichtigste: The spinal cord passes signals between the brain and the body.
It also controls reflexes without asking the brain.
It runs protected in the vertebral canal of the spine.
In adults it is about 45 centimetres long.
31 pairs of spinal nerves leave the spinal cord.
The brain and spinal cord together form the central nervous system.
A severe injury to the spinal cord can lead to paraplegia.

abschnitte.text: The **spinal cord** lies in the **vertebral canal**, a tunnel formed by the vertebrae. It begins at the foramen magnum, where it passes into the brain. In adults it ends at about the level of the first or second lumbar vertebra. It is about as thick as a little finger and about 45 centimetres long.

The spinal cord is surrounded by three membranes, the **meninges**. Between them is a clear fluid that cushions shocks. On the outside, the bones of the spine protect it. In this way the delicate nerve tissue is well secured.

The spinal cord is like a **data motorway** between the brain and the body. Signals from the skin and organs run upwards to the brain. Orders from the brain to the muscles run downwards. 31 pairs of **spinal nerves** leave the spinal cord and reach all parts of the body.

Some reactions are dealt with by the spinal cord entirely on its own. If you touch something hot, it switches the signal straight to the arm muscles. These **reflexes** are very fast because the detour via the brain is left out. The knee-jerk reflex is also controlled in the spinal cord.

If the spinal cord is badly injured in an accident, the signals can no longer get through. This causes **paraplegia**: below the injury you can no longer move or feel anything. In Switzerland, many of those affected are treated at the Paraplegic Centre in Nottwil in the canton of Lucerne. Researchers are working on reconnecting injured nerves one day.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tunnel in the spine in which the spinal cord lies.
A nerve that leaves the spinal cord and supplies the body.
The brain and spinal cord together.
Paralysis after an injury to the spinal cord.

gewusst: The spinal cord is shorter than the spine because the bones grow faster than the nerve tissue as you grow.
Doctors sometimes take fluid from the lower back because no spinal cord can be injured there any more.
Swiss researchers at EPFL in Lausanne have enabled paralysed people to take their first steps again with electrical implants in the spinal cord.

teile.einleitung: Post-traumatic stress disorder, PTSD for short, is a mental illness. It can arise after a person has experienced something extremely distressing. The good news: PTSD can be treated.
wichtigste: PTSD arises after a traumatic event, for example a serious accident, war, violence or a natural disaster.
Not all people who experience a trauma get PTSD.
Typical are flashbacks: what was experienced returns unwanted, as if it were happening right now.
Many people affected avoid triggers, that is, stimuli that recall the trauma.
In hyperarousal the body stays constantly on alert.
Effective treatments are, for example, trauma-focused psychotherapy and EMDR.

abschnitte.text: A **trauma** is an experience that is so threatening that it completely overwhelms a person. Examples are a serious accident, war, violence or a natural disaster. Directly afterwards many people show an **acute stress reaction**: they tremble, are confused or as if numbed. This reaction is normal and usually fades again within hours to days. But if the complaints last a long time, PTSD can develop.

An important feature of PTSD is unwanted re-experiencing. In a **flashback** pictures, sounds or feelings of the trauma suddenly appear very vividly. Experts also speak of **intrusions**, that is, memories that force themselves on you. They are often set off by a **trigger**: a sound, a smell or a place that recalls what was experienced. That is why many people affected try to avoid such stimuli.

Many people with PTSD are constantly tense. This is called **hyperarousal**, in German Übererregung (overexcitement). People affected sleep badly, are irritable, find it hard to concentrate and are easily startled. Their body behaves as if the danger were still there. This is very tiring and can burden everyday life at school, at work and in the family heavily.

As early as the First World War it was noticed that many soldiers suffered badly after the fighting. People then spoke of **“shell shock”**. Many of these complaints would today be assigned to PTSD. As a diagnosis in its own right PTSD was included in 1980 in an American handbook of mental disorders. With the **ICD-11**, the disease classification of the World Health Organization, **complex PTSD** was added. It follows long-lasting, repeated traumatisation, for example after long captivity.

PTSD is well treatable. What has proved especially good is a **trauma-focused psychotherapy**, in which you work through what was experienced step by step and in a safe setting. A well-known method is **EMDR**, which Francine Shapiro developed. In it you move your eyes back and forth in a targeted way while thinking of the memory. People who listen and give support are also important. In Switzerland doctors, psychotherapists and, for young people, the advice line 147 help.

gewusst: Only some of the people who experience a trauma develop PTSD. Many recover by themselves with time.
The abbreviation EMDR stands for “Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing”.

teile.einleitung: The stroke volume is the amount of blood that a ventricle ejects in one heartbeat. Together with the heart rate, it determines how much blood the heart pumps through the body per minute.
wichtigste: The stroke volume of an adult at rest is about 70 ml.
Stroke volume = end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume.
The ejection fraction is the share that is ejected.
Stronger filling leads to a greater stroke volume (Frank-Starling).
The afterload is the resistance against the ejection of blood.
Endurance athletes have a greater stroke volume.

abschnitte.text: The heart fills with blood in **diastole** and pumps it out again in **systole**. At the end of filling, the **end-diastolic volume** is in the ventricle, and after ejection the **end-systolic volume** remains. The difference is the **stroke volume**. In a healthy adult it is about **70 ml** at rest.

If the end-diastolic volume is 130 ml and the end-systolic volume 60 ml, you get 130 minus 60, so **70 ml**. The **ejection fraction** says what share of the filling is ejected. With a stroke volume of 60 ml and a filling of 120 ml, that is **50 per cent**. The stroke volume times the heart rate gives the **cardiac output** per minute.

The **preload** is the **stretch of the ventricle at the end of filling**. According to the **Frank-Starling mechanism**: if the ventricle is filled more, it contracts more strongly. **Stronger filling** therefore leads to a **greater stroke volume**. In this way the heart adapts by itself to the amount of blood flowing back.

The **afterload** is the **resistance** against which the heart has to eject the blood, for example a high blood pressure. The higher the afterload, the harder the heart has it. An effect that raises the force of contraction is called **positive inotropic**. The stress hormone adrenaline acts in this way.

Endurance training enlarges the **stroke volume**. Because the heart pumps more blood with each beat, it has to beat less often at rest. That is why **endurance athletes** often have a very **low resting heart rate**.

gewusst: At rest, a heart pumps about 5 litres of blood per minute.
In some top athletes the resting pulse is below 50 beats per minute.

teile.einleitung: A saddle joint is a joint whose joint surfaces are shaped like a riding saddle. The best-known example is the thumb saddle joint in the hand. It makes our thumb so mobile and skilful.
wichtigste: A saddle joint moves around **two main axes**.
The joint surfaces are **curved like a riding saddle**.
The **thumb saddle joint** lies between the trapezium bone and the first metacarpal bone.
It makes it possible to **oppose** the thumb to the other fingers.
A saddle joint can hardly turn about its own long axis.
Arthrosis in the thumb saddle joint is called **rhizarthrosis**.

abschnitte.text: A saddle joint gets its name from the shape of its joint surfaces. They are **curved like a riding saddle**: upwards in one direction, downwards in the other. Two such surfaces fit exactly on each other, like a rider on a saddle. As a result the joint can move around **two main axes**. You can move it forwards and back and to the side.

The most important saddle joint in humans is the **thumb saddle joint**. It lies between a wrist bone, the **trapezium**, and the **first metacarpal bone**. Thanks to it we can **oppose** the thumb to the other fingers. This movement is called **opposition**. It is the basis of many gripping movements.

A **ball-and-socket joint**, like the shoulder joint, is even more mobile. It can move around three axes, so it can also turn about its own **long axis**. That is exactly what a saddle joint can **hardly** do. A **hinge joint**, like the middle joint of a finger, moves around only one axis. The saddle joint therefore lies in between.

The thumb saddle joint makes the **precision grip** with thumb and index finger possible. With it we hold a pen, button up a shirt or pick up a small bead. The opposed thumb also helps with a strong grip. Besides humans, **many apes** can also oppose their thumb to the other fingers.

Because the thumb saddle joint is used constantly, its cartilage wears down over the years. Such wear is called **arthrosis**, and in the thumb saddle joint it is called **rhizarthrosis**. It causes pain when gripping, for example when opening jars. Older people are often affected. Splints, exercises and sometimes an operation can help.

gewusst: Without the opposable thumb, many everyday things such as writing or brushing your teeth would be very difficult.
The thumb has only two finger bones, the other fingers have three.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, school dental care looks after healthy children’s teeth. Children learn in kindergarten and at school how to brush correctly. In many municipalities there is also a yearly dental check-up.
wichtigste: School dental care takes place in kindergarten and at school.
A school dental care instructor practises tooth brushing with the class.
In many municipalities there is a check-up with the school dentist every year.
Disclosing tablets make dental plaque visible.
You practise correct brushing on a model set of teeth.
A good mid-morning snack is, for example, an apple and wholemeal bread, with water.
School dental care helps to prevent tooth decay in children.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, **school dental care** has long been part of everyday school life. It takes place in **kindergarten and at school**. It is regulated by the cantons and often organised by the **municipalities**. The aim is that all children have healthy teeth, wherever they live. Its most important purpose is to prevent **tooth decay**. This means holes in the teeth caused by bacteria in the plaque.

Several times a year, a **school dental care instructor** visits the class. She shows on a large **model set of teeth** and a large toothbrush how to brush correctly. Then the children practise themselves. With **disclosing tablets** the plaque becomes coloured. This way you can see exactly which spots you forgot when brushing. Often there is also a toothpaste or gel with **fluoride**, which strengthens the enamel.

In many Swiss municipalities, schoolchildren go **every year** for a **dental check-up** with the school dentist. There they check whether the teeth are healthy and whether decay is developing. This way problems can be recognised and treated early. Crooked teeth are also noticed at the check-up.

What you eat and drink is important for the teeth. School dental care recommends a mid-morning snack such as **an apple and wholemeal bread**. Sweets and sugary drinks feed the bacteria in the mouth, which make acid and attack the enamel. The best drink for break is **water**. Anyone who does not snack constantly in between gives the teeth time to recover.

gewusst: Since the 1960s, children in Switzerland have had clearly less tooth decay, also thanks to school dental care.
In Switzerland you can buy table salt with fluoride, which is also meant to protect the teeth.

teile.einleitung: Snow goggles protect the eyes from the glaring light in the snow. The Inuit in the Arctic were already making snow goggles. Today in the mountains we wear ski goggles and glacier glasses.
wichtigste: Snow reflects a great deal of sunlight and UV radiation.
The Inuit made snow goggles from wood or bone.
Instead of lenses they had narrow slits.
Even with clouds you need eye protection in the snow.
Glacier glasses have side shields against light.
Pain from too much sun often comes only hours later.

abschnitte.text: Fresh snow reflects a large part of the sunlight and the **UV radiation**. In the mountains, the radiation is also stronger than in the valley. The light is still strong **even with clouds**. That is why you always need protection for the eyes in the snow, even on grey days.

In the past the **Inuit** in the Arctic carved snow goggles from **wood or bone**. Instead of lenses they had **narrow slits**. Through these small openings only a little light falls into the eye, but you still see enough. In this way they protected themselves from the dazzling light on ice and snow.

Mountaineers wear **glacier glasses** on glaciers. They have very dark lenses and **side shields against light**. These stop light from falling into the eye from the side. In the Swiss Alps they are part of the equipment on high-mountain tours.

**Ski goggles** should **fit tightly to the face** so that no wind and snow get in. Sometimes they mist up inside. This happens because **warm, moist air** from the face cools on the cold lens. Many ski goggles therefore have two lenses and small ventilation slits.

Without protection, the bright light can damage the eyes, which is called **snow blindness**. The eyes then hurt, water and are sensitive to light. The tricky thing is that the symptoms usually come **only a few hours later**. Usually it heals again after a few days.

gewusst: Slit goggles work even without glass, because the small opening limits the light.
Fresh snow reflects much more light than a meadow.

teile.einleitung: **Rheumatoid arthritis** is a chronic inflammation of the joints. In it, the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own tissue. Without treatment, the joints can be destroyed over time.
wichtigste: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease of the joints.
At first it is usually the knuckles and middle finger joints that are affected on both sides.
A long morning stiffness of the joints is typical.
Anti-CCP antibodies in the blood are especially typical of the disease.
Methotrexate is regarded as the most important basic medicine.
Women are affected more often than men.

abschnitte.text: In rheumatoid arthritis, the **joint lining** becomes inflamed first, a thin layer inside the joint. It swells, and the joint becomes warm and hurts. Typically the **knuckles and middle finger joints** are affected first, and on **both hands**. Later other joints can also become diseased. Over time the inflammation can damage cartilage and bone.

A typical sign is long **morning stiffness**. After getting up, the joints are stiff and hard to move, often for longer than half an hour. Many of those affected also feel tired and weak. In some people, firm lumps form under the skin, for example at the elbow. These are called **rheumatoid nodules**.

Rheumatoid arthritis is an **autoimmune disease**. In it the immune system makes antibodies against the body itself. The **rheumatoid factor** is one such antibody, directed against the body’s own **IgG**, another defence protein. The **anti-CCP antibodies** are especially specific. If they are found in the blood, this points strongly to this disease.

Early treatment is important so that the joints are not destroyed. **Methotrexate** is regarded as the most important **basic medicine**. It dampens the overactive immune system. If that is not enough, **biologics** are used, for example infliximab or adalimumab. Many of them are aimed at the inflammatory messenger substance **tumour necrosis factor alpha**.

**Women** develop rheumatoid arthritis more often than men. The disease often begins in middle age but can occur at any age. Smoking raises the risk. Besides medicines, physiotherapy and occupational therapy also help to keep the joints mobile. In this way many of those affected can lead a largely normal life.
