gewusst: Rheumatoid arthritis is one of the most common inflammatory joint diseases, and about one per cent of people are affected.
Children too can develop a similar joint inflammation, which is called juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

teile.einleitung: With a squint, the two eyes do not look in the same direction. In children, early treatment is important so that both eyes learn to see well.
wichtigste: With a squint, the eyes look in different directions.
Each eye is moved by six outer muscles.
In the first months of life, a slight squint is normal in babies.
Treating early is important, otherwise one eye learns to see poorly.
Often glasses and an eye patch help.
In very strong squints, the eye muscles are sometimes operated on.

abschnitte.text: Normally both eyes look at exactly the same point. With a **squint**, one eye deviates, for example it looks inwards, outwards, upwards or downwards. Each eye is moved from outside by **six muscles**. If they do not work together exactly, a squint can arise.
In the **first months of life**, babies often squint a little. Their eyes are only just learning to work together. If the squint stays longer, an eye doctor should examine the child.

The brain gets a different picture from a squinting eye than from the straight one. So that nothing appears double, it pays less attention to the picture of the squinting eye. This eye then learns to **see poorly**, which is called **amblyopia**. The younger the child, the better this can still be changed.

Often **glasses** help to line up the eyes correctly. In addition, the **better eye** is often covered with an **eye patch**. That way the weaker eye has to work and is trained. In very strong squints, an **operation on the eye muscles** can help.
If someone suddenly starts to squint, they often see **everything double**. The brain has not yet learned to block out one picture. A sudden squint should be checked by a doctor quickly.

gewusst: Many children wear their eye patch only a few hours a day.
Squinting eyes can still be healthy, it is mainly about how they work together.

teile.einleitung: The pulse is the heartbeat that you can feel in blood vessels, for example at the wrist. It shows how often the heart beats per minute. Doctors and paramedics check the pulse to find out how a person is doing.
wichtigste: The pulse shows how often the heart beats per minute.
You can feel it at the wrist or at the neck.
In adults, the resting pulse is usually between 60 and 100 beats per minute.
Children have a faster pulse than adults.
With sport, excitement or fever, the pulse rises.
Trained athletes often have an especially low resting pulse.

abschnitte.text: With every heartbeat, the heart pumps a surge of blood into the arteries. This makes the vessel walls stretch briefly, like a wave in a garden hose. This **pulse wave** can be felt with the fingers in some places. The number of beats per minute is called the **pulse rate**.

Lay your index and middle finger on the inside of your wrist, below the thumb. That is where the **radial artery** lies. Count the beats for 15 seconds and multiply the result by four. You can also feel the pulse well at the neck, next to the larynx.

In adults at rest, the heart usually beats 60 to 100 times a minute. Children have a faster pulse, and in newborn babies it is over 100 beats. Well-trained endurance athletes often have a **resting pulse** of under 60, because their heart pumps more blood with every beat. The regularity of the pulse is also important.

When running or cycling, the muscles need more oxygen, so the pulse rises. Excitement, fear, heat, fever or coffee also make the heart beat faster. In sleep, on the other hand, the pulse falls. A pulse that is too fast is called **tachycardia**, one that is too slow bradycardia.

In an emergency, paramedics and doctors quickly check breathing and circulation. Today many people also measure their pulse with a sports watch or a fitness band. They use light to measure how the amount of blood under the skin changes. A very irregular pulse can be a sign of a heart disease.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of heartbeats per minute.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
The pulse when you are sitting or lying quietly.
A heartbeat that is too fast.

gewusst: In a long human life the heart beats about 2 to 3 billion times.
A shrew has a pulse of several hundred beats per minute, a blue whale only a few.
Even in ancient China, doctors examined the pulse very closely to recognise illnesses.

teile.einleitung: Sour is one of the basic tastes that our tongue recognises. We taste it when a food contains acid, for example lemon or vinegar. The sour taste can also warn us about spoiled food.
wichtigste: Foods taste sour when they contain **acid**.
**Vinegar** is a sour liquid from the kitchen.
**Yoghurt** tastes slightly sour.
For **sauerkraut** you need **white cabbage**.
Spoiled **milk** tastes sour.
The sour taste can warn us of **unripe or spoiled food**.

abschnitte.text: Our tongue can recognise five **basic tastes**: sweet, **sour**, salty, bitter and umami. We taste sour when a food contains **acid**. The acid is recognised by sensory cells in the taste buds. A signal then goes to the brain. Many people like a little acid because it makes food taste fresh.

Especially sour are **lemons** and the green **lime**. They contain a lot of **citric acid**. Anyone who bites into a lemon **screws up their eyes and mouth**. That is a quite natural reaction. Redcurrants, rhubarb and unripe apples also taste sour. Lemon juice is often used in salad dressings, drinks and for baking.

Some foods turn sour through tiny living things: **lactic acid bacteria**. They turn sugar into **lactic acid**. This is how milk becomes **yoghurt**, which tastes slightly sour. For **sauerkraut** you slice **white cabbage** finely, add salt and leave it to stand for a few weeks. In Switzerland, sauerkraut belongs, for example, to the Bernese platter.

**Vinegar** is a sour liquid that stands in almost every kitchen. It contains **acetic acid**. It is used for salad dressings and for pickling vegetables such as gherkins. The acid makes food keep longer, because many bacteria multiply badly in it. Vinegar is also used for cleaning and descaling.

The sour taste can warn us **of unripe or spoiled food**. Unripe fruit often tastes very sour. **Milk** that was left open too long or not kept cool also turns **sour**. Then bacteria form acid in it. If milk smells and tastes sour, you should not drink it any more.

gewusst: There is acid in the stomach too: it helps to digest food.
Sauerkraut contains vitamin C and used to be taken along on long sea voyages.

teile.einleitung: Not every stimulus is noticed. A sound can be too quiet, a light too weak. The **stimulus threshold** is the limit from which our senses only just perceive a stimulus.
wichtigste: The stimulus threshold is the smallest strength of stimulus that is only just perceived.
A stimulus below this threshold is called **subliminal**.
With age, the hearing threshold for high notes rises.
In the dark, the stimulus threshold of the eye falls, so you see weaker light.
The difference threshold is the smallest difference between two stimuli that you still notice.
A nerve cell sends its signal according to the all-or-nothing principle.

abschnitte.text: Every sense has a **stimulus threshold**. It is the smallest strength of a stimulus that you only just notice, for example the quietest audible sound. If a stimulus is weaker, it is called **subliminal**. It is there but is not consciously perceived. The threshold is not the same in everyone and can also change.

Sometimes it is not a question of whether you notice something, but whether you notice a difference. The **difference threshold** is the smallest difference between two stimuli that you can still tell apart. According to **Weber’s law**, it depends on the basic strength: if with 100 grams you only just notice 2 grams more, then with 1000 grams you need about 20 grams. So the difference must always make up roughly the same proportion. The law is named after the German researcher Ernst Heinrich Weber.

If you stay in the dark for a longer time, the stimulus threshold of the eye **falls**. You then see even very weak light, which is called dark adaptation. With increasing age, on the other hand, the hearing threshold for high notes **rises**, so they are heard less well. Pain also has a threshold. With sunburn the skin is inflamed, the pain threshold has fallen, and even a light touch hurts.

Individual **nerve cells** also have a threshold. If a stimulus stays below it, nothing happens. If the threshold is exceeded, the cell sends out a signal, and always at full strength. This principle is called the **all-or-nothing principle**. The brain recognises a strong stimulus by the cell sending more signals per second, not by stronger signals.

gewusst: Young people often hear high whistling tones that adults can no longer perceive at all.
It takes about half an hour until the eyes have got used to the darkness completely.

teile.einleitung: In **restless legs syndrome**, people feel a strong urge to move their legs in the evening and at rest. The condition can disturb sleep badly but is well treatable.
wichtigste: Another name is **Willis-Ekbom disease**.
The complaints occur at rest and in the evening and improve with movement.
Iron deficiency can trigger or strengthen the disease.
Dopamine agonists are often used.
In kidney failure the disease occurs especially often.
The diagnosis is made mainly from the complaints in conversation.

abschnitte.text: **Restless legs syndrome**, RLS for short, is a disease of the nervous system. It is also called **Willis-Ekbom disease**, after two doctors who described it. Those affected feel an unpleasant tingling, pulling or tightness in the legs. With this comes a strong urge to move the legs. The complaints occur **at rest** and above all **in the evening** or at night and **improve with movement**.

Because the complaints begin when lying down, many of those affected find it hard to fall asleep. In a sleep laboratory, sleep is studied with **polysomnography**, a measurement of many body values during the night. In many people with RLS it shows **periodic limb movements**, that is, regular twitches of the legs during sleep. During the day those affected are then often tired. That is why good treatment is important.

In many people no cause is known, and the disease often runs in families. Sometimes, though, another illness is behind it, and then it is called **secondary** RLS. An important trigger is **iron deficiency**. RLS occurs especially often in **kidney failure**, that is, when the kidneys work badly. The doctor makes the diagnosis mainly **in conversation** from the typical complaints.

With iron deficiency, it helps to add iron. **Dopamine agonists** are often used, medicines that work like the messenger substance dopamine. With longer use, **augmentation** can occur. This is a worsening of the complaints caused by the medicines themselves, which then appear earlier in the day or more strongly. In this case the doctor adjusts the treatment.

gewusst: As early as the 17th century, the English doctor Thomas Willis described the typical complaints.
A short walk or stretching exercises in the evening can ease the complaints.

teile.einleitung: So that we can see something even in the twilight, the eye needs an especially light-sensitive substance. This is **rhodopsin**, also called **visual purple**. It sits in the rods of the retina.
wichtigste: Rhodopsin is the visual pigment of the rods.
It consists of the protein opsin and retinal.
The body makes retinal from vitamin A.
In light, 11-cis-retinal is rearranged into all-trans-retinal.
Rhodopsin absorbs light most strongly at about 500 nm.
It is a G-protein-coupled receptor and activates transducin.

abschnitte.text: The retina has two kinds of light-sensing cells: **cones** for colour vision and **rods** for seeing in little light. In the rods sits the visual pigment **rhodopsin**. In German it is also called **Sehpurpur**, visual purple, because it looks reddish violet. It is so sensitive that even very little light triggers a reaction. That is why at night we see with the rods, but hardly any colours.

Rhodopsin consists of two parts. The larger part is the protein **opsin**. In it sits a small molecule, **retinal**. The body makes retinal from **vitamin A**. If vitamin A is missing, night blindness can develop.

In the dark, the retinal is present as **11-cis-retinal**, a bent form. When a particle of light, a **photon**, strikes it, it is rearranged into **all-trans-retinal** and straightens out. This also changes the shape of the opsin. Rhodopsin absorbs light most strongly at about **500 nm**, that is, blue-green light. After that the retinal has to be rebuilt into the bent form.

Rhodopsin belongs to the **G-protein-coupled receptors**. These are receptors that pass on a signal through a so-called G-protein. Illuminated rhodopsin activates the G-protein **transducin**. This closes channels in the cell membrane, and the rod **hyperpolarises**. That means the electrical voltage at the membrane becomes more strongly negative, and this is how the signal to the nerve cells arises.

gewusst: Unusually, rods are not excited by light; instead they release less messenger substance in light.
A single rod can react to a single photon.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes things do not go smoothly at school: with reading, with arithmetic or with feelings. Then the school psychological service can help. It advises children, young people, parents and teachers.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the cantons are responsible for the school psychological services.
A consultation usually costs families nothing.
It looks into, for example, a reading and spelling disorder or dyscalculia.
The conversations are covered by confidentiality.
The specialists have mostly studied psychology.
In many cantons, young people may also get in touch themselves.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, schooling is a matter for the **cantons**. That is why the **school psychological services** are also organised by canton. Each canton decides itself how they are set up and where they have their advice centres. For families a consultation is usually **free of charge**. Often a teacher or the family gets in touch after they have talked to each other.

An important task is **assessment**. Children solve tasks and tests, and the specialists look closely. In this way you can recognise, for example, a **reading and spelling disorder**, also called dyslexia. A particular weakness in arithmetic is called **dyscalculia**. Once it is clear where the difficulty lies, suitable support can be planned, for example extra tuition.

The service also advises on worries, fears, quarrels or problems with behaviour. It helps families, for example, with the question of the **right time to start school**. It also supports when it is a matter of special schooling or a change of class. In many cantons **young people can get in touch themselves** if they want help.

For the conversations, **confidentiality** applies. That means: what you say is not simply passed on. The specialists have mostly completed a **degree in psychology** and often an additional training for children and young people. They work closely with schools, parents and other specialist bodies so that a child can learn well.

gewusst: The school psychological service is called something slightly different depending on the canton, for example school psychology advice centre.
Teachers can also ask the service for advice on how best to support a child.

teile.einleitung: A wheelchair is a chair with wheels. It helps people who cannot walk or can only walk with difficulty to move around independently. So that they can get everywhere, ramps, lifts and wide doors are needed.
wichtigste: A usual wheelchair has **2 large drive wheels** and small wheels at the front.
On the large wheel is the **handrim**, with which you propel the wheelchair.
An **electric wheelchair** runs on a motor and a battery.
A **ramp** helps to get over a step.
In houses with several floors, a **lift** helps.
The wheelchair symbol usually has a **blue** background.

abschnitte.text: A wheelchair has a seat, a backrest and footrests. At the back are **2 large drive wheels**, and at the front are small wheels that turn in all directions. This makes it easy to steer. Many wheelchairs can be folded up. Then they fit into the boot of a car.

abschnitte.titel: With arm power or a motor
abschnitte.text: On the outside of the large wheel, an extra ring is attached, the **handrim**. You push the wheelchair forward with your hands on it and also brake it. This takes a lot of strength in the arms. An **electric wheelchair**, on the other hand, runs on a **motor** and a **battery**. You usually steer it with a small lever, the joystick.

Even a single step can be a big obstacle for people in a wheelchair. A **ramp** is a sloping surface that you can drive up. In houses with several floors, a **lift** helps. Wide doors and low buttons are also important. Buildings without such obstacles are called **barrier-free**.

The well-known symbol shows a figure in a wheelchair, usually white on a **blue** background. You see it in car parks, at toilets and at entrances. It shows: here is space or access for people with disabilities. The especially wide parking spaces are reserved for them so that they can get in and out easily.

In Switzerland there has been the **Disability Equality Act** since 2004. It requires, for example, that railway stations, trains and buses gradually become barrier-free. In **Nottwil** in the canton of Lucerne stands the Swiss Paraplegic Centre. There people with a spinal cord injury are treated and learn everyday life in a wheelchair.

gewusst: There are sports wheelchairs with slanted wheels that are especially nimble, for example for basketball.
With practice, some people in wheelchairs can balance on the back wheels.

teile.einleitung: REM sleep is a special phase of sleep. In it the eyes move quickly back and forth, and we dream especially vividly. Several times a night, REM sleep and other sleep phases alternate.
wichtigste: REM stands for “rapid eye movement”.
In REM sleep we dream especially vividly and in pictures.
Most skeletal muscles are almost completely relaxed during it.
The brain is almost as active as when awake.
In adults, REM sleep makes up about 20 to 25 per cent of the night.
Newborn babies spend about half of their sleep in REM sleep.

abschnitte.text: The abbreviation **REM** stands for the English **“rapid eye movement”**. During this phase of sleep, the eyes move quickly back and forth under the closed lids. REM sleep was discovered and described in the **1950s** by the American researchers **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman**. They observed sleepers in the laboratory.

In REM sleep we **dream** especially **vividly and in pictures**. If you wake someone in this phase, they can often remember their dream well. At the same time most **skeletal muscles are almost completely relaxed**. That makes sense: it means we do not act out the movements from our dreams. Only the eye muscles and the breathing muscles go on working.

REM sleep is also called **“paradoxical sleep”**. Paradoxical means contradictory. Although you are sleeping deeply, the **brain is almost as active as when awake**. **Heartbeat and breathing** also become **more irregular** than in the calm phases of sleep. Researchers suspect that REM sleep is important for processing what we have experienced and for consolidating what we have learned.

A night consists of several **sleep cycles** of about an hour and a half. In each cycle, light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep follow one another. At the start of the night, the REM phases are short, and **towards morning** they last **longest**. In adults, REM sleep makes up about **20 to 25 per cent** of the night. **Newborn babies** even spend about **half** of their sleep in REM sleep.

gewusst: Many animals, for example dogs and cats, also have REM sleep. Sometimes their paws twitch.
If you wake from a dream in the morning, you have often just woken from a REM phase.

teile.einleitung: A placebo is a dummy medicine without a real active substance, for example a sugar pill. Remarkably it can still work, because the person expects an improvement. This effect through expectation is called the placebo effect.
wichtigste: A placebo is a remedy without a real active substance.
The placebo effect is an effect that arises through expectation.
Placebos work mainly for pain, nausea and tiredness.
The opposite is the nocebo effect, in which expectation harms.
In drug trials real remedies are compared with placebos.
In double-blind trials neither patients nor doctors know who gets what.
A placebo cannot cure a serious illness.

abschnitte.text: A **placebo** looks like a real medicine, but contains no active substance. Mostly it consists of sugar or starch. The word comes from Latin and means “I shall please”. A sham treatment, for example a pretended operation, can also serve as a placebo.

If a person expects that something will help, their body reacts to it. The brain can then release its own pain-relieving substances, the **endorphins**. Trust in the doctor and attention also play a part. This effect through expectation is called the **placebo effect**.

New medicines must prove that they work better than a placebo. For this one group gets the real remedy and another a placebo. In a **double-blind trial** neither the participants nor the doctors know who receives what. This prevents expectations from distorting the result.

Expectation can also harm. Whoever fears that a remedy has side effects sometimes feels them although they received only a placebo. This is called the **nocebo effect**, from the Latin word for “I shall harm”. That is why it matters how doctors speak about treatments.

Placebos help mainly with complaints that you feel yourself, for example pain, nausea or sleep problems. A broken bone, an infection or cancer they cannot cure. It is interesting that larger or coloured pills often work more strongly than small white ones. A plaster and comfort for a grazed knee also work partly like a placebo.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dummy medicine without an active substance.
The substance in a medicine that has the actual effect.
A test in which neither patients nor doctors know who gets the real remedy.
A negative effect that arises only through bad expectation.

gewusst: Placebos can even work when you know that they are placebos.
Expensive dummy medicines sometimes work better than cheap ones in experiments.
Sham treatments are sometimes also used in research on operations, to test real procedures.

teile.einleitung: The incisors are the teeth right at the front of the mouth. You see them first when someone laughs. With them we bite pieces off food.
wichtigste: The incisors stand at the front in the middle, top and bottom.
An adult has eight incisors: four at the top and four at the bottom.
They have a thin, sharp, straight edge at the front.
With them you bite off, for example, a piece of apple.
An incisor usually has only one root.
In children the lower middle incisors often fall out first.

abschnitte.text: In the mouth, the teeth stand in two arches, one at the top and one at the bottom. Right at the front in the middle sit the **incisors**. At the top there are four and at the bottom also four, so eight altogether. Next to them follow the pointed **canines** and further back the broad **molars**. Each kind of tooth has a different job when eating.

An incisor is flat at the front and runs to a thin, straight **cutting edge**. That is why it works a little like a small knife. When the upper and lower incisors bite on each other, they separate a piece off. Chewing and grinding are then done by the molars. The incisors also help with speaking, for example with sounds like “s” or “f”.

The visible part of a tooth is called the **crown**. It is covered with **enamel**, the hardest substance in the body. In the jawbone sits the **root**. An incisor usually has only a single root, molars often have two or three. Inside the tooth lies the tooth nerve with fine blood vessels.

Small children first have **milk teeth**, among them also eight incisors. At about six years old, the **changing of teeth** begins. Usually the two middle incisors at the bottom wobble first. Beneath them the permanent teeth are already growing and push the milk teeth out. The permanent teeth have to last a lifetime, so good brushing is worthwhile.

In **rodents** such as the beaver, the squirrel or the mouse, the front gnawing teeth keep growing all their life. When gnawing wood or nuts they wear down again. The tusks of the elephant are also lengthened incisors. Human teeth, by contrast, do not grow back. That is why you should not open bottles with them or bite on hard things, because a corner can break off.

gewusst: The gnawing teeth of the beaver are orange at the front because their enamel contains iron.
The tusks of an elephant are really giant incisors.
Enamel is the hardest substance in the whole human body.

teile.einleitung: Peristalsis is the name for the wave-like muscle movements in the digestive tract. They push the food from the gullet to the end of the gut, without our having to think about it.
wichtigste: Peristalsis is wave-shaped muscle movements in the digestive tract.
Circular and longitudinal muscles work together in it.
The gut wall consists of smooth muscle, which works involuntarily.
The enteric nervous system controls peristalsis.
Because muscles push the food, you can even swallow in a handstand.
A mouthful needs only a few seconds through the gullet.

abschnitte.text: In **peristalsis** the muscles of the digestive tract contract one after another. This creates a **wave** that pushes the contents on bit by bit. You can imagine it like toothpaste that you squeeze out of a tube. This movement exists in the gullet, stomach and gut.

In the wall of the gullet and gut there are two layers of muscle. The **circular muscles** constrict the tube. The **longitudinal muscles** shorten it. Together they produce a continuous wave. This is **smooth muscle**. It works by itself, and we cannot control it consciously.

The **gullet** is about **25 centimetres** long. After swallowing, the muscle wave carries a mouthful into the stomach in **a few seconds**. Because the muscles actively push the food, this works even against **gravity**. That is why you can swallow even in a handstand, although it is unfamiliar.

Peristalsis is controlled by the **enteric nervous system**. It lies in the gut wall and contains many millions of nerve cells. It is sometimes called the **“belly brain”**. When gas and liquid move in the gut, you sometimes hear it **rumble** and **gurgle**. This is especially loud when the stomach is almost empty.

abschnitte.titel: When it no longer goes on
abschnitte.text: Sometimes the movement runs in the wrong direction. In **vomiting** the abdominal muscles and diaphragm contract strongly, and the stomach contents are pressed upwards. Dangerous is a **bowel obstruction**. Here the gut is blocked or paralysed, and the contents no longer get on. This is an emergency that must be treated quickly in hospital.

gewusst: Astronauts too can eat quite normally in weightlessness, because peristalsis pushes the food on.
The word peristalsis comes from Greek and has to do with “wrapping around” and “contracting”.

teile.einleitung: Red bone marrow is a soft tissue inside some bones. It is the factory for our blood: this is where red and white blood cells and platelets are made. Without red bone marrow, the body could not survive.
wichtigste: Red bone marrow **makes blood cells**.
All blood cells come from **blood-forming stem cells**.
In newborn babies there is red bone marrow in almost all bones.
In adults it lies mainly in the **pelvis, vertebrae, ribs and breastbone**.
An adult makes about **2 million** red blood cells per second.
The hormone **erythropoietin (EPO)** from the kidney stimulates the making of red blood cells.

abschnitte.text: In **newborn babies** there is red bone marrow in almost all bones. With age, in many bones it is replaced by **yellow bone marrow**, which consists mainly of fat. In adults most of the red bone marrow lies in the flat and short bones: in the **pelvis**, in the **vertebrae**, the **ribs** and in the **breastbone**. There it fills the fine hollow spaces in the spongy bone tissue.

All blood cells are made in the red bone marrow. Their origin is the **blood-forming stem cells**. Through many divisions, these become **red blood cells**, which transport oxygen, **white blood cells**, which fight off disease-causing agents, and **platelets**, which stop bleeding when there is a wound. Blood cells do not live long and have to be replaced constantly. That is why the bone marrow works without a break.

Blood-forming bone marrow is red because it contains many **red blood cells** and fine **blood vessels**. An adult makes about **2 million** new red blood cells there every second. How many are needed is controlled, among other things, by the hormone **erythropoietin**, **EPO** for short. The kidney releases it when the blood has too little oxygen. Then the bone marrow makes more red blood cells.

Sometimes a doctor has to look at the bone marrow more closely. To do so she usually takes a small sample from the **iliac crest**, the upper edge of the pelvic bone. In severe blood diseases such as **leukaemia**, a donation of **blood stem cells** can save lives. The stem cells of a healthy person then replace the diseased bone marrow. In Switzerland you can register as a stem cell donor.

gewusst: Bone marrow is one of the tissues in the body that make the most new cells.
In a stem cell donation, the cells are today usually collected from the blood, not directly from the bone.

teile.einleitung: Proteins are vital building blocks of all living things. The body needs them to build muscles, cells and many important substances such as enzymes and hormones. They consist of long chains of small building blocks, the amino acids.
wichtigste: In German, proteins are also called Eiweisse.
The body needs proteins to build muscles, cells and many important substances.
Proteins consist of chains of amino acids.
For humans, 20 different amino acids are important.
Some amino acids must be taken in with food.
Enzymes, antibodies and many hormones are proteins.
Meat, fish, eggs, milk, pulses and nuts contain a lot of protein.

abschnitte.text: **Proteins** are large molecules made of many small building blocks, the **amino acids**. These line up one after another like beads on a string. Then the chain folds into a very particular shape. What job the protein does depends on this shape.

Muscles, skin, hair and nails consist to a large extent of proteins. **Enzymes** are proteins that speed up chemical reactions, for example in digestion. The red blood pigment haemoglobin transports oxygen, and antibodies fight off disease-causing agents. The hormone insulin is also a protein.

A lot of protein is found in meat, fish, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt. Plant foods such as lentils, beans, chickpeas, tofu and nuts are also good sources. In the gut, the proteins are broken down into amino acids. From these the body then builds its own proteins.

Adults need about 0.8 grams of protein per day for every kilogram of body weight. Children and teenagers who are growing need proportionally a little more. The body cannot make nine amino acids itself; they are called **essential amino acids**. A varied diet normally supplies enough of them.

The blueprint for every protein is stored in the **DNA**. In the cells, small factories called ribosomes read this plan. They join the amino acids together in the right order. In this way a human being can make tens of thousands of different proteins.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small building block from which proteins are put together.
A protein that speeds up chemical processes in the body.
An amino acid that you have to take in with food.
A tiny cell factory that builds proteins.

gewusst: When you fry an egg, the egg white turns white because the proteins change through the heat.
Spider silk is a protein and, in proportion to its weight, very strong.
The word protein comes from the Greek proteuo, meaning “I take first place”.

teile.einleitung: Polysomnography is an examination in the sleep laboratory. During a whole night many body signals are recorded at the same time, in order to recognise sleep disorders.
wichtigste: In polysomnography you measure brain waves, eye movements, muscle tension, breathing and more.
The recording is evaluated in epochs of 30 seconds.
An arousal is a brief waking reaction of at least 3 seconds.
Pulse oximetry measures the oxygen saturation of the blood.
Leg movements are measured at the anterior tibial muscle at the front of the shin.
In the first night many sleep worse, which is the first-night effect.

abschnitte.titel: A night in the sleep laboratory
abschnitte.text: Whoever sleeps badly or is very tired during the day is sometimes sent to the **sleep laboratory**. There you spend a night in a quiet room. Small **electrodes** and sensors are attached to the head and body. They record many signals all night. This examination is called **polysomnography**, which means roughly “multiple sleep recording”.

The **EEG** measures the brain waves. In addition there are measurements of the **eye movements** and the **muscle tension**. Sensors at the **nose and mouth** record the airflow. A sensor on the finger measures with light the **oxygen saturation** of the blood, which is called **pulse oximetry**. Electrodes over the **anterior tibial muscle at the front of the shin** record movements of the legs. Often a **video camera** also runs.

The recording is divided into **epochs** of **30 seconds** each. To each epoch the sleep stage that predominates in it is assigned. In this way a picture arises of the course of the night with light sleep, deep sleep and **REM sleep**. Short **arousals** are also counted. These are waking reactions of at least **3 seconds**, in which the brain waves become faster. People affected often do not notice them.

Often people look for **pauses in breathing** in sleep, **sleep apnoea**. In it the oxygen saturation falls again and again. With **video polysomnography** you can also recognise **REM sleep behaviour disorder**. In it the normal relaxation of the muscles in REM sleep is missing, and people affected hit or kick in their dreams. **Periodic leg movements** can also be counted.

abschnitte.titel: First night and measuring at home
abschnitte.text: Many people sleep worse in the **first night** in the sleep laboratory. The unfamiliar surroundings and the cables disturb. This is called the **first-night effect**. That is why measurements are sometimes made over two nights. Simpler is **polygraphy** at home. It records mainly breathing and oxygen, but as a rule measures **no brain waves**. That is why it cannot determine the sleep stages.

gewusst: During a night you go through several sleep cycles, each lasting about an hour and a half.
In REM sleep the eyes move quickly back and forth, hence the name, from the English “rapid eye movement”.
